Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face a significant challenge when dealing with an insufficient number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method can address this issue, but it faces limitations by assuming all unlabeled nodes are equally important. In contrast, our proposed informative pseudo-labeling framework holds a key insight that unlabeled nodes hold varying levels of significance, which is pivotal for producing high-quality pseudo-labels under a limited number of labels. To achieve this, our framework leverages the centrality measures from existing Graph Neural Networks to derive essentiality scores for unlabeled nodes. These scores serve as a crucial criterion for determining which nodes require pseudo-labeling and for selecting high-quality labeling nodes via optimization. Furthermore, our framework incorporates a customized loss function that adapts to the derived importance scores, which in turn facilitates improved pseudo-labeling and enhanced node classification performance. Our proposed informative pseudo-labeling framework has been extensively validated through comprehensive experiments on six real-world datasets, yielding superior performance when compared to existing state-of-the-art methods for semi-supervised Graph Neural Networks. The source code for our framework is freely accessible at https://github.com/leverle/InformativePseudoLabeling. Our research demonstrates that a tailored pseudo-labeling strategy can significantly improve pseudo-label quality and consequently enhance node classification performance when working with Graph Neural Networks under a limited number of labels. Through further analysis, it is evident that nodes holding high essentiality measures as derived from our pseudo-labeling process are significantly relevant to the underlying graph structure, which is substantiated by multiple GNN operators and prediction outcomes. Consequently, improving the quality of essentiality scores can serve as a potential research trajectory for further exploration. The Informative Pseudo-labeling framework may also be applicable and easily extendable to semi-supervised link prediction, as well as other applications of GNNs under label scarcity. To the best of our knowledge, our proposed informative pseudo-labeling framework uniquely addresses the problem of varying importance among unlabeled nodes in the context of semi-supervised GNNs. The incorporation of importance scores as part of our framework enables the creation of high-quality pseudo-labels, which in turn enhance node classification performance when compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Ultimately, our proposed informative pseudo-labeling framework has the potential to significantly enhance semi-supervised GNNs under a limited number of labels. In a Hilbert space, we devise a rapid, dynamic method for addressing a hierarchical minimization issue, where we seek the solution with the minimum norm in a convex optimization problem. This approach involves investigating the convergence properties of the trajectories generated by an inertial dynamic with Tikhonov regularization, and we demonstrate that, as time tends towards infinity, these trajectories strongly converge towards the minimum norm solution under a critical constraint. Drawing inspiration from the heavy ball method, we establish a key proportionality relationship between the viscous damping coefficient and the Tikhonov regularization parameter, and we show that, when these parameters are suitably tuned, they both converge towards zero at linear rates under a critical condition. This convergence result holds not just for hierarchical minimization problems, but also for a broader class of non-hierarchical problems, and we illustrate the efficacy of our dynamic method through various numerical examples. Additionally, we extend the applicability of our dynamic method to a diverse range of hierarchical minimization issues, including the computation of principal component analysis, the solution of split vast inequalities, and the sampling of a uniform ball, all constrained to a stick manifold. In particular, we show that the method enables us to efficiently navigate a dynamic of sampling on a stick manifold in just one iteration. Furthermore, we extend the applicability of our dynamic method to diverse problems of non-hierarchical minimization, and we illustrate the efficacy of our method through a range of numerical examples. To safeguard users against misinformation in the near future, distinguishing deep learning model-generated content will be essential. For this purpose, researchers have compiled a dataset consisting of deep learning model-generated headlines and genuine headlines, and conducted a study where participants attempted to identify the fabricated headlines. A novel computational strategy called Action-CSA is introduced, enabling the global exploration of reaction pathways through optimization of the Onsager-Machlup action using conformational space annealing. Action-CSA is capable of sampling multiple reaction pathways without initial guesses and successfully captures both the most dominant pathway and a variety of alternative routes. Pathway diversity is maintained through a crossover operation, facilitating the efficient sampling of pathway space. Action-CSA is evaluated by identifying reaction pathways for alanine dipeptide and hexane, demonstrating strong agreement between the approach and extensive molecular dynamics simulations regarding the most dominant reaction pathway. Moreover, Action-CSA identifies a significant number of additional reaction pathways compared to the transition path sampling method, highlighting its ability to capture alternative routes with lower reaction rates. Furthermore, Action-CSA is capable of predicting reaction pathways for peptides that undergo ring-flipping, a phenomenon observed in MD simulations. By identifying a distinct mechanism involving ring-bridging, the Action-CSA results provide a novel structural explanation for ring-flipping peptides. These results indicate that Action-CSA is a reliable strategy for the comprehensive exploration of reaction pathways, extending existing transition state theory to complex systems. Action-CSA is also suited for parallel processing, allowing it to efficiently sample reaction pathways, even for systems as large as peptides of six amino acids. As such, Action-CSA is an invaluable tool for the systematic investigation of reaction pathways in various chemical and biological systems. In the future, integrating Action-CSA with extensive molecular dynamics simulations could help accurately classify reaction pathways with high confidence. Action-CSA results, if combined with simulation data, could aid in the detection and inhibition of reaction mechanisms within real biological processes. However, Action-CSA's focus on lowest energy pathways may overlook less dominant but statistically occurring reaction mechanisms, particularly those involving deceleration as reaction rates approach zero, a problem first identified in prior research. As such, integrating Action-CSA with simulation data will not entirely solve the aforementioned problem. Ultimately, Action-CSA's findings highlight its capacity to identify reaction mechanisms that can be exploited or inhibited, as reaction flux occurs optimally when the system operates at the reaction's rate constant. As such, facilitating or impeding reaction flux may constitute a valuable strategy in chemistry, biology, and medicine. In the future, the integration of Action-CSA with experimental datasets could uncover reactions that can be manipulated or inhibited, thereby shedding new light on chemical and biological processes at the atomic level. This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for value filling. Building on the established SUPER and SQL-Decode frameworks, the work introduces a unified model, SUPER-Decode, to integrate benefits from both approaches. Experimental evaluation on the SuperGLUE dataset demonstrates that SUPER-Decode outperforms both individual frameworks. Moreover, analyzing decoding paths from SUPER-Decode reveals that SQL-Decode's systematic exploration contributes substantially to improvement in complex queries. Overall, the results indicate that integrating decoding methods can lead to notable progress in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing. As a result, the model achieves top-tier performance on the SuperGLUE dataset, achieving 73.9% in value filling and 59.4% in column selection tasks. Furthermore, the full model reaches 59.3% in SQL execution on the dataset. Insights from the analysis further suggest that streamlining value filling targets and decoding mechanisms can be crucial for optimizing this parsing task. In complex multi-robot systems, accurately navigating while avoiding potential collisions with other robots is a significant challenge, largely due to the unpredictable movements of fellow robots. To tackle this, our method develops a data-driven strategy where each robot continually determines and follows a safe trajectory that minimizes a probability-optimized measure of closest approach with other robots, rather than relying on probabilistic assessments of potential collisions. Inspired by risk-aware decision-making concepts, our method integrates distributionally robust CVaR to account for the uncertainty of other robots, thereby enhancing the data-driven prediction and mitigation of unexpected robot behaviors. By utilizing convex optimization to obtain optimal solutions, our method can also leverage evolutionary techniques to generate approximate solutions, thereby maintaining real-time efficiency and scalability for real-world applications. Simulation outcomes reveal substantial improvements in navigation quality and a significant reduction in navigation time, with increased visibility of other robots, making our method a valuable resource for optimizing multi-robot systems. The techniques presented here also have viable applications in other domains involving uncertain environments, such as autonomous driving. Research on spoken dialogue systems has typically relied on a shortlist of the top ASR hypotheses for interpreting meaning and monitoring the dialogue flow.  Nevertheless, confusion networks comprising multiple ASR hypotheses appear to more accurately capture language uncertainties, although they were previously considered impractical due to computational costs.  This paper explores the possibility of employing confusion networks in a variety of dialogue management tasks and compares their effectiveness with the traditional method of using the top ASR hypotheses.  To accomplish this, a model of confusion networks is generated utilizing the most likely n ASR hypotheses and their corresponding n most likely n sentences generated by an ASR system.  Experimental results indicate that dialogue management policies developed using confusion networks, when combined with sequence-to-sequence models trained on confusion networks, yield significantly better results, up to a 114% improvement over current standards, which involve policies trained on sequence-to-sequence models trained with only the top ASR hypotheses.  This improvement holds true across both offline simulations and online deployments.  Online deployments have shown that utilizing confusion networks results in a 3.1% decrease in dialogue quality metric scores compared to a system that never speaks incorrectly, indicating a path towards achieving error-free dialogue flow.  Additionally, the models trained with confusion networks show increased ability to reason about language uncertainties and employ more conservative responses when encountering uncertain context information.  Importantly, the models' ability to reason about uncertainties is substantiated by analysis of the models' internal workings during offline simulations.  This research lays the groundwork for leveraging confusion networks in dialogue management and highlights their potential to help develop more sophisticated and accurate models of language uncertainties, which in turn can facilitate the achievement of error-free dialogue flow.  Looking ahead, one promising area of exploration is the application of neural attention mechanisms to model the relationship between utterances based on the likelihood values derived from the confusion network model.  Another promising area of exploration is the application of confusion networks to other tasks such as data-to-text and question answering, which also deal with uncertainties in language, as well as the use of neural networks to model the relationship between utterances based on the likelihood values derived from the confusion network.  Finally, the benefits of using confusion networks to improve the design of dialogue management policies through combinatorial optimization are shown via offline simulation results.  In particular, the results indicate that utilizing confusion networks yields a 0.13% increase in WER for the METR-DE dataset, which consists of data from an online e-commerce dialogue application. A critical factor in secret sharing schemes is the count of minimal qualified subsets, as knowing this value results in the richest possible access structure. Specifically, this structure contains participants in all feasible Boolean combinations of the minimal qualified subsets, yielding the maximum complexity given the number of subsets. Every access structure can be considered a subset of this universal structure when having the same number of minimal qualified subsets, thereby the universal access structure is the most complex given the subset count. It is demonstrated that the complexity of this universal structure, with 2^n minimal qualified subsets, is asymptotically equivalent to the maximum complex structure with the same subset count. Furthermore, this structure is achieved by a shared data distribution with specific security and non-redundancy properties and a specific threshold value. 

A shared data distribution with m subsets, each containing n participants, is defined as follows. Every subset consists of participants with consecutive IDs, starting from i, for 1 ≤ i ≤ n and i + |R| ≤ n, where R is the repair set of the scheme and has the largest possible size of (n - 1) / 2. 

Using the universal access structure with 2^n minimal subsets, a shared data distribution with 2^(log*n + log*(n^(-1)) + epsilon) minimal qualified subsets is achieved. This was proven through the absolute boundedness of R in the scheme, resulting in the achieved complexity being asymptotically equivalent to the universal access structure with the same subset count. Furthermore, this structure is attained by a shared data distribution with specific security, non-redundancy properties, and a threshold value of (1 + epsilon')n for a small, fixed positive epsilon', where epsilon' is directly proportional to epsilon.

Notably, using the optimal estimators does not necessitate a complete characterization of the states, as we demonstrate in our research that identifying just three key parameters suffices for several families, whereas others require four, leading to promising opportunities for future enhancement of quantum measurement precision. We extract variance values from raw data and compare them to simulated results, revealing optimal performance in line with quantum estimation theory. This study investigates whether an even more basic method could achieve continual learning results by solely fine-tuning a pre-trained model on each new task with available data. To achieve defense against data memory and covariance changes, a simple task preconditioning using a handful of easy-to-classify images is also considered. Experiments on standard continual learning benchmarks confirm the proposed frozen pretraining method's efficacy, yielding a notable improvement in performance compared to the widely adopted Incremental Learning approach and competing continual learning methods. These results, along with additional analysis, are provided in the published paper. The code for these results can be found on the official GitHub repository for this research, which is located at https://github.com/neginpas/iCL2022FrozenPretraining. A related technical report containing supplementary information, including detailed experimental results and additional comparisons, can be accessed at arXiv:2206.11630. A high-quality demo showcasing the proposed continuation learning method can be viewed at https://vison.github.io/vison-demo/. As social media increasingly influence public perceptions globally, researchers have focused on tackling the pervasive issue of hate speech online. This pernicious problem gives rise to real-world consequences, such as heightened social divisions and violent crimes. Previous studies have employed automated hate speech detection methods, but they often fall short by overlooking broader social and contextual nuances. Furthermore, few attempts have been made to explore the explainability of such systems, which hinders their usefulness in practice. To address these shortcomings, we investigated the feasibility of integrating multi-layered contextual knowledge into hate speech detection models, employing both statistical and transformer-based architectures. We also introduced an approach to elicitating contextual knowledge, accompanied by an explainability evaluation that demonstrated the models' ability to learn human-intuitive patterns. Our experiment, involving over 22 million annotated tweets, revealed significant improvements in model performance when contextual features were considered, across both datasets and languages. Notably, our best-performing model achieved AUC-1 scores of 0.9452 (Spanish) and 0.9406 (English). The contextual knowledge extracted also underscored the importance of nuanced context-based hate speech classification. These findings, accompanied by the open-sourcing of our code and data, aim to foster further research on the incorporation of contextual knowledge in hate speech detection models. As a result, our models can serve as a foundation for subsequent work, helping to mitigate the devastating impact of hate speech on society. We explore the behavior of large networks of theta neurons, deriving degree-based mean field equations that capture the overall dynamics of these networks. By assuming random connections, we analyze the effects of varying in- and out-degree distribution widths on synaptically and gap junction coupled networks. Our findings reveal that the out-degree distribution has no impact on synaptically coupled network dynamics. Broadening the in-degree distribution of inhibitory networks eliminates oscillations and narrows the bistability range in excitatory networks. Conversely, in gap junction coupled networks, in-degree distribution variations shift the onset points for collective oscillations. Many of these results persist in networks of more biologically accurate neurons. These results, based on simplifying assumptions, are confirmed with spiking neuron model simulations, demonstrating qualitative agreement despite quantitative disagreements. The mean field framework provides an valuable first glance into large networks of coupled neurons. However, for accurate predictions, particularly in scenarios with diverse connection widths, additional biologically informed methods should be employed.

This study introduces a general framework for the capacity region of a complex interference channel, with its capacity defined by a linear program involving channel characteristics. We also identify a fundamental lower bound for this capacity region, expressed as a convex combination of individual spectral mutual information rates. We investigate how this lower bound approaches the actual capacity region as specific channel parameters change. Furthermore, a new algorithm is proposed for estimating the capacity region of a general interference channel for a given signal-to-noise ratio. We also analyze the efficiency of various cooperative algorithms, assessing their gains over half-duplex and full-duplex schemes. We present the findings of our analytical and numerical analyses. We conducted our analysis using a modified version of the SIC cooperative strategy, which involves sequential use of Sisso and direct transmission methods. We compared our algorithm's performance to the achievable correlation limit, yielding substantial gains over half-duplex and full-duplex approaches, and showed that the increase in efficiency over the achievable lower bound is modest, especially for higher SNR values. We also observed that the increase in efficiency over the achievable lower bound is consistent across a wide range of SNR values. We aim to determine whether the Equation-of-State of the nuclear substance can be identified by examining both flow characteristics and multi-particle correlations in nuclear collisions. To this end, we utilize a dynamic nuclear-substance transport model to simulate high-energy nuclear collisions, varying the nuclear substance's Equation-of-State to replicate observations of different flow characteristics and multi-particle correlations. We discover that the nuclear substance's Equation-of-State can be successfully replicated for heavy nuclei, such as gold, by incorporating a state with a specific temperature and entropy change. However, the same approach does not apply to lighter nuclei, such as calcium, indicating a need to consider distinct nuclear substance parameters. Furthermore, we observe that the flow characteristics of positive and negative pions differ slightly, and the flow coefficient varies among different particles, suggesting a way to establish the nuclear substance's Equation-of-State using data specific to particular particle types. We investigate the nuclear substance's Equation-of-State using a state-of-the-art thermal model, finding that the model's temperature and entropy change differ significantly from those predicted by earlier studies, implying a need to consider a state with three distinct components: separate pressures for protons and neutrons, and a temperature that exceeds the limits of the nuclear substance's stability. Considering this unusual property of the thermal model, we propose that the nuclear substance's Equation-of-State is determined by a combination of the three-body forces and quantum effects, such as those associated with pion-nuclear-substance interactions. To establish the nuclear substance's Equation-of-State, we examine multi-particle correlations while accounting for effects that may influence pion observations, such as pion-nuclear-substance interactions. We discover that taking these effects into consideration allows us to establish the nuclear substance's Equation-of-State using data specific to pions, deuterons, tritons, and helium-4, thereby allowing us to distinguish whether these correlations arise from a state with a specific temperature and entropy change or a state boundary. The study indicates an opportunity to investigate novel states in heavy nuclei by means of in heavy-ion collision experiments. A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an effective neural network architecture that processes graph data, extensively applied across multiple domains. Unlike traditional neural network models, GNN can operate in a decentralized manner, facilitating communication among neighboring nodes and potentially leading to more efficient control mechanisms in wireless communication systems. However, wireless channel disruptions significantly reduce the robustness of GNN predictions. To address this limitation, we develop methods to assess the robustness of decentralized GNN predictions in various wireless communication systems, focusing on a binary classification model. We evaluate GNN performance in both unstructured and structured communication environments using synthetic data for a synthetic wireless communication task. Moreover, we demonstrate that a simple training approach significantly improves the GNN's prediction robustness in wireless channels. Our research contributes to the understanding of the GNN performance in wireless communication systems and sets forth guidelines for the effective deployment of GNN algorithms in these systems. Furthermore, our work provides insights on the feasibility of using wireless communication systems to optimize the performance of GNN models. Overall, our paper offers valuable knowledge on the effective deployment of GNN algorithms in wireless communication systems, an area that has not been extensively researched in the literature. The threat of homicide death tolls has raised concerns worldwide and demands attention from the scientific community and society at large. A crucial aspect of addressing this issue lies in understanding which groups are disproportionately affected. The present Study provides a comprehensive overview of homicide death tolls in Brazil, focusing on variations according to demographic factors, including sex, age, race, skin colour, and educational background. Utilizing data collected by Brazil's Ministry of Health between 2010 and 2017, the research utilized Multiple Correspondence Analysis and explored relationships via adjusted logistic regression. The findings indicate that males are approximately six times more likely than females to experience homicide death tolls. Those aged 15-24 are significantly more at risk than their older and younger counterparts. Individuals of black or mixed race individuals have higher mortality rates than their white counterparts. Additionally, it has been discovered that individuals without a formal education are nearly three times more likely to experience homicide death tolls than their educated counterparts. The analysis also reveals that homicide death tolls are more concentrated in specific regions, such as Northeast Brazil. The research highlights that public policy interventions are required to address the distinct challenges faced by various demographic segments. Furthermore, it is essential for governments and the community to acknowledge the devastating impact of violence on young people. The study demonstrates the efficacy of statistical analysis in identifying patterns of correlations within complex datasets, which can be utilized to inform policy and action. The proposed use of MCA and logistic regression analysis may appeal to researchers working with large population datasets, as it requires minimal personal data. The present Study contributes to the body of existing research on population-level consequences of violence by exploring the distinct challenges faced by various demographic segments. The research highlights that effective solutions to address homicide death tolls require a tailored policy approach that addresses the distinct challenges faced by different demographic segments, rather than a one-size-fits-all strategy. The analysis suggests that efforts to combat violence should prioritize addressing the factors that distinguish high-risk groups from their peers, such as disparities in education and race. The research emphasizes that addressing homicide death tolls is a pressing public health concern that demands the attention of governments and the community at large. We investigate a stochastic gradient descent algorithm that employs exponentially decreasing step sizes to minimize smooth, strongly-convex functions. Our analysis demonstrates that, with an optimally chosen decay rate, the algorithm permits the adjustment of the step sizes solely based on observed function values and invariance to function transformations, while still achieving a convergence rate of $\mathcal O(1+\varepsilon)$. For optimality, we establish upper and lower bounds for the convergence rate under this scheme. Furthermore, we extend this approach to jointly minimize a smooth, strongly-convex function and a convex, Lipschitz function, and show that, by utilizing a specially constructed sequence of decay rates, the algorithm can be designed to run concurrently without any adjustments, and still achieve a convergence rate of $\mathcal O(\log^2(T)+\varepsilon)$. Additionally, applying this methodology to stochastic convex-concave Nash games reveals that the algorithm can be used to solve this complex multiplayer problem with an optimally engineered decay rate of $\omega_t=\omega=\frac{\kappa}{\log(t)}$, and still achieve a convergence rate of $\mathcal O(1+\varepsilon)$, where $\kappa$ represents the convexity constant of the game's utility functions. Through straightforward extensions, these outcomes also offer faster rates for solving multiple-player convex-concave non-parallel games and sequential optimization problems with adaptive step sizes. Similar to previous research, the algorithm's application to Nash games utilizes an engineered $\omega_t$ whose value depends solely on the iteration index $t$, and not on the number of players. Nevertheless, the presence of $n$ players does influence the optimal choice of $\omega=\omega_t$ decay rate, which is reflected in a $\frac{\kappa}{n\log(t)}$ decay rate for $\omega$. It is demonstrated that this engineered decay rate permits the concurrent design without any adjustments, and still achieve a convergence rate of $\mathcal O(1+\varepsilon)$. Variants of axions known as axion-like particles (ALPs) also appear in modified theories of gravity and fundamental particle interactions.  The decay rate of these axions or ALPs is generally low (10^-5 to 10^-11 GeV), making detection challenging but possible with the help of astrophysical observations and particle tests.  The axion oscillation amplitude relies on the size of the initial nonabelian gauge interaction, and current astrophysical evidence suggests large ALP decay rates of over 10^-12 GeV.  The proposed research aims to study the reverse process of axion or ALP decays within the framework of nonabelian Higgs mechanisms.  The reverse process, though theoretically possible, is highly unlikely due to the constraints of nonabelian Higgs mechanism.  An alternative approach to reverse decays is explored through mass-dependent coupling modifications and found that the reverse process is generally forbidden.  However, under exceptional conditions of high-energy interactions and long-range ALP coupling, the reverse process becomes theoretically feasible but constrained by the hierarchy problem and current astrophysical evidence, implying that the energy scales of such reverses are likely capped at 10^16 GeV or lower.  An unexplored yet possible outcome of reverse decays is that three particles from the same multiplet are emitted in a single event, and future particle experiments should consider this additional decay pathway. Developing robots with skilled hands that can effectively grasp and manipulate objects is an essential yet complex challenge. In comparison to other object-grasping fields, dexterous grasping has been understudied, mainly due to a shortage of extensive datasets. To address this issue, our study introduces DexGraspNet - a large-scale simulated dataset - designed specifically for robotic dexterous grasping, paired with an efficient data generation approach utilizing Unity Simulations. By employing statistical sampling, our method enables high-speed simulation data generation, significantly expanding available resources for dexterous grasping. As a result, our dataset comprises 1.3 million demonstrations of novel 3D objects grasped by a 6-DoF robotic hand, totaling 6 million demonstrations in total. In contrast to a prior hand-grasping dataset, our simulated object-grasping demonstrations exhibit (1) lower object rotation around the grasp axis and (2) lower grasp table elevation. We validate the advantages of training a dexterous neural policy using DexGraspNet by demonstrating that policies trained on this dataset (1) generalize better to objects with unseen shapes and (2) produce stable object orientations during grasp execution. Notably, our findings show that object rotation can be adequately predicted without relying on object rotation data. Instead, our data reveals that DexGraspNet encodes object shape drifts, which serve as sufficient predictors. Moreover, our integration of KF predictions yields significant improvements in grasp success rates by 5% and our end-to-end dexterous policy training accounts for an additional 4% improvement. We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and channel pruning to effectively transfer critical information flow from a powerful teacher model to a more efficient student model. Unlike previous techniques that collapse this information, InDistill leverages layer-wise pruning of the teacher's intermediate stages, aligning their widths with those of the student, thereby enabling direct information distillation without an intermediate encoding step. To facilitate knowledge transfer, we employ a curriculum learning strategy that prioritizes layer-wise difficulty and critical learning periods. Through these advancements, InDistill significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving enhanced results on a range of image classification benchmarks, including a 16.7% compression improvement on ResNet-50 for ImageNet at comparable accuracy to the full model. Two submersion functions from the set of two-dimensional real numbers to the set of real numbers are defined, and their respective level set foliations are examined. The equivalence of these functions topologically implies the topological equivalence of their foliations. Conversely, this relationship is not always valid; however, we define a specific class of linear-like functions with sufficient complexity and provide criteria under which the converse is true. This class includes functions whose iterates converge uniformly to their limits as well as functions whose Hausdorff dimensions of invariant sets are strictly less than one. In addition, we demonstrate that the set where two topologically equivalent functions differ is compact and strictly invariant under both functions. Furthermore, we prove that both functions exhibit the same locally connected open sets and that their compact invariant sets are equally distributed in a specific proportion. This research focuses on a specific scenario involving a 2D marine ice sheet with a grounding line, though the approach can be extended to other contact issues like subglacial cavitation. A primary challenge arises from the analysis due to ice's nonlinear rheology, the implementation of a power-law based friction boundary condition, and the presence of rigid modes in velocity space, resulting in a semicoercive variational inequality. To tackle this complexity, a mixed formulation is explored that incorporates a Lagrange multiplier, followed by a finite element approximation analysis. This research derives error estimates by employing a specially constructed projection operator to account for rigid modes, leveraging a Korn-type inequality, under the condition that rigid modes do not exceed one. To validate the approximation, it is applied to a specific analytical test case, known as the lifted Bessel variational inequality, allowing for a more in-depth examination of the method's performance. Furthermore, the proposed formulation is utilized in a computational study on the West Antarctic Ice Sheet, shedding new light on the role of rigid modes in enhancing Inverse Problem solutions, known as "anti-stable modes". This research reveals that these additional degrees of freedom can significantly contribute to improved Inverse Problem solutions when included, though their influence might be negligible when solely viewed from an analysis perspective. To facilitate practical applications, a Python-based tool is utilized for generating the projected problem, illustrating the feasibility of this approach for marine ice sheet models, as well as other contact-related issues involving Stokes variational inequalities. Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe. Furthermore, we found that outflows from our selected galaxy share similarities with those from lower-mass galaxies similar to the Milky Way, suggesting that our understanding of outflows applies broadly to galaxies across various masses and environments. Our research also utilized NOEMA's spatial resolution to detect a hidden gas cloud near the center of the galaxy, which contains about 200 million times the mass of our sun; the cloud is largely absent of the galaxy's star-forming regions, but the exact reason for its location is still unclear. Finally, we found that outflows do not fully account for how gas is moving in and out of the galaxy, suggesting that other processes such as gas absorption and the movement of gas in and out of the galaxy's central region may play a significant role. A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau is examined, along with an efficient method for estimating its value from data. The proposed method significantly reduces computational time by adapting a standard approach, allowing for quicker calculations when dealing with larger datasets. The modified approach specifically identifies key components in its underlying Hájek projection, leading to a notable runtime improvement for fixed-dimension datasets. The method's time complexity scales as O(n log n) when dealing with datasets of a given dimension, rather than the previous O(n^2) scaling. This implementation is demonstrated with a synthetic dataset, prior data, and an examination of correlations among variables in the Boston house prices challenge, showcasing its practical applications and efficiency. The associated R package named kendalltau can be accessed through the following repository: https://github.com/mkapata/kendalltau. A Python implementation of the code is available at https://bit.ly/3Qs3H0A. For further extensions or discussions regarding the code, feel free to contact the author at mkapata@imt.liges.in. A presentation outlining the work in detail can be found at https://tiny.cc/KendallTau. The presented work contributes significantly to the statistical field of nonparametric correlation estimation by offering a faster method, thereby making it more applicable in various situations. The estimated correlation measure has an asymptotic normal distribution and efficiency comparable to previously published results, while significantly reducing computational time. The approach specifically yields an estimate with a mean squared error (MSE) of (nu*h^3/(6*sigma^2))*(1 + (1/(nu*h)))*((3*(nu+h)/4)*((1)/(n-1))) as demonstrated, where nu is the degree of freedom, h is the estimated value, and sigma is the standard deviation. The new method exhibits efficiency of (nu/(nu+h))^2, approaching 1 as data size increases, indicating its high precision. Euler characteristic is a fundamental, widely recognized topological invariant with numerous past uses, especially in studies involving random fields. Our primary objective is to illustrate its application in high-dimensional spaces. While employing more powerful invariants like homology remains an active area of research, employing the Euler characteristic in high-dimensional spaces is still useful for various reasons. Some reasons include its computational efficiency compared to other more complex invariants, the availability of open yet significant research questions regarding its variation properties in high-dimensional spaces, and the relatively limited understanding of more powerful invariants for several problems. We examine Euler characteristic's variation properties using random fields and extend it to multi-variable spaces. We then test it on several synthetic and real-life datasets, demonstrating its practicality. Our findings include its application in modeling data variability by employing random fields with specific properties and its use in analyzing texture patterns within magnetic resonance images of retro-ocular tissues. We establish that the Euler characteristic provides a compactness invariant, offering a straightforward approach for identifying unique features in multi-variable images. We also discuss potential enhancements using more powerful invariants from topological data analysis. Our software is hosted on the GitHub platform (https://github.com/3dfck/EulerChar), enabling reproducible evaluations. This second paper verifies the efficacy of the facet pivot method, confirming it can solve linear programming problems in at most n - d iterations, motivated by Smale's mathematical problems as outlined in his 'On the Mathematical Foundations of Studying the Brain'. The third paper is being prepared to present computational analyses and extensive comparative studies of several other proposed algorithms for linear programming. Theoretically, the Hirsch Conjecture remains valid for specific classes of polytope structures, prompting further inquiry into the validity of each type of polytope. Effective countermeasures against these deceptive attempts are vital for the safe integration of facial recognition technology. Current approaches have shown limitations, often becoming overly specialized in training datasets and struggling to adapt to unseen attack methods and environments. In this research, transfer learning is applied from the vision transformer model to tackle the challenge of detecting unknown anti-spoofing attacks. Despite initial expectations, however, its successful application in autonomous vehicle development has been hindered by the challenges of accurately framing learning problems and collating comprehensive datasets. particularly when it comes to complex tasks like road navigation and vehicular control. This paper argues that the difficulty in defining autonomous vehicle learning problems and compiling datasets stems from the necessity of developing a comprehensive road map. To tackle this obstacle, we present a novel data-driven strategy for creating an accurate road map by leveraging graph theory and network analysis. The proposed framework utilizes a hierarchical graph comprising of macro-road segments and corresponding micro-lane markers to facilitate automatic vehicle learning. To evaluate the efficacy of our approach, we implemented an end-to-end graph autoencoder to assess the efficacy of the learned road map. The results indicate that our method successfully enables autonomous vehicle learning and showcases its potential by demonstrating self-driving capabilities through simulated off-road driving and a challenging first-person MOGATL challenge. Additionally, we make our source code and datasets freely available online. Furthermore, the implications of our method are discussed in terms of extending the capability of autonomous driving beyond standard training data, with potential applications in standardization and data set creation. The research further investigates the implications of autonomous learning on cogntive and artificial intelligence and examines the possible role of autonomous systems in developing robust general intelligence. However, a major limitation in Asynchronous PEAs (APEAs) arises from idling computing nodes after each solution evaluation. As solution quality typically increases over time, APEAs tend to suffer from Evaluation Time Bias (ETB), where the goal of improving solutions becomes entwined with the passing of time. Consequently, passing time acts as a dominant selection force that diverges remaining solutions from their optimal counterparts. We investigate ETB and its effects on convergence in multi-objective optimization problems, along with providing two possible remedies - a novel termination criterion and using a population size that fluctuates over time. Results from comprehensive experiments using CMA-ES on multi-objective test functions demonstrate that acknowledging ETB can significantly boost the computing time it takes to reach a satisfactory Pareto-frontward progress. We start by showcasing ETB's influence on quality around its onset and optimizing function evaluation delay. From a computational standpoint, we examine the time required to achieve a satisfactory progress for both optimized and unacknowledged ETB scenarios, also evaluating the effectiveness of our proposed solutions over a set of multi-objective optimization problems. Conclusively, our findings underscore the importance of acknowledging ETB in Asynchronous PEAs to optimize performance, alongside offering concrete strategies to mitigate its negative consequences. As such, these strategies are proposed to address a considerable practical issue affecting high-performance computing in evolutionary algorithms. Lastly, the report highlights ongoing challenges in domain adaptation, specifically the potential for results to be skewed by image-to-image translation techniques that memorize target labels, and suggests future areas of exploration and investigation. This finding has an additional consequence: for k-means algorithms using concave assignment functions and data points within a convex area, we can determine a standardized version of the function that ensures all local optima converge to the global optimum. As a result, this standardized function has a global optimum that is both continuous and decreases monotonically. Moreover, we can calculate the quantity of improvement from the global optimum to any local optimum, all without requiring prior knowledge of the global optimum. These results are also relevant to multi-modal optimization problems, as they offer a method to differentiate between local optima and the global optimum based on the value of the objective function. We present two applications – an alternative method for spatial clustering and a novel approach to continuous optimization – to demonstrate the practical utility of these findings. The theoretical insights from this research can be extended to other clustering algorithms through a transformation, thereby opening up further applications. These extensions include the Chinese restaurant process from the fields of statistics and computer science and the best cluster problem from bioinformatics, where our method allows us to distinguish between local maxima and global maxima without requiring prior knowledge of the global maximum. We can also transform other clustering problems to meet the required conditions, such as the spatial clustering and continuous optimization problems mentioned earlier. This research provides a comprehensive understanding of the nature of local optima in kernel k-means algorithms, specifically in regards to their location, behaviour, and relationship with the global optimum. As a result, this work offers a solid theoretical foundation for the development of more effective clustering algorithms. To demonstrate its utility, we present an alternative method for spatial clustering that focuses on the specific characteristics of the data points. This approach allows for the differentiation between local and global optima without the need for further adjustments, thereby meeting the requirements for the theoretical guarantees outlined in this research. Ultimately, this study contributes valuable insights into the behaviour of local optima in kernel k-means algorithms, opens up new avenues for the development of clustering algorithms, and presents practical applications of these findings. Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate a latent image's sharpness and a blurred image's blurry kernel, given just one blurry image. Past research has proposed using a specific distribution, such as a Gaussian or Laplacian, to model the blur kernel, but in reality, the amount and type of blur can vary significantly. This paper presents an innovative approach to tackle this challenge by using a mixture kernel structure to model kernel distributions. By drawing inspiration from Gaussian Mixture Models, we develop a probabilistic model that allows the number of components, mean, and variance to adapt during training. To prevent the model from assigning too much weight to a specific component, we use a Dirichlet prior. By assuming that the intensity of the blur within a patch is drawn from the estimated distribution, we derive the training and inference procedures. To validate our approach, we compared it with state-of-the-art methods on standard datasets and found that it consistently outperformed these methods. Additionally, we analyzed the effect of the model parameters on image deblurring quality and found some interesting insights. This research suggests that using a mixture kernel structure is a promising approach for handling complex blur patterns effectively. Incorporating deep neural networks into robotic systems poses a significant problem due to the lack of reliable measures for their output predictions. Traditional methods relying solely on training data are insufficient as they fail to consider real-world scenarios. However, a novel approach developed in this paper Grounded Uncertainty Pool (GUP) addresses this limitation by taking into account a robot's sensory and physical interactions. GUP begins by isolating features impacting the robot's observations and physical interactions, then uses these isolated factors to define multiple candidate distributions for the robot's environment. By sampling from these distributions, GUP generates synthetic data, utilizing this synthetic data to calculate an uncertainty measure for predictions based on real data. The approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through successful prediction of sensor data, navigation in uncharted terrain, and reliable object detection even in real-world scenarios where data is insufficient. The full implementation of GUP is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/aspn-analysis/GUP. Additionally, a corresponding video illustrating GUP's application can be found at https://youtu.be/fIE8O0mH0E. Furthermore, a detailed discussion on the motivations and limitations of GUP can be accessed at https://docs.ros.org/foxy/src/gup/README.md. The integration of advanced traffic forecasting technology significantly improves urban transportation systems' efficiency. However, traffic predictions based on full road scene images result in suboptimal outcomes due to issues like traffic congestion, obstructions, and camera distortions. To enhance prediction accuracy in such scenarios, we propose dividing test data into smaller spatial segments and training models to predict patches independently. This approach enables the accommodation of temporary road obstacles and camera distortions by leveraging the models for full patch predictions. We examine multiple techniques for pooling patch predictions, including averaging, categorical ordering, and blending methods, and compare their effects on prediction performance. Moreover, we examine the performance of traffic video encoding architectures, including CSINet, implicit spatial terms, autoregressive models, including CRF, Kurtosis, Minorax, and Novelty, on three traffic video datasets, showing that our method outperforms baseline models with improved coarseness, allowing the proposed technique to achieve results comparable to current state-of-the-art traffic forecasting models on single test locations. On the KITTI-360 dataset, we specifically address traffic video forecasting challenges by achieving a high MS-SSIM of 0.9701, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method. The code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/quantvast/TrafVideo4Forecasts. Ultimately, we aim to establish a standardized benchmark, referred to as TrafVideo4Forecasts, for evaluating the performance of traffic video forecasting models. Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging is a critical factor in diagnosing and treating neuropsychiatric disorders. Current deep learning-based methods primarily utilize data from patients with healthy or Alzheimer's disease. This raises concerns about their performance in other domains, such as patients with epilepsy and hippocampal resections. We have developed and validated an open-source, state-of-the-art deep learning method that uses an extended 2D multi-orientation approach for automatic hippocampus segmentation. We have also made public some private datasets that were previously not accessible, allowing for a comprehensive evaluation on five different datasets in comparison to 11 published methods. Our novel approach demonstrated excellent results on four datasets, achieving a mean dice score of 0.866, and mean absolute surface error of 1.661 mm, and a mean center distance error of 1.875 mm. The method also showed good generalizability to unseen datasets, and we recommend its use as the current top-performing solution for the community. We also conducted additional analyses on the impact of data augmentation and the influence of MR scanner properties on hippocampus segmentation, which are provided in the accompanying documentation. Our research focuses on the lower proton radiation belt at an altitude of approximately 5 Earth radii. Previous studies suggested that this radiation belt is primarily formed by the radial diffusion mechanism. To investigate the lower radiation belt, we ran a global electromagnetic simulation with the UNRAR model to analyze a 28 MeV proton's orbit at an altitude of around 5.1 Earth radii. To mimic the effects of a radial diffusion mechanism, we specified an equilibrium distribution with protons in the phase space. The results of our time-dependent simulations indicate that a stable equilibrium was achieved within a 10 Earth year timeframe. In contrast, time-integrated phase space density maps of protons showed significant discrepancies relative to the equilibrium distribution, especially for protons with higher energy. Additionally, we found that a radial diffusion mechanism does not predominantly contribute to the formation of the inner proton radiation belt in the specified altitude. To further clarify the radiation belt formation, we investigated the longitudinal distribution of protons in the equilibrium and found that near-equilibrium proton distributions at different longitudes exhibited periodic variations every 2.7 years. Consequently, a time-averaged radial projection of proton density showed significant discrepancies when calculated over a 4-year and a 10-year period. Notably, a score of studies have utilized a 10-year timescale in their research. In the context of radiation belt physics, our findings imply that a 10-year timescale may not be sufficiently long to capture the complex orbital dynamics of trapped particles. Moreover, combining the results of multiple-year simulations may introduce inaccuracies in modeling these complex particle orbits. The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task
approach, training existing relation extraction models alongside knowledge graph
link prediction to ultimately boost the models' overall performance and achieve
predictable gains in accuracy. We evaluated the effectiveness of this method on
the FB15K-237 and WN18RR datasets, observing a significant 1.2% increase in
F1 score on the FB15K-237 dataset and confirming our hypothesis that related
tasks can enhance the performance of each other. We are one of the first groups to
exploit the connection between these two semi-related tasks. The code used in
our study is publicly accessible on our GitHub profile at the provided link.

This study introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Developed based on the critical recognition that inverter delay is a complex interplay of multiple process variables and load capacitance, the proposed model incorporates parameterized equations derived using Curve Fitting Toolbox in Matlab to accurately capture these dynamics. In comparison to simulation results generated by SPICE and the BSIM4 transistor model, the analytical delay model exhibits remarkably high precision, demonstrating an average error of less than 2% across an extensive range of technological parameters and output loads. As a result, the proposed model presents itself as a computationally efficient solution for various applications involving CMOS inverter delay analysis, particularly in the contexts of technology transfer, design parameter analysis and optimization, and performance benchmarking. Furthermore, this model serves as a highly suitable starting point for the development of delay models describing the behavior of more complex digital circuits. This work was presented at the 2014 International Symposium on Microelectronics. Furthermore, the predictive capabilities of the model regarding inverter delay have been recently explored, demonstrating that it accurately predicts changes in delay resulting from alterations in CMOS inverter structure. This study provides statistical analysis indicating the relative importance of individual process variables on inverter delay, in line with the findings of recent technical literature. As a case study, the model has been used to quantify the delays of CMOS inverters manufactured under different technological conditions, thereby facilitating the quantitative comparison of inverter delay across disparate technological frameworks. Additionally, the analytical delay model has been successfully extended to express the behavior of CMOS inverters in the presence of non-linear output loads. This study presents analytical models of radio frequency power amplifiers, emphasizing the importance of accurately characterizing the distortion behavior of such devices. Furthermore, the analytical delay model represents a valuable educational tool, capable of being utilized in tutoring circuits involving deep submicron technology. The ventral temporal cortex is crucial for object recognition, but the link between visual objects and living animates remains poorly understood, despite being intimately linked in human experience. We present a survey of existing research focusing on how the brain processes animates, objects, and hybrids within specific domains, and introduce a theory to explain the variability seen in brain areas associated with animates. Two theoretical models are proposed to account for this variability: the first posits that animates are processed as complex objects, integrating individual components such as parts and function, while the second proposes that animates are simply distinct from inanimate objects, with no inherent characteristics. We support our hypotheses with existing brain imaging studies, outlining a potential research framework that could test these ideas and provide a framework for integrating knowledge across distinct areas of research. The interplay between objects and animates has significant implications for computational models and the design of future machines, especially those seeking to comprehend the world through visual means. The study also highlights opportunities for interdisciplinary research at the intersection of neuroscience, computer science, and philosophy. Quasi-periodic oscillations type C, typically observed in low-hard and hard-intermediate states of black hole X-ray transients, have been investigated using the MAXI J1535-571 data collected by Insight-HXMT. By applying a novel time-dependent Comptonization model and a relativistic reflection model, we observed distinct correlations between the seismic features and the hardness-intensity diagram. Specifically, we identified the seismically affected spectrum in the low-hard state and found that the seismic amplitude exhibits a characteristic "double-horned" pattern during the outburst. Our findings also suggest that type C QPOs in low-hard states are related to corona instabilities rather than truncation. These results imply that the inner edge of the corona is likely to be semi-infinite, and when broken, it causes "flickering" that can be observed in the hardness-intensity diagram. Additionally, we discovered a positive correlation between the seismic amplitude and the cooling photon index, indicating that photon trapping increases as the inner edge of the corona moves closer. As the photon trapping effect strengthens, the seismic pattern transitions from a "double-horned" to a "single-horned" shape. Moreover, we observed a positive correlation between the seismic amplitude and the width of the broad iron line, indicating that the seismic mechanism shifts from being fuel-driven in the low-hard state to being jet-fed in the hard-intermediate state. These findings demonstrate that Seismology of X-ray transients can be an effective tool for investigating the properties and behavior of jet-fed plasmas. Moreover, by differentiating between various mechanisms driving QPOs, researchers can obtain a more in-depth understanding of the inner accretion flow. Finally, we verified the accuracy of previous interpretations related to the Seismic feature width and its association with the inner edge of the corona or the boundary between the standard and jet-fed regimes. Moreover, we determined the QPO amplitude to be inversely correlated with the width of the iron broad line during the hard-intermediate state. In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to being brittle due to their potential for overfitting on the policies of their training partners. As a result, they may perform poorly when introduced to agents with different strategy preferences during testing. To address this issue, we propose a technique known as inter-agent zero-shot evolution, which aims to improve the test-time adaptability of MARL agents. By applying evolutionary strategies to vary the actions taken by training agents, we can create a robust variant of each MARL agent through multiple generations, simultaneously adapting to the diverse strategies of potential test-time counterparts. Experimental findings confirm that MARL agents developed with this method exhibit enhanced cross-agent robustness, improved communication efficiency, and increased adaptability to unfamiliar agents, surpassing the performance of baseline methods. The proposed approach can be utilized as an off-the-shelf test-time adaptability solution for MARL agents. We introduce MatSim, a comprehensive synthetic dataset, benchmark, and 
approach designed to leverage computer vision for identifying and 
transferring similarities and transitions across materials and textures. 
MatSim enables one-shot learning, empowering the identification of any 
material regardless of the context or circumstances using only one or 
multiple examples. Visual material recognition is a crucial element in 
several industries such as manufacturing, construction, and logistics, 
where it can be applied on a large scale like analyzing images from drones 
or industrial equipment. Our dataset consists of 472 synthetic families, 
featuring 77 materials and 25 environments that expose 10 transformation 
types. We develop an unsupervised and domain-adaptive vision model, 
MatSimV2, that can be adapted to any new material with only one example. 
We achieve this through a combination of our new synthetic dataset 
characteristics and an advanced neural architecture that incorporates 
unsupervised domain adaptation, multi-scale semantic feature extraction, 
and local detailed texture feature preservation. In our experiments, we 
successfully apply MatSimV2 to 1) known materials with new domains (domain 
adaptation), and 2) unseen material domains with only one example (one-shot 
learning). We showcase MatSimV2's capability to process real-world images 
in challenging scenarios, significantly outperforming baseline models in both 
supervised and unsupervised settings. The MatSim dataset and our 
approach, including code and models, can be accessed at https://github.com/npatlas/MatSimV2.

To effectively manage consumer behavior, the study shows that the pricing plan must account for various economic factors that influence consumers' decision-making processes, involving complex optimization problems. Given the inherent uncertainty and risk involved, the authors explore the feasibility of implementing a dynamic pricing plan that offers guaranteed revenue to the energy provider. The investigation leads to a recommendation of a quota-based pricing strategy, which balances the needs of the energy provider for revenue assurance and consumers seeking fair incentives to shift their peak-time energy consumption. The proposed quota-based pricing plan involves the sale of two separate energy packages with predetermined quotas, priced at different rates to reflect their varying levels of risk to the energy provider. The quota for the primary energy package is calculated based on consumer willingness to pay and his/her historical energy consumption, while the selection of this package incurs a lower rate than the secondary energy package. The sale of the secondary energy package beyond its quota is subject to higher pricing, resulting in an increase in the seller's revenue. The study demonstrates through simulation that the quota-based pricing strategy can effectively provide the seller with an optimal revenue and the seller's risk of revenue loss due to abusive usage of the pricing plan is minimized to 7%. The evaluation of pricing plan fairness involves an objective analysis of consumer satisfaction and the revenue earned by the seller at different quota values, resulting in an optimal value that balances both requirements and minimizes system risks. The study shows that the pricing plan can effectively achieve its purpose by reducing peak-hour energy consumption, promoting a fair incentive to the energy provider, and ensuring the revenue earned is commensurate with consumer willingness to pay. The particular architecture of the pricing plan allows for consumer satisfaction to vary inversely with his/her abuse of the pricing plan, while keeping revenue earned by the seller consistent through appropriate quota setting. The research on extremely metal-poor stars within the Local Group offers valuable insights into the early chemical evolution of galaxies and the process of star formation. To explore the nature of metals within these stars, we conducted a statistical analysis based on measurements of the iron abundance in their atmospheres. Our focus lies in the local group galaxies, specifically those containing very faint, extremely metal-poor stars whose origins are still unclear. Utilizing the Fe/H ratio, we carried out a statistical analysis and constructed a binary distribution to represent the metallicity of stars at their birth, influencing the chemical evolution of galaxies. In the different galaxies, we observed distinct patterns and correlations, allowing us to draw comparisons between M31, M33, Sagittarius Dwarf, Fornax, Carina, Sextans, and the Milky Way. Our results indicate possible discrepancies at low metallicity, specifically at Fe/H < -2.0, between the observed distributions and a two-component model consisting of dark matter and stars. Notably, we discovered that the model overestimates the number of metal-poor stars within the Milky Way, Sgr I, and Sextans, whereas it underestimates it in the cases of M31, M33, Fornax, and Carina. In an effort to minimize systematic errors, we performed a thorough analysis of the data while addressing issues such as random and edge-brighting effects, resulting in consistent results across the various galaxies. Our results may be explained by the presence of discrete star-forming events, dark matter substructures, or other factors, and can be used to test the metallicity distribution of stars within different galaxy environments. Additionally, our method allows us to derive constraints on the metal content of stars at their birth, thereby contributing to the understanding of the process of star formation in the various galaxies of the local group. The obtained results can be utilized in future cosmological simulations to test the metallicity distribution of stars. This paper examines trends in global annual fire seasons to determine their present-day characteristics. To achieve this, we incorporate various meteorological data into a fire potential index by using Kalman filter-based time series analysis. This approach yields a concise metric enabling the identification and characterization of regional and global fire seasons. By applying this method to multiple meteorological datasets, we have developed a statistical model that estimates regional fire season lengths and frequencies using European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasting reanalysis data. Our analysis reveals that the majority of global regions experience fire seasons ranging from one to three episodes per year. Notably, we found no significant increase in regional fire season length or frequency, although certain regions, such as those in Africa and Indonesia, have experienced slight decreases in fire season frequency since 1980. Conversely, regions with increasing annual burn areas, such as western Canada and the southern United States, also exhibit extended fire seasons. Interestingly, while regional fire characteristics often contradict long-term trends in burned areas, they more closely align with changes in burn frequency. This finding implies that previous findings of widespread burn area increases were likely due to recurring fires rather than increasing fireline lengths, and that regional fire activity is more closely linked to climate variability frequency than to changes in burn intensity. Overall, our analysis highlights the value of regional fire activity metrics, such as frequency and season length, in understanding present-day fire trends. Moreover, we found that regional fire characteristics are significantly impacted by extreme weather conditions, such as El Niño and La Niña events, and that prolonged fire seasons are more common in regions with previous burn histories. In particular, we found that recurring fires in regions with frequent fire activity often result in extended fire seasons. Finally, we suggest that regional fire activity responses to climate change are more likely to be detected at the frequency rather than the burn area density level. Based on our analysis, we recommend that regional fire managers and researchers focus on tracking regional fire frequency rather than burn frequency to anticipate and prepare for changing fire activity conditions. By incorporating different meteorological datasets, this approach yields similar regional fire characteristics, suggesting that the underlying physics remain consistent. We've conducted a thorough examination of eight distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages. These measures have different prerequisites for data annotation, yet our analysis covers all scenarios. We've performed a statistical analysis of the correlations among these measures, as well as between them and typological characteristics. This analysis was conducted on a substantial dataset of 102 languages. Interestingly, we discovered a significant correlation among most of these measures, suggesting they are largely measuring the same aspect of language structure. Specifically, we found that languages with more complex morphology, as gauged by Principal Component 1, tend to have more auxiliary verbs, multiple verb forms, and greater word frequency within word lists. These results have important implications for researchers choosing methods to quantify morphological complexity for languages with limited or no written records. This, in turn, can impact assessments of language acquisition abilities. Furthermore, we found that certain typological features, such as the use of ergative cases, can influence the outcomes of such measures. This phenomenon is particularly noticeable in PC1, where speakers of languages employing ergative marking tend to score lower than their counterparts speaking accusative-only languages. It also appears that ergative cases disrupt the relationship between morphological complexity and auxiliary verbs within ergative languages. This disruption, in turn, correlates with a greater effect of ergative marking on PC1 scores. These findings highlight the beneficial role ergative cases play in understanding the intricacies of language structure. Finally, we provide recommendations for researchers and acquisicians on how to effectively use these measures, considering both the presence of auxiliary verbs and ergative cases. By quantifying this complexity, researchers can assess language acquisition abilities, though our results suggest ergative cases pose a particular challenge for such assessments. This research focuses on reducing the complexity of parametric partial differential equations (PPDEs) by finding an accurate approximation space for the solutions of the equations. Given limited information, we integrate two key sources: a reliable set of solutions (containing the solution at specific target points) and an untrustworthy set of solutions (possibly inaccurate due to random or systematic errors). An initial prediction of the approximation space is refined through multiple iterations, ensuring its accuracy and stability by minimizing errors and bound growth. The approach is demonstrated on exact PPDE solutions and in conjunction with a case study involving fractal image compression, yielding significant findings. The latter reveals that our method effectively uses trustworthy data to mitigate the influence of untrustworthy data, while untrustworthy data with localized accuracy contributes to better approximations. Furthermore, the efficacy of our method is compared to alternative reduction techniques in terms of producing high-quality fractal images. The results suggest that our approach yields more robust and accurate outcomes. The proposed method's potential extension to reducing the dimensions of incompressible Stokes equations is also explored. Computational experiments conducted with PPDE reduction reveal that our approach leads to marked speed increases while maintaining accurate solution bounds. These findings indicate that our method's reliability in using inaccurate data without compromising accuracy is a valuable asset. The approach's potential for real-world applications is further solidified through its successful implementation in a case study involving financial option pricing, where it consistently produced precise solution bounds despite using inaccurate data. In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has become the predominant approach. Each time an ad is about to be delivered, advertisers formulate bidding strategies by considering various factors such as the value of the ad, probabilities of conversion, and the cost per bid. Research has shown that optimal bidding strategies align with Expected Utility Maximization under specific assumptions about an ad's effectiveness. However, the single-type advertisement model used in this study does not accurately account for advertisers who have multiple products or varied levels of quality, all of which can impact an ad's ability to generate sales or demand. Additionally, the probabilistic nature of an ad's effectiveness can be described by different distributions, such as logistic or normal distributions, which further complicates the model. Therefore, to better address these limitations, we developed a new Bayesian hierarchical model that enables each advertiser to characterize the distribution of an ad's effectiveness using a Dirichlet process, effectively creating a cluster of similar single-type advertisers, all of which can then inform and influence each other's bidding strategies, specifically by considering an ad's conversion rate and the cost per bid. Our empirical findings reveal that incorporating a Bayesian hierarchical model yields bidding strategies of improved quality and increased revenue compared to situations in which advertisers are assumed to be homogeneous in terms of their effectiveness. However, the practical implementation of our proposed model comes at the cost of increased complexity, specifically with respect to computational requirements, for instance in terms of the amount of time needed to process a request in a Google data center environment. To address this challenge, we suggested simplifying the model by clustering a large number of advertisers into a smaller number of groups, for instance by considering the co-advertising behavior of these advertisers, which in turn enables us to efficiently ensure that the probability distribution over effectiveness is consistent across a group of similar single-type advertisers, thus facilitating efficient computation and the development of robust bidding strategy code using standard approaches such as the alpha-beta gamma slide algorithm. Empirical analysis confirms the efficacy of our proposed strategy.
