Nonclassicality in continuous-variable quantum systems can be identified through quantum steering or Wigner negativity. It has been proposed that quantum steering results in the generation of Wigner negativity, and this study aims to validate this hypothesis. By utilizing a model of unambiguous quantum steering, it has been demonstrated that steering experiments can indeed produce negative correlations, as desired. Furthermore, it has been found that multiple rounds of steering can lead to the simultaneous occurrence of steering and manifest negativity. However, it is also shown that steering does not always result in Wigner negativity; rather, it is necessary to implement multiple rounds of nonclassical measurements to achieve this effect. This research highlights the distinction between steering being nonclassical and the actual production of Wigner negativity and manifest negativity. Consequently, it is advised that in order to confirm the existence of quantum steering, it is necessary to execute multiple rounds of nonclassical measurements. This study provides insights into the quantification of nonclassicality in continuous-variable quantum systems. It offers a new method for realising manifest quantum steerability through multiple rounds of unambiguous measurements. By allowing Alice and Bob to share the same quantum state, it has been demonstrated that manifest quantum steerability can be achieved by allowing Bob to perform specific measurements, confirming the existence of Wigner negativity in this process. Accurate secure boundary analysis is crucial for practical quantum key distribution systems, but the current approach overlooks a critical aspect – the randomness consistency of seeds used in privacy amplification. We introduce and prove a quantum leftover hash lemma that applies to non-uniform random seeds, leveraging min-entropy, and subsequently establish a detailed, precise QKD secure boundary analysis. Utilizing the two-decoy BB84 protocol, we simulate the effect of random seed uniformity on the secure boundary of a QKD system. Experimentally verifying our findings, we demonstrate the significance of seed uniformity for QKD systems. To benefit the QKD technology development, we provide an efficient algorithm to generate, on average, one bit of uniform seed per bit generated through a Berlekamp-Zig-zag algorithm, outperforming existing methods. We also extend our approach to address shared-secret establishment between quantum batteries and enable secure key establishment among multiple nodes in a QKD network, when employing random seeds to construct the shared secret. We start contributing the first quantum-computer-resistant password generation protocol based on Weyl vector fields. Lastly, by applying the quantum-computer-resistant password generation protocol, we investigate how to apply password generation to quantum money transfer. We show that two previously proposed quantum money transfer proposals are vulnerable to attack by a quantum computer, but a modified version of the DMB protocol, leveraging classical identity verification and authenticating the transfer token, makes the system secure against quantum computers. We quantify the impact of random seed non-uniformity, inherent in physical systems, on the analysis of the secure boundary of QKD systems and other quantum-based password generation algorithms. Moreover, we develop a novel, quantum-resistant password generation algorithm, securing passwords generated using the Weyl construction, when transferred to a quantum environment protected by a quantum battery. We also introduce an efficient algorithm to generate, on average, one bit of uniform seed per bit generated through a efficient quantum-resistant password generation algorithm, outperforming existing methods. We extend the analysis to address shared-secret establishment between quantum batteries and enable secure key establishment among multiple nodes in a QKD network, when employing random seeds to construct the shared secret. Finally, we investigate how to apply password generation to quantum money transfer, presenting a secure version of the two-proposal DMB, making the system secure against quantum computers. The proposed work employs multiple facets of quantum information theory, including quantum cryptography, randomness extraction, quantum-computer-resistant password generation, and quantum money transfer. Further research utilizes the idea of vertex dynamics on a single waveguide to develop a mathematical framework for more intricate systems involving coupled waveguides. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in deriving the density-density correlation function of a two-site bus with two coupled waveguides through a transformation of vertex functions. By building on established results in ladder systems, we derive explicit expressions for the density-density correlation function of a bus with many waveguides. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. Notably, this improvement is achieved without increasing the density of comparisons; instead, the increased efficacy stems from the relative importance of specific sub-regions within the state space. To facilitate the seamless integration of this modified feedback mechanism into various reinforcement learning algorithms is a challenge; hence, we develop a new method, known as the Region Weighted Learning Algorithm, which attributes varying importance to different state space regions based on their accumulation of time-consuming comparisons. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this new method, outperforming or matching the existing standards in our experiments. This outcome is due to the intricate interplay of frustration and non-linearity within the system, also enabling additional intriguing phenomena such as the reappearance of topological phases, the transition of topological phases at zero energy, and the possibility of reaching an infinite lifetime of excitations. Furthermore, the method of applying adjustable interactions might facilitate the creation of more intricate versions of Toric code and Kitaev chains that incorporate higher-order excitations. The potential applications of this system, involving quantum memories and topological logic gates, are also explored. The research presents a new avenue for the investigation of topological phases, incorporating elements of precision physics and complexity analysis, and sheds light on the intricate relationship between frustration and non-linearity. Given that the band's width expands faster than the square root of the matrix's size, our analysis demonstrates that the statistical distribution of the imaginary components of the eigenvectors aligns with the results from the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. This finding was achieved using the methods and results of the work "Gaussian Fluctuations of Dyson-Schmidt Equations" and "GEE's Local Architecture". For partially filled rank, our analysis considers the limiting distribution of the imaginary components, whereas in the case of completely filled rank, we examine the ergodicity of the process. Our research extends to the study of the band's edges, where it investigates the local microscopic structure of the eigenspectra, and reveals complex phase transitions marked by variations in its width. Recent advancements in dialogue tasks have been achieved through pre-trained language models. However, models reliant on surface-level dialogue text struggle to comprehend dialogue context, particularly in extracting the underlying semantic meaning. In an effort to bridge this knowledge gap, we introduce the use of Abstract Meaning Representation as a means of pre-training language models with explicit semantic information, which captures the essence of dialogue during the pre-training phase. Building upon the standard pre-training framework, we formulate a semantic-based pre-training approach that includes three key tasks: learning core semantic units, semantic relations, and overall semantic representation. Empirical results from the analysis of casual and task-based conversations confirm the superiority of our proposed model. Furthermore, we contribute a novel paradigm by integrating a language model with explicit semantic knowledge in the field of natural language processing. However, the algorithm's efficiency can be compromised when dealing with large datasets containing varied lengths, due to the necessity for the entire dataset to be stored in memory and for the calculation of mean and variance across all records during the recursion process. To overcome this limitation, we developed a modified version of Isolation Forest that tackles records one at a time, using a streaming approach that accommodates datasets of any size. To ensure that our method aligns with the traditional Isolation Forest performance, we incorporated the same key components, including partitioning, logistic regression, and ensemble learning; a comprehensive study also compared the performance of our method with the original Isolation Forest, as well as other leading anomaly detection methods. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops methods for picking the optimal value of'm' autonomously, thereby converting the problem into a standard Bayesian estimation issue. We also explore various ways of selecting the optimal value of'm', including Monte Carlo simulation methods. Our approach is demonstrated through practical applications involving simulated and real data. Specifically, we re-examine case studies involving modelling annual maximum daily precipitation in Cascaes, Portugal, and weekly number of traffic accidents in London. Our analysis shows that using'm' = 0.5 yields satisfactory results, making parameter choice a bit more confined, although still a degree of freedom remains. Further study is suggested to incorporate additional information such as modelling the changing levels of extreme occurrence frequency over time. By incorporating time trends, the estimation process could become dependent on another factor, offering a degree of additional control over the estimation process. There's been a growing trend in the study of natural language understanding with a renewed focus on commonsense representation and reasoning in recent years. This renewed interest has led to the creation of new commonsense knowledge graphs that aim to provide a foundation for reasoning tasks. Despite these efforts, there's still no unified consensus on assessing and building these graphs, resulting in an array of disparate benchmarks and a lack of analysis of their underlying characteristics. This study aims to address these gaps by introducing a unified set of commonsense data sets, encompassing a range of language and graph-based formats, to facilitate a comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art models and assess their graph-based attributes. Our analysis reveals that these models often fail on certain dimensions of commonsense knowledge, with notable weaknesses observed in reasoning tasks involving multi-step processes, context-aware information, and data related to human lifestyles. What's more, we find that these models demonstrate equality biases, with a notable disparity in their performance with respect to data sets representing diverse commonsense knowledge across different languages. Our research highlights the importance of further exploring these neglected areas of commonsense knowledge to facilitate more well-rounded understanding and mitigate potentially harmful implications for real-world applications. We introduce the data processing pipeline developed for the Hi-GAL survey. This critical component is an integral part of the Herschel satellite project that's mapping the Galactic plane's inner regions. Leveraging a combination of Herschel Interactive Standard Environment capabilities and new, custom-designed tools, our pipeline effectively handles data reduction tasks. These include accurate data filtering, noise assessment, and efficient map generation, which utilizes a highly modified ROMA algorithm previously validated on several key projects. This work extensively examines the properties of Hi-GAL Science Demonstration Phase data to ensure the reliability of our processed products. These products, along with the corresponding raw data, will be publicly available through the Hi-GAL Data Access Layer. Our analysis of the 65 $\nu$/$I_{100}$ flux density map shows a high degree of linearity, with a correlation coefficient greater than 0.99. The resulting maps have a root-mean-square noise of around 2 MJy/sr at 100 $\mu$m, along with an absolute uncertainty in the 130-500 $\mu$m flux densities of about 5% due to the data reduction process. This achievement represents a significant milestone in the data reduction history of the Hi-GAL survey. Our processed data will facilitate a precise comparison between observed and predicted spectral energy distributions, thereby improving the cataloging process. Ultimately, a vast collection of cataloged objects will be generated, encompassing sources like giant molecular clouds, HII regions, molecular outflows, and star-forming clouds among others. These catalogs will significantly enhance our understanding of the SFR (star formation rate) in the Galaxy and the associated properties of its molecular gas. Recent photometric studies of the first population stars within the galactic globular clusters revealed heterogeneity in metallicity, contrasted to the cluster's evolutionary status as red giants. This phenomenon suggests an internal star formation mechanism within the clusters. Our investigation involved an analysis of the interstellar lines of the brightest red giant stars within NGC 2808, focusing specifically on the iron content and specific magnetic hydrogen lines. Our analysis, conducted through high-resolution spectroscopy, explored whether multiple-star populations within NGC 2808 are defined by varying iron levels, and whether multiple stellar populations within the cluster are characterized by distinct iron content. Our results reveal multiple star populations within NGC 2808, designated as Blue Horizontal Branch (BHB) and Blue Straggler (BS), exhibiting a correlation between iron content and spatial distribution. BHB stars within NGC 2808 are found in the upper-right section (positive Fe and Delta Excess), whereas BS and BHB stars within the cluster are found throughout the middle section (negative Fe and Delta Excess). Our results also show that the mean iron content of BHB, BS, and Red Horizontal Branch (RHB) stars within NGC 2808 differs by 0.04, 0.04, and 0.10 magnitudes, respectively. We derive an analytical solution for the complete first exit time statistics of an overdamped single file with absorbing boundary conditions, after which we apply these findings to investigate the speed-accuracy relationship, examining how this property is influenced by the mean squared displacement and the entropic repulsive forces within the system. Subsequently, we modify the boundary conditions to investigate the single file character, while replicating the initial speed-accuracy relationship by adjusting the entropic repulsive forces. Finally, we outline the potential next steps in further exploring the properties of an overdamped single file, involving the incorporation of harmonic potentials. By taking this approach, we are able to elucidate the interplay between slow diffusion and entropic forces, thereby shedding light on the behavior of single file systems, especially at large time scales, with key implications for nanomechanical systems and their dynamics. Through our thorough analysis, we derived new insights into the properties of ideal overdamped single files, generated novel IPKZ diagrams, and developed a comprehensive understanding of the dynamics of slowly-moving particles, thereby contributing to the richer understanding of one-dimensional physical system behavior. We hope that the new concepts introduced will inspire experimental validation and highlight ongoing challenges, particularly the absence of a single file realization with boundary conditions, thereby guiding future research efforts to tackle these difficulties. We conclude by outlining the potential for the development of single file-based devices, highlighting the inherent single file character of Mott insulators, as well as the potential for the creation of optical traps utilizing the entropic force. Quantum Mechanics contradicts the universally accepted causal relationship equation, Bayes' rule. While it appears to hold for quantum systems, the conventional understanding is insufficient. We propose an improved formulation of Bayes' principle that adheres to the principles of Noether, while its classical equivalent is invalid. Bayes' operator, responsible for this transformation, is a quantum analog of projective measurement, enabling us to derive Markov chains and master equations associated with it. We demonstrate that it is possible to express quantum correlation time as a function of system size, albeit only under specific conditions. Additionally, it is shown that the improved Bayes' formula is applicable to causal observation of quantum systems at arbitrary scales. Therefore, it offers a potential solution to the consistency problem within quantum generalized Bayesian approaches and quantum decision theory. We utilize an optimal quantum clock to compare the performance of classical and quantum decision-making methods with increasing levels of risk and uncertainty. Quantum prediction methods based on the Feynman-Hellinger map or quantum relative entropy are more effective in such scenarios, surpassing a classical binary choice and outperforming a quantum binary decision method only when incompatibility reaches a certain critical threshold. We also explore potential applications of the improved Bayes' formula in causal quantum analysis of complex networks and the principle of total probability in quantum mechanics. Moreover, it is shown that entropy-like functions apply only to discrete quantum systems, whereas continuous ones require a modified definition. We establish a correspondence between causal quantum operators and quantum stochastic processes, including the diffusion of Schrödinger, Lévy, and teleportation. Furthermore, it is found that the improvement to Bayes' rule resolves the consistency problem within quantum generalized Bayesian approaches and quantum decision theory, and the use of causal quantum operators for decision-making yields higher returns when the options are partially transitive. Finally, it is shown that the improved Bayes' formula allows for the interpretation of Markov chains and master equations as causal operators in certain instances, and the model of optimal quantum clock accuracy matches the experimental precision of quantum interferometry, a result consistent with classical Cramér-Hermitian accuracy. The improved Bayes' formula's validity for quantum correlation time applies only if the improvement factor is finite. Under infinite correlation times, it is possible to derive causal quantum operators from the quantum consistency principle. We initially reported a method for reducing system size effects in theoretical physics, but it appears this method has been previously suggested by Strestnianski. We compared our original method to Strestnianski's method and found them to be equivalent. The confidence in our initial publication and the validation of the underlying theory prompted us to explore its application to various physical equations, including the hydrogen gas equation of state, the hydrogen gas spectrum, and the hydrogen gas viscosity, as well as the equation of state for helium gas and paraffin fluid. We also discovered that finite size corrections can provide additional insights not accounted for in low-order thermodynamic equations, such as viscosity. Building upon the NIST equation of state for hydrogen gas, we developed the H2* equation of state, and were able to match the experimental Helium-4 equation of state, while predicting that hydrogen gas will deviate from the ideal gas law at lower temperature and pressure values. Furthermore, the thermodynamic and transport properties calculations for hydrogen and helium gas revealed a new phenomenon, in which the finite size effect on the transport properties shows a non-monotonic relationship with temperature. Also, the paraffin fluid correlation found through its finite size effect on the viscosity helped accurately forecast the viscosity measurement gap for the Space Shuttle External Fuel System Liquid Hydrogen Pump. These applications demonstrate that the finite size effect theory is versatile and can be used in practical engineering projects. We made the NFIE code, which calculates the finite size effect on the thermophysical properties, available to the scientific community through an open-source project that can be accessed at https://bit.ly/fife-open-source. Additionally, the theoretical and experimental predictions for the finite size effect on the transport properties, especially for hydrogen, helium, paraffin, and air can be explored at the newly launched website: https://bit.ly/fife-predict. Moreover, the website hosts the newly developed theoretical hydrodynamic models for hydrogen, helium, paraffin, and air to calculate the flow instabilities that can occur when liquid fuels undergo thermal gradient in storage tanks, such as those for the Space Shuttle External Fuel System Liquid Hydrogen Pump. Lastly, the website features a hydrodynamic prediction for the gravity-driven flow in the storage tank, illustrating the potential to mitigate the occurrence of flow instabilities that can lead to liquid puddle formation. In summary, the finite size effect theory and its practical applications, including the newly developed theories and models, can be explored at the website mentioned above.

Astronomers observing far ultraviolet wavelengths from Earth's orbit have a major limitation in detecting continuous spectra from objects due to the blocking effects of air and Earth's surface in this spectral range. Since hydrogen atoms can absorb specific observed signals, researchers have long wanted a far ultraviolet absorption cell with controlled atomic composition to study absorption and gain a deeper understanding of observed signals from space. 

In our research, we have successfully developed such an absorption cell by filling it with hydrogen and measuring the cell's hydrogen density, which is crucial for reconstructing original spectra through division by the cell's absorption spectrum. 

In this study, the cell's design, the methods of measuring hydrogen density, and the procedures we followed are detailed out. Moreover, we have also determined that while the cell provides nearly 80% absorption at high hydrogen densities, its current composition is not uniform, which results in additional complex absorption features beyond those of pure hydrogen, thereby necessitating further improvement in cell design. 

Ultimately, by combining data from multiple cell orientations, and through careful examination of both the cell's absorption and the unabsorbed signal from the object, it is possible to nearly completely remove the cell's absorption, thereby allowing for accurate reconstruction of original far ultraviolet spectra from space. 

In theory, by employing this correction technique, it becomes feasible to detect objects with very low signal strengths, thereby broadening the scope of far ultraviolet astronomical research. 

In practice, however, several technical limitations, such as the difficulty of controlling atomic energy states and the lack of precision in measuring hydrogen density, restrict the accuracy of spectrum correction. 

In particular, it is found that the cell's absorption can barely be subtracted due to high levels of signal loss, and accordingly, accurate far ultraviolet spectral analysis of observed signals from space still requires considerable improvement in measurement precision, particularly calibrating the cell's absorption using death stars or other planetary objects, which is clearly highly unfeasible with current technology. 

In the future, advanced techniques such as the utilization of wavelet denoising can provide reliable spectrum correction despite limitations in precision, thereby paving the way for extensive research in far ultraviolet astronomical science. 

Wavelet denoising technique was also tested in subtracting the cell's absorption, and as a result, accurate far ultraviolet spectral analysis of observed signals from space remains limited mainly by technical problems, which can potentially be resolved with the development of advanced technologies.

Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from large databases comprise two main components: a neural network that converts an image into a transformation-resistant vector, and a high-performance data structure that quickly matches similar images. This paper addresses the challenge of optimizing the performance of these algorithms by generating a superior vector representation of each image, tailored to efficiently detect and retrieve similar images from massive databases. Traditional image representation learning techniques solely aim to minimize the distance between vectors of identical images or maximize the margin between vectors of different images, often resulting in poor performance when detecting and retrieving images across diverse databases. In contrast, we propose a method to learn an adaptive image representation that simultaneously enhances image copy detection and retrieval. This method employs a learning technique that incorporates a data structure and a different loss function to transform the input image. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated by the development of a retrieval system that surpasses the current state-of-the-art performance on image search benchmarks. The proposed method and its implementation as part of the Pytorch framework are available at https://github.com/Runting/image-search. Our work significantly advances the field of weakly-supervised image copy detection and retrieval, allowing the creation of efficient systems with minimal human input, where a single model can handle diverse database scenarios. The output image representation can also be used for other tasks beyond retrieval, including image compression and generation. The study further contributes to the field of neural activation utility, providing insights into the role of high-activated image regions in the context of image copy detection and retrieval. The work also introduces a high-performance data structure that indexes activated image regions, enabling the efficient location of relevant images and their applications. Ultimately, our approach offers promising avenues for the development of image-assistance technologies. The study further examines the relationship between human visual attention and neural network activation, highlighting their shared underlying mechanisms and the role of high-activated regions in image composition. The work also introduces a new theory explaining why deep neural networks achieve high levels of imaging performance, suggesting that activation can serve as a more direct and interpretable indicator of human visual attention and network learning than other existing models. The study suggests that different feature maps respond to the presence of diverse visual stimuli, and their activations blend to convey image semantic interpretation. The work further proposes a technique to visualize the image semantic interpretation conveyed by the different feature maps of the first fully-connected layer in CNNs, including those during the process of image recognition. The flat section in the dispersion evolution graph can be entirely attributed to the particles spreading according to their local mean velocities. Consequently, we reject the notion of a dispersionless transport regime in this context. The flat section does, however, confirm the existence of a dispersionless vortex state, which we discovered in numerical simulations without any previous theoretical anticipation. The width of the plateau is found to be proportional to the square of the particle's running speed and inversely proportional to the height of the potential barriers. The time frame of this relatively stable spread width is effectively capped by the Maxwell-Boltzmann relaxation time, but we noticed that its upper limit is actually the time it takes for the particles to reach their local mean velocities. The findings suggest that microscopic nonlinear diffusion rates could be predicted from higher-order approximations of the microscopic Fokker-Planck equation, which would be particularly useful in designing nanoscale devices with enhanced diffusion properties. The development of a phase space diffusion equation could offer further insights, potentially shedding light on the origin of the nonlinear diffusion phenomenon. The possibility of leveraging intrinsic noise to improve diffusion properties could open new avenues for the design and rectification of nanoscale devices using an innovative strategy that relies on the symbiotic relationship between Brownian motion and intrinsic noise. We investigate the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum on the angular momentum of a charge q moving in a uniform magnetic field. The orbital angular momentum generated is due to photons in the vacuum that emit an energy back to the charge in proportion to n^2, a greater increase than that of the -2n\hbar of a charge in a Landau level. This leads to an energy given by $-\frac{q^2 B^2 n^2}{\hbar} $ in an area of the order $\frac{1}{n^2}$ the vacuum contribution exceeds that from the charge's kinetic energy for n less than a certain value, $n_{eq}$. The $n_{eq}$ is the point at which the sum of the charge's kinetic and vacuum energies equals the absolute value of the charge's potential energy; $n_{eq}$ increases as the square of the size of the magnetic flux over $\hbar$; for a given magnetic field, $n_{eq}$ is a maximum possible integer. The primary goal of Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) is to accurately classify various entity types, often exceeding hundreds, by considering the context of each mention. However, the common approach to acquire supervised training data through distant supervision introduces label noise by assigning type labels without considering the context. In order to mitigate this noise, FG-NET research adopts a flat label framework where all mentions are labeled with a single type. As the existing datasets in FG-NET often exhibit a hierarchical label structure (e.g., person_name), we aim to model this label hierarchy in a hyperbolic space. Our study indicates that representing labels in a hyperbolic space leads to improved entity typing performance when compared to traditional Euclidean spaces. Furthermore, by adapting the learning objective to minimize the distance between label representations, we are able to effectively address the issue of noisy distant supervision labels. Our proposed approach yields superior results on the FG-NET datasets in 2020. The code used in this study is publicly available at: https://github.com/zwang20/hyperbolic-fgnet. Our research also includes an analysis of entity typing datasets where the label hierarchy is unclear and developing accurate FG-NET datasets where the label hierarchy is unclear. Our research also finds that FG-NET benefits from a learning-to-rank mechanism when combined with the hyperbolic space method. Our research further investigates the applicability of hyperbolic space in other FG-NET related tasks, including multi-task learning. In various real-world scenarios, factors like weather, traffic or fiscal policy, beyond the agents' control, can impact game dynamics. Often, the equilibrium observed doesn't align with the actual cost functions of the agents. This research proposes the use of Nash Fixed Point Networks, a new class of neural networks, capable of predicting game equilibria using context. N-FPN architecture integrates data-driven approaches with constraints related to available agent actions, making it more efficient for learning and prediction tasks. N-FPN models can also leverage a recent backpropagation method and utilize novel techniques for avoiding computationally costly operations. Experimental results illustrate N-FPN's effectiveness on both atomic and non-atomic games. To highlight N-FPN's advantages, learning curves and a comprehensive analysis of several non-atomic game benchmarks are presented. Furthermore, the framework is demonstrated on a complex large-scale game simulating football tournaments, showcasing N-FPN's ability to make policy recommendations using neural networks. These recommendations, taking into account game context, yield a lower cost of living for players compared to a scenario without context. All related code and models are available for public access. N-FPN also opens new avenues of research, and its potential applications extend to sectors affecting society, including those impacting public health. A proposed model using a unique approach to process these languages is presented, utilizing the GLOVE algorithm to convert word forms into dense vectors independent of context, thereby addressing the resource shortage. Additionally, the model incorporates character-based models to account for words that cannot be broken down, thereby improving its robustness and effectiveness. It has been demonstrated that the suggested model achieves the best results on recently gathered datasets for four Indian languages and outperforms a contextual language model on a related task in a third tested language. Furthermore, the research includes an exploration of factor impacting summarization model performance, which highlights the resource shortages as a significant factor and suggests potential solutions. As an open-source contribution, the model is shared with the research community to facilitate further study and evaluation. Recently, Variation Autoencoders have emerged as a preferred choice for unsupervised learning of intricate probability distributions. Compared to traditional autoencoders, VAEs exhibit enhanced reconstructive capabilities, making more accurate approximations possible even in the presence of noise, as opposed to Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. By utilizing a hierarchical series of probabilistic layers, VAEs formulate a generative process that involves ancestral sampling, thus serving as directed graphical models. Training a VAE entails optimizing the variational minimum description length objective, which strikes a balance between reconstructing observations and capturing the data-generating distribution in an approximate sense. Our objective is to employ this framework for learning the underlying statistical structure of a continuous dynamical system from time series observations, focusing on a version of the Lotka-Volterra dynamics. By combining this system with random noise, we create a model that resembles observations from the dynamical system, allowing us to capture its approximate, continuous characteristics in a probabilistic sense. Our results indicate that the learned models can accurately predict future time series segments, both in terms of the generated samples and the predicted future segments. Furthermore, the approximate posterior distribution of the hidden state variables, learned during the training process, enables us to accurately assess uncertainty in the state variables, a capability that is showcased in our analysis. As a directed model, the VAE generates observations by ancestral sampling, thus allowing us to analyze the influence of specific variables on the posterior distribution of the hidden state variables. By investigating the scenarios in which the variables become irrelevant, as indicated by the uncertainty in the posterior distribution, we can pinpoint the time intervals at which the model fails to account for the data. By identifying the variables with high posterior probabilities, as indicated by the uncertainty in the posterior distribution, we can pinpoint the time intervals at which the model is most effective, a capability that is shown to correlate with the data-driven insights from the scalar indicator of variability. The model's capability to predict future time series segments, both in terms of the generated samples and the predicted future segments, is evaluated in the context of the data-driven insights from the scalar indicator of variability, thus showing a positive correlation. A novel approach to quantizing log-likelihood ratio storage utilizing deep learning is presented. It was discovered that average L-values from the SoftFEC project could be effectively represented using a 5-bit scalar or 6-bit vector scheme, resulting in a significant 30% reduction in memory usage compared to earlier work. To achieve this, two custom quantization techniques were developed: the Iterative Log-Linear (ILL) method, optimized through deep learning, and the Direct Linear (DL) method, also optimized through deep learning. Notably, while the ILL method allows for high-quality L-value quantization across the entire probability range, the DL method excels within specific, yet frequently occurring, communication scenarios. Both quantizers were also applied to capture spatial logic variable dependencies, leading to further performance gains. Employing these quantizers, a deep neural network (DNN) was trained to reconstruct unordered logic bit vectors from the quantized L-values. The DNN was designed to operate in parallel with the quantizers, at the storage node or at the edge of the network, in both cases concurrently computing the message packet. To evaluate its performance, the DNN was tested using 128,000 stored L-value vectors from the SoftFEC project, quantized using the proposed schemes, and assessed using the Bit-Flipping Ratio (BFR) metric. By combining the DL method with the DNN, it was possible to achieve a 98.97% bit accuracy with only 6 bits per vector memory usage. Conversely, the ILL method required 5 bits per vector memory usage and resulted in a bit accuracy of 98.63%. To validate the DNN's potential in real-world communications, its performance was evaluated using 128,000 L-value vectors from various, commonly employed modulation schemes, including QAM-16, QPSK, 16-QAM, 64-QAM, and QAM-256. Notably, the DNN exhibited a bit accuracy of 98.64% using the ILL method and a bit accuracy of 98.40% using the DL method. Both quantizers demonstrated consistent performance across the tested modulation schemes. Consequently, the proposed deep learning-based quantization scheme allows for high-quality L-value quantization, resulting in a significant reduction in memory usage while facilitating reliable logic bit reconstruction from the quantized values. This innovation has the potential to significantly enhance the efficiency of wireless communication systems equipped with memory storage capabilities. This not only simplifies but also strengthens and generalizes previous findings, including those for full-bracket average methods, hyperbolic systems, and $C^r$ dynamical systems. Furthermore, the proof can be adapted to handle partially expanding systems and linearization methods. We obtain similar results for the $L^p$ norm in place of the H\"older norm. This paper examines a unique category of nonlocal games, denoted by $(G,\psi)$, in which two players engage in a one-round game using bipartite states independent of the game itself. We concentrate on a specific case when this state is highly entangled, specifically, a noisy version of the maximally entangled $|Phi_0^{(d)}(p)$, derived from the Schrödinger representation, and investigate the most efficient strategy for the first player to employ. Our analysis yields two main findings. Firstly, a strict limit is established on the probability that the first player can achieve an advantage over the best local outcome through access to these highly entangled states, and this limit diminishes rapidly as the states become even more pure. Secondly, a strict limit is established on the most optimistic outcome of the first player, and this limit decreases rapidly as the states become even more pure. As a consequence of these findings, the exact capacity of quantum channels is precisely determined in cases where the channel sends noisy maximally entangled states to local states. We also outline the general methodology to determine the exact capacity of any quantum channel. Furthermore, the analytical method we've introduced holds promise for analyzing complex optimization problems beyond capacity theory for quantum channels. We demonstrate its applicability to solving a wide range of optimization challenges within combinatorial games. In particular, the method provides a precise limit on the most optimistic outcome of the first player in a wide range of games, and this limit increases rapidly as the states become even less pure. We also outline potential future applications to other areas within quantum computing. -- Established researchers in the relevant fields of quantum computing may leverage the theoretical framework developed here to contribute meaningfully to optimization problems beyond capacity theory for quantum channels. Recent research includes precise calculations of the influence of viscosity on photon emission in these collisions, taking place at RHIC and LHC. Thermal photons exhibit anisotropic movement patterns known as v_n coefficients, which are calculated considering and excluding viscosity effects. Surprisingly, the viscosity effects significantly impact these coefficients, more so than viscosity effects in hydrodynamic flow anisotropies, with variations persisting after suppression due to differences in elasticity and medium opacity. This phenomenon is attributed to the viscosity effects disrupting photon emission in a manner consistent with photonic processes in isotropic systems, thereby reducing the significance of initial anisotropic movement patterns, whereas hydro dynamics minimizes this difference by promoting isotropic movement. If the hypothesis test is declared significant at an interim assessment, the experiment can be concluded immediately, and the confidence intervals will be marked with a validity indicator to reflect any potential bias in estimating ATE. Software developers who perform maintenance tasks encounter multiple change requests 
submitted by software system users, presenting the difficulty of choosing suitable 
search terms for concept location during maintenance activities. A proposed technique 
QUICKAR leverages the knowledge from change requests to guide software search, 
utilizing text analysis and natural language processing to identify relevant information 
in each request without requiring domain knowledge. Implemented in an IDE plugin, 
the effectiveness of QUICKAR has been demonstrated in comparison to typical search 
methods applied by software developers, resulting in the discovery of 19% more 
relevant results on average. Evaluations also included a simulation of developer 
practice, reinforcing QUICKAR's benefits in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, 
theoretical analyses validated QUICKAR's average performance in conjunction with 
existing search methods. Based on these outcomes, we believe that QUICKAR may 
enhance the efficiency of software maintenance activities. 

A companion video detailing the implementation and evaluation of QUICKAR can be 
accessed at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jss.2022.113.106.

Adaptive synchronization in interactions, or entrainment, involves the participants in a conversation adapting or matching each other's distinctive vocal traits. To better grasp how people adapt to each other's communication style during conversations, it's necessary to analyze various acoustic characteristics and compare them through multiple measurement techniques. This work introduces a novel turn-level metric, referred to as the Neural Entrainment Envelope, developed using a deep autoencoder model that identifies patterns unique to each speaker in a pair. Experimenting with over 800 conversational dialogues between trained individuals, we found significant evidence supporting the hypothesis that communication style plays a crucial role in entrainment, revealing a significant increase in the selection of words that are characteristic of the other speaker as the level of entrainment grows. Furthermore, we found that entrainment can be predicted with high accuracy based on the alignment of acoustic traits at the turn level. These findings confirm the role of communication style in the entrainment process and suggest that predicting how much two individuals will synchronize in a conversation is feasible by analyzing their speaking patterns at the turn level. Finally, we compare our proposed metric with other conventional methods for measuring entrainment and discuss the implications of our findings. This research marks a significant breakthrough in understanding how communication style influences the entrainment process through deep acoustic feature analysis, providing a fresh perspective in this field. It also showcases the advantages of using a two-step structure of pre-trained CNNs and autoencoders in measuring acoustic similarity. To facilitate future research, we are releasing our code and data open-source. At the time of our study, the 13DB dataset was the largest available dataset for entrainment analysis; subsequently, a new dataset has been developed, known as the EASIE dataset, and we plan to replicate our work using this larger dataset to verify the findings and ensure their generalizability. Prior to our study, the most prominent approach for measuring entrainment involved comparing the similarity of speech segments from the BCIHC dataset as described in the work by Boldencourt et al. [2000]; however, this technique compares the similarity of the entire speech at once. In contrast, we develop a novel approach for measuring entrainment based on the similarity of the structure in the turn-level as well as the deep acoustic features in the spectrogram. An inquiry-based method, utilized in various scientific fields, has proven effective in teaching. Nevertheless, this approach has yet to be widely adopted in software testing education. We developed a testing tool called Inquiria, which makes possible for students to learn the axiomatic testing theory by solving inquiry-based exercises. Inquiria's exercise database comprises over 400 open-ended problems, accompanied by simple program examples, designed to promote critical thinking, abstraction, and technical creativity. Domain adaptation has been applied extensively to handle distribution shifts across various fields like vision, language, and multimedia. Most existing domain adaptation techniques leverage domain-invariant features by utilizing both source and target domain data. However, when source data is inaccessible due to privacy concerns, this strategy becomes impractical. To resolve this issue, we propose a novel method that adapts source models via hypothesis transfer without requiring access to source data. This approach involves a semi-supervised learning technique that iteratively utilizes entropy minimization and augmented data to create tight Gaussian mixtures in the target feature space. As the source model converges, domain confusion increases, resulting in more accurate target predictions. Experimental results on multiple public datasets demonstrate that our method yields significant improvements of up to 19.9% compared to state-of-the-art alternatives. Additionally, our method showcases a desirable trait of semi-supervised mutual enhancement – adaptative performance can be either fully parameter-free or feature. To facilitate widespread use, the proposed method has been implemented as a highly efficient and self-contained Python library compatible with the Adas framework, allowing users to be trained on diverse deep learning architectures. This includes support for popular models like ResNet, Vision Transformer, and Mixup. Further implementation details are documented on the repository's GitHub page. The repository's address is https://github.com/nina-ai/semisup_domain_adaptation. A comprehensive analysis of nuclear power systems designed for Deep Space transport is presented, utilizing a cutting-edge Gas Core Reactor (GCR) integrated with a magnetohydrodynamic generator. A novel GCR design with enhanced characteristics compared to existing models is proposed and validated, capable of generating 200 MW of electricity within a 200 ton system. This GCR consists of a spherical cavity within a molybdenum-92 enclosure surrounded by a 50 cm thick liquid beryllium reflector, utilizing a fuel mixture of Xe, C, and LiAlH4, and a heat transfer medium of Kr, embedded in a porous graphite structure. Thermal calculations reveal 200 MW of fission heat output, and a 75% efficiency power conversion results in a significant output of 150 MW. This system is proposed for the Russian Space Nuclear Power Initiative, aiming to improve space power systems with reduced mass and enhanced safety. A space-specific safety assessment of the proposed GCR is conducted, incorporating the unique safety considerations for Deep Space applications. Based on the analysis, it is concluded that enhanced GCR designs with improved safety characteristics can be developed and may alleviate some space-specific safety concerns. Thus, it is suggested that further space-specific safety assessments of Gas Core Reactor designs be conducted to facilitate the development of reliable and safe nuclear power systems for Deep Space applications. These discussions are limited to space nuclear power systems, but the arguments may be extended to other space-specific nuclear safety concerns. Furthermore, an economic assessment of the proposed GCR is conducted, and the results indicate that the cost effectiveness of the proposed GCR is comparable to existing space nuclear power systems. This study demonstrates that the radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTG) mass efficiency model can be reproduced with the proposed GCR, RTGs being primarily fueled with alpha -emitting radioactive isotopes, the GCR being fueled with 238U, the proposed GCR being capable of generating 5.96 times more electricity per fuel mass than a typical RTG. Consequently, the study offers a mass efficiency comparison model for radioisotope power systems. Lastly, some future perspectives for further development of the proposed GCR are outlined, a comprehensive listing of the proposed GCR performance parameters, system design, and thermal characteristics is provided. This study presents a novel neural network architecture for particle physics research that leverages localization in time-of-flight and double-sided area detectors. Utilizing particle interaction patterns, the proposed Domain-informed Neural Network (DiNN) model offers a more efficient alternative to traditional multilayer perceptron (MLP) methods. A comparative assessment of DiNN and MLP is conducted through simulated analyses of synthetic data generated from standard analysis procedures. The results demonstrate the superiority of DiNN over MLP in terms of analysis efficiency, while DiNN's domain-specific output also serves as a valuable full analysis model prior for high-level physics interpretations. To validate this, we employ a transfer learning approach from a trained DiNN model to a physics-based generator network, resulting in significant improvements in the reconstruction of physics features. Ultimately, the concept of transfer learning on domain-aware neural networks may have far-reaching implications for the extraction of complex scientific features from data. Additionally, this methodology may be adapted and applied to multiple experimental particle physics research facilities, such as various versions of LHCb and future experiments like PANDA and ALICE. Code implementations for the DiNN model can be accessed through the following link: https://github.com/lhcbsu-dienn/Domain-informed-Neural-Network. Simulation data and additional model-related resources are available upon request at contact@lhcbsu-dienn.org.

The development of models for stellar, substellar, and planetary atmospheres heavily relies on accurate input data, specifically opacities, but various discrepancies often occur due to outdated or incomplete information about atomic and molecular interactions. In an attempt to bridge this gap, we compiled a comprehensive database of pre-calculated absorption coefficients for crucial atmospheric molecules such as MgH, SiO, TiO, and H2O, spanning a wide range of wavelengths, pressures, and temperatures. These calculations yield notable improvements in the spectral characteristics of Earth-like and super-Earth planets as well as hot Jupiters, specifically in terms of reflected light and atmospheric escape characteristics. Furthermore, we analyzed the influence of line list accuracy on the spectral properties of M stars, discovering significant line list adjustments are necessary to align our model predictions with observed spectral features. The incorporation of our revised data is anticipated to enhance the precision of transit, eclipse, and atmospheric-scale models for various types of celestial bodies. This test is based on the distribution of the first several eigenvalues of the covariance matrix, allowing us to create confidence intervals for each possible number of stochastic trends. This research examines the impact of disorder on the correlation between bulk and boundaries in two-dimensional topological insulators of higher order. We explore two specific scenarios: one focusing on the relationship between bulk and corner states, and the other examining edge and corner correlations. We establish the existence of mobility gaps for bulk-corner correspondence and clarify the topological properties defining these gaps. Interestingly, corner states prove to be resilient to disorder due to their protection by exceptional points. Conversely, corner states stemming from disorder-induced flat bands lack this protection. We also identify mobility gaps for edge-corner correspondence and prove that while disorder cannot eliminate corner states, it can eradicate bulk states within mobility gaps. Moreover, we demonstrate the presence of flat bands guarantees the persistence of boundary states, and importantly, the mobility gaps for edge-corner correspondence can be eliminated when the system transitions from a topological insulator to a topological phase transition. This research provides a clear understanding and clarifies the impact of disorder on the boundary modes of higher-order topological insulators. Furthermore, we propose a proposal for detecting a mobility gap through measurement of a Aharonov-Bohm oscillation's period. The period is shown to be proportional to the system's area, offering experimental validation of our conclusions. The mobility of bulk-corner correspondence is amenable to verification via measurements of bulk resistance, Hall resistance, and their temperature dependencies. We suggest an experiment utilizing graphene-based 2D topological insulators to investigate the bulk-corner correspondence. The distinct disorder-insensitivity of corner states is easily verifiable through capacitance measurements. The existence of a mobility gap can be confirmed through Hall coefficient measurements as a function of temperature. We highlight the perspectives and the crucial questions surrounding higher-order topological insulators, and outline future research directions to explore and study these fascinating topological systems. The unique corner states protected by exceptional points have potential applications in nanoelectromechanical systems and other fields. The concept of a mobility gap offers a quantitative measure of bulk-boundary correspondence and can facilitate the efficient design of topological insulators. The flat bands play a pivotal role in numerous important materials and systems, and understanding the impact of disorder on bulk states in mobility gaps may facilitate predictions and analyses of real materials. The persistence of boundary states in disordered higher-order topological insulators highlights their robustness and great potential for applications. The transition from a topological insulator to a topological phase transition can be investigated through measurements of Hall resistance, and the sensitivity of bulk states to disorder offers avenues for explorations. In contrast, geometric model-based approaches can leverage sparse data and provide robustness against occlusions, but these geometric representations may fail to capture patterns such as texture patterns or lighting effects. This research introduces a new model leveraging the four-dimensional light field representation of $E(\omega_{x,t})$ to effectively capture view-dependent phenomena. It specifically employs a convolutional encoder operating on the four-dimensional representation $E(\omega_{x,t})$ to capture 2D and 2D+time patterns, and uses a latent code derived from a set of provided reference images to encode low-frequency geometry and high-frequency details. To address the challenge of dealing with moving objects, latent style codes for each reference image are learned that isolate pattern shifts due to object motion. By optimizing these latent codes, the latent style codes can be predicted for unseen views, enabling accurate novel view synthesis, especially in scenarios with moving objects. Extensive evaluations on benchmark datasets indicate the proposed approach outperforms prior methods, specifically notable for view-based rendering with moving objects. A recent competition, the 2021 Image Similarity Challenge, introduced a benchmark dataset to evaluate state-of-the-art image copy detection methods. With over 200 participants involved, the winning entries are subjected to both qualitative and quantitative analysis in this paper. Key findings indicate that the most challenging transformations for the participating algorithms are extreme cropping of images, incorporation into unrelated content, combined with pixel-level disturbances. Notably, the winning approaches employed training with robustly augmented data, self-supervised learning methods, score normalization techniques, explicit identification of overlays, and pair-wise image comparison utilizing global descriptors. With regard to the performance metrics, the winning entries exhibit notable success in the pre-trained configuration, albeit with room for improvement in developing more robust methods to handle image alterations. Additionally, the results show that the conventional detection pipeline outperforms recent self-supervised methods and further analysis is needed to fully assess the latter's effectiveness in the image copy detection domain. With analysis complete, the paper presents relevant observations, drawing actionable guidance for future research, and providing an implementation framework that enables the reproduction of the results using widely applied deep learning models. The dataset used in this work can be accessed at https://www.imagelab.uwy.se/imagedetection/challenge/. Our implementation code can be found at https://github.com/AndreasKahler/ImageChallenge2021. Finally, a related video providing an in-depth explanation of the results can be accessed at https://www.youtube.com/watched. Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a critical concern in the distributed training process. To address this gap, we have created an innovative approach that reconciles the scalability of communication and data privacy during federated training. To achieve this, we integrated the Sparse Federation technique, which reduces communication overhead, alongside the FedBoost framework, which enhances privacy. However, the initial combination of these techniques resulted in reduced convergence rates due to incomplete gradient updates. To overcome this challenge, we employed a strategy where the client computes variance estimates using aggregated gradients while bypassing the FedBoost computation phase to accumulate a full batch of gradients. To enhance privacy, we introduced differential privacy and found that it enhances the convergence rate while maintaining the benefits of sparse communication. Our experiments demonstrate superior performance over previous methods in various settings, achieving up to 32x faster convergence for a specific benchmark with the same level of accuracy, as well as better results for a specific application with improved accuracy and reduced training time. This work delves into the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory, introduced by Lin and Palfrey (2022), within the context of multi-stage incomplete information games. In such scenarios, players simultaneously uncover peers' relevant characteristics and problem-solving abilities as the game unfolds. The study provides the first comprehensive characterization of the dynamic CH solution for two-person games with correlated uncertainty and reveals that policies from high-level cognitive types exhibit a "partially observable link" property. Building on this finding, the study also defines the dynamic CH solution for games between groups, extending existing results that typically restrict problem-solving abilities to binary choices. The study also demonstrates that, in games with correlated uncertainty, the dynamic CH solution differs significantly from the linear demand solution. Furthermore, the study shows that policies from high-level cognitive types can be accurately represented by a polynomial-sized mixed-integer program. The study also introduces a novel algorithm, originally designed for the single-stage CH problem, to generate dynamic CH equilibrium values through a novel procedure, originally designed for the single-stage CH problem. The study's findings further reveal that, in games with uncertain uncertainty, the dynamic CH equilibrium values exhibit a doubly-continuous nature. The study's numerical results indicate that both the dynamic CH policy link property and the dynamic CH equilibrium values can be effectively approximated with reasonable computational efficiency. The study's findings are illustrated using two-person linear demand games, where the dynamic CH policy link property is shown in scenarios with varying problem-solving abilities. The study's findings also show that the dynamic CH theory can be effectively applied in games with renegotation options, where the dynamic CH equilibrium values can be effectively approximated through various approaches. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, which combine multiple sub-models to determine the output, have become an essential component of most machine learning applications, particularly in neural networks and statistical analysis. Nevertheless, training these models poses significant difficulties due to the unsatisfactory local minima of conventional algorithms and inadequate sampling methods. In our work, we introduce a novel generative adversarial network (GAN) technique for learning MoE parameters without relying on reparameterization techniques. By dividing the learning process into two hidden Markov chains that converge to a unique, stationary solution, our approach ensures the existence of at least one saddle point with optimal parameters, thus evading local minima. Moreover, our technique enables the extraction of a unique, dense posterior distribution over parameter spaces, which can be applied to diverse MoE structures. Our findings demonstrate that traditional algorithms fail to yield satisfactory results for MoE models, whereas our proposed GAN method achieves superior outcomes with reduced variability. Additionally, our technique successfully generalizes to challenging tasks, such as multi-modal data classification, speech synthesis, target detection, and neural architecture search. The source code for our method is publicly available on our GitHub repository. Experimental results indicate that our proposed GAN approach significantly outperforms conventional algorithms in learning MoE models. While quantum gravitational effects generally break global symmetries, their presence may hold significant value in understanding both particle physics and cosmology. Discovering well-maintained global symmetries could provide a valuable insight into the properties of gravity. A statistically significant detection of cosmic birefringence in the Cosmic Microwave Background may signify a previously undiscovered, though spontaneously broken, global symmetry in nature. A potential explanation for this phenomenon could be a very light, electromagnetically interacting pseudoscalar field, which must be protected from the effects of gravity. We demonstrate that a certain upper limit on the gravitational disruption of global symmetries would be required for this scenario to be feasible. Such a bound would have far-reaching implications, influencing the development of theories of quantum gravity as well as numerous models in particle physics. Moreover, our result is applicable to numerous other models involving light fields that may have significant cosmological roles, such as quintessence or dark matter. Although our focus is on global symmetries, our bound could also impact theories of time reversal violation, a topic with significant ramifications in particle physics. The development of more precise constraints on cosmic birefringence could substantially lower this bound, thereby broadening the scope of feasibility for quantum gravity models and particle physics theories. In particular, our findings open the possibility for electromagnetically interacting axions to be produced coherently in dark matter halos, a promising idea for future investigations. Lastly, our bound establishes a connection between phenomenology in gravity and particle physics that may be pursued in related research. Our research presents new findings based on far ultraviolet (FUV) detection of a globular cluster, NGC 4147. A comprehensive analysis using FUV, U-band, and U-band photometry revealed 185 potential binary stars within the cluster, comprising 135 previously undetected binary-stellar systems and existing binary star members, including 4 newly identified binary blue straggler members. Our analysis further indicates that the cluster's blue horizontal branch stars and blue straggler stars exhibit distinct nature, characterized by a difference in mass between the two groups. By examining the cluster's FUV brightness in relation to color, we identified a correlation affecting both blue and red giant regions, indicating the presence of a widespread mass-segregation pattern across the cluster. Based on FUV detection of F-stars, we estimated a mass-separation threshold of ~1.4 M_sun for blue straggler stars, whereas a broader range of masses exists for horizontal branch stars. Our analysis further suggests that a mass-separation occurs within the cluster's blue straggler population, assigning a theoretical origin to the variety of BSS properties found across GC members. The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to empower deep neural networks (DNNs) with the ability to draw from past experiences and adapt to unfamiliar tasks. This capability is especially vital in scenarios where task-specific data are scarce or recoverable at significant expense.  Despite extensive research on employing pre-trained DNNs as a starting point for additional tasks, the underlying factors contributing to their success remain poorly understood.  This study investigates the role of DNNs' architectural characteristics, including their depth and width, feature extractor homogeneity, and the influence of the training environment in terms of computational resources and data variability, among other factors, aiming to provide insights into their role in transferability.  We also examine the impact of adapting learning strategies, such as training data augmentation and batch normalization parameter freezing, to make predictions in unfamiliar environments.  Our research employs a combination of both quantitative and qualitative assessment strategies, including empirical studies involving image classification tasks. Our findings reveal that the transferability of pre-trained DNNs declines with an increase in architectural complexity, the complexity of the initial training environment, the homogeneity of the feature extractors, and the discrepancy between the initial and target learning settings.  We show that incorporating small, randomly initialized DNNs as a starting point can enhance transferability. Additionally, freezing the batch normalization layers during adaptation learning may also yield positive outcomes. We believe that our research contributes significant insights to the DTL domain. This knowledge can aid in the development of more effective policies to facilitate DTL applications in a variety of domains. The findings from this research are further substantiated through an interactive visualization of the outputs from a convolutional neural network, bridging the gap between the experimental findings and the qualitative assessments. nonlinear interference points can be analyzed using a normal distribution. We analyze several

Service-oriented computing utilizes services as building blocks for constructing distributed systems. Traditionally, orchestrating cloud-based services centered around business process execution, particularly with BPEL's focus on services as processes. However, recent shifts towards alternative service representations based on mathematical functions have led to a shift in perspective. This shift has led to a notion of services as adaptable, exchangeable functions, particularly with the concept of cloud functions in BigFlow. This chapter explores this representation, identifying both advantages and limitations, and considers its implications for process orchestration, organizing distributed functionality, and defining service composition methods. Furthermore, we reflect on the potential effects of adopting functions as the basic service unit on service-oriented computing paradigms and tools, evaluating aspects such as service abstraction, reuse, composition, execution, deployment, management, and risks. crucially, we analyze how this service representation influences key risks, defining, and dividing them into hazards and opportunities. Ultimately, we provide an outlook on the role of service representations, suggesting that different applications may require different service paradigms, and highlight the need for expertise in service-oriented computing to curate these representations, ultimately paving the way for services as a prominent application development and deployment paradigm. Our analysis reveals that the conditions generating the Thakurta metric, previously investigated in a study by Böhm et al., involve a single black hole feeding on non-interacting isotropic dust throughout the entire universe. This leads to a realization that the processes driving black hole growth are connected to universal properties rather than localized occurrences. Moreover, radiation, primordial black holes, and dark matter cannot provide the required energy to sustain Thakurta black hole growth, and such a solution cannot be applied to binary black hole systems. Ultimately, we conclude that the Thakurta metric does not accurately represent the growth of cosmic black holes, and, therefore, existing restrictions on primordial black hole abundance derived from LIGO-Virgo and CMB data remain relevant. Lastly, we note that a thorough examination of black hole properties across various cosmic contexts is long overdue from a cosmological perspective. Extremely large, overparameterized models have achieved impressive success. In this research, we investigate whether the requirement for massive models might be partly attributed to computational limitations inherent to the learner itself. We also examine whether these constraints are exacerbated under robust learning conditions. Our paper achieves two significant outcomes: 1) we formally prove that learners bounded by specific computational resources are compelled to employ highly complex models when performing certain learning tasks; 2) our study of robust learning reveals that these bounds increase exponentially with the level of robustness, even for learners restricted by simple computational resources. We also relate our results to empirical observations on overparameterization in learning. Our work contributes to a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between computational constraints and the necessity of overly large models in learning theory. Our research also sheds light on the computational complexities inherent to robust learning problems. We utilize tools from cone-overlapping algorithms, computational circuit structures, and Sanov's theorem to derive analytical evidence for the inherent difficulties of robust learning. Our paper further investigates these complexities by generalizing commonly applied techniques in robust learning into the framework of circuit learning and proving that these methods may incur an exponential increase in computational cost for certain tasks. We also provide lower bounds for computational efficiency in robust learning under specific constraints, which complement our general bounds, thereby establishing strict limits on the performance and efficiency of robust learning algorithms. Our study into the structural mechanisms behind overparameterization in learning sheds new light on the general practice of using extremely large models, which we consider as a necessary evil due to the strict limitations imposed by the learner's computational capabilities. Our research also contributes to an improved understanding of the trade-off between the complexity of these models and the level of robustness required for learning tasks. Our paper further explores the duality between the constraints on learner computational resources and the amount of data required to achieve robust learning goals. Our study also reveals the presence of inherent trade-offs between robustness, data requirements, and learner complexity under various computational resource limits. Our results also provide insights into the limitations of adaptive methods in robust learning and the inherent risks of divergence when learners employ complex models that beyond a certain limit begin to exhibit unstable behavior. Our research also identifies avenues for future advancements along these three dimensions, thereby offering a framework to quantify and explore their relationships. Our paper further derives analytical evidence for the exclusivity of robust learning algorithms using circuit learning structures, which generalizes commonly applied techniques into the framework of circuit learning and provides strict limits on their performance and efficiency. - The Bohr set's radius is at a minimum of $\delta |H|$,
- Each translated image of $H$ can be expressed as a combination of integers from different prime factors.

This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings where residents have multiple transportation options at their disposal. To remain competitive, ridepooling services must balance high pool participation rates against minimizing detours for users. We propose a Branch-and-Cut algorithm to tackle this challenge, leveraging insights from established route paths to identify and exclude non-viable solutions, thus enhancing lower-bound estimates for arrival times. Additionally, this technique allows us to introduce new valid inequalities that accelerate solution finding. We conducted an extensive analysis involving up to 120 customers and 20 vehicles, incorporating pre- and post-routing improvements to ensure lower bounds are not exceeded. The results show that our method consistently outperforms a conventional mixed-integer programming model, significantly reducing solution times in the process. Specifically, we observed an eightfold improvement in obtaining optimal solutions and a twentyfold improvement in obtaining lower bounds when infeasibility applies. Furthermore, we observed that our method is highly effective even when forced detours occur, thus demonstrating its potential for significant cost savings. We estimate that our method can yield annual savings of up to 2.64 euros per user, with similar reductions likely in other major cities. In terms of scalability, our results suggest that our method is capable of handling systems with up to 500 customers and 50 vehicles, although solution times are expected to rise exponentially beyond this threshold. To further optimize performance, we outline promising research avenues for integrating artificial intelligence into the process, thus paving the way for the widespread adoption of ridepooling services in urban settings. Elaborating on this concept, we introduce a learning system that anticipates optimal matching strategies based on given criteria. Using a supervised learning approach, we train neural networks to replicate specific linear programming-based matches and demonstrate their efficacy in replicating the behavior of state-of-the-art solvers. Moreover, we show that incorporating this method using a gradient boosting technique achieves an accuracy rate of 85% that of a highly specialized solver, with results obtained within a 100 ms time frame. As such, we believe that this technology is poised for seamless integration into ridepooling services. In practice, we simulate its performance over a large synthetic dataset and compute total travel times equivalent to a 2.64 euros annual savings per user. According to our estimates, this technology is within reach based on current advancements in deep learning and cyber infrastructure. Finally, we outline a framework for regularly monitoring and comparing compensation policies in urban transportation systems, thus providing a framework for regular assessment and improvement.
