This study explores multi-modal pretraining techniques for product data in E-commerce, addressing limitations in current methods which struggle with modality-noise and modality-missing. We present LST-Modality, an innovative pretraining approach incorporating a potential completion space to tackle these issues. This novel method leverages a latent space to identify missing modalities and employs a second latent space to integrate modalities, utilizing a contrastive learning strategy. Furthermore, we introduce a novel modality that utilizes product indices instead of traditional image and text, enhancing learning capacity and efficacy. The word-level contrastive learning is replaced with a novel instance-level contrastive learning, resulting in the proposed LST-Modality framework. Experimental evaluations confirm its superior performance on visual product reconstruction and cross-modal retrieval tasks. The framework's source code and pre-trained models are made available for future reference. The research suggests that leveraging statistical potential surfaces can improve learning effectiveness, and provides insights on utilizing statistical distributions as an alternative to probabilistic augmentation for completing modalities. The proposed concept of potential space opens up new avenues for exploring latent geometric structures. The index modality introduces a novel paradigm for utilizing structural information across various domains. The research demonstrates that utilizing instance-level contrastive learning yields enhanced efficacy and efficiency. The experiments indicate a notable increase in model generalizability when utilizing the potential space over traditional methods of augmentation. Importantly, the research highlights the LST-Modality framework's potential for utilization across E-commerce applications. The research and implementation aim to inspire advancements in visual product reconstruction and cross-modal retrieval, and provides useful lessons for researchers working in related fields. The pre-trained models will be made available online. A recent deep learning method called Deep InfoMax (DIM) allows an unsupervised extraction of long-term brain image sequences. Based on this approach, we are analyzing the evolution of a brain region typically linked to epilepsy in a large group of patients over many years. As some patients may experience epilepsy symptoms for many years, we are exploring whether there's a noticeable change in the brain area over time and whether there's a correlation with symptoms. Using data from the Mesial Temporal Sclerosis (MTS) cohort, we analyzed recaptured brain MRI scans of 222 patients taken an average of 7 years apart using a modified version of the DIM approach. Each patient's brain sequence was compared to a control group, and we quantified the difference using a statistical metric, correcting for anatomical variations. We found a noticeable and significant difference in the brain sequence development in patients who experienced more symptoms than those who experienced fewer or no symptoms, based on annual evaluations of their condition. This distinction became more pronounced over time, correlating with clinical findings. This research shows that using the DIM approach on long-term MRI sequences could help diagnose patients with temporal lobe epilepsy who may develop into refractory status. Furthermore, we propose utilizing the method to predict epilepsy outcome based on brain sequence development over time. Finally, we suggest combining the method with a supervised model to improve the detection of significant changes in the mesial temporal lobe. The findings and code have been made publicly available.

An analysis of local interactions reveals an enhancement of spin-orbit coupling in the paramagnetic phase when electron-electron interactions intensify. Increasing interactions below the antiferromagnetic critical value also yields increased spin-orbit coupling in the antiferromagnetic phase, however with diminishing gains. Furthermore, we investigate how spin-orbit coupling affects the magnetic phase diagram, discovering that high spin-orbit coupling yields a gain in stability for the antiferromagnetic phase and an increase in the Néel temperature. An orbital analysis of the self-energy shows that the electron dynamics are concentrated in the x-y orbitals during all stages, while under strong electron-electron interactions within the antiferromagnetic phase, the electron dynamics shift to the diagonal orbital, indicating reduced inter-orbital transfer with increasing interactions. An investigation of the electron pair shows that the electron pair breaks apart under the influence of spin-orbit coupling in the paramagnetic phase, whereas in the antiferromagnetic phase, the electron pair remains intact, yet the electron dynamics in the x-y orbitals indicate a broken pair with diminishing gains. Consistent with these findings, the electron pair remains detached from the lattice, as indicated by the electron-pair wave function. In contrast to Weyl semimetals, the electron pair does not converge to a detuned state, as the electron binding energy to the lattice differs from the energy detuning. Therefore, the electron binding energy can be considered as a product of the orbital overlap and the electron-lattice coupling. Given the regulatory restrictions on medical software and the scarcity of comprehensive labeled medical datasets, our approach revolves around predicting a model's performance in an unfamiliar setting using its predicted outputs alone, without requiring any modifications to its training process or assumptions about its original data source. This "black-box" model assessment technique is based on conformal prediction and is being evaluated across various medical image datasets and distribution shift scenarios, such as changes in medical institution, imaging technology, or clinical settings. By promoting more effective evaluation methods for AI models, we hope to standardize clinical assessments, enhance AI system robustness and credibility, and foster the development of reliable medical tools. This research aims to reduce uncertainties surrounding AI model deployment, making medical AI a more reliable tool for both medical professionals and patients. Given its versatility, our method can be readily applied to other domains, such as consumer electronics, with the potential to enhance trust in AI systems across multiple fields. The Asymmetric Numeral System (ANS) was developed as a entropy coding method using a custom encoding engine derived from the finite state transducer, originally producing a redundancy of 0.5 bit per symbol with a high probability of representation. This paper explores improvements to the ANS encoder by addressing limitations in its initialization process, which contributes to the overall redundancy. A modified encoder is proposed and its efficiency assessed using a combination of theoretical and empirical analysis, indicating a significant decrease in redundancy of 0.125 bits per symbol, resulting in a minimal rate of 0.375 bits per symbol. This modified encoder is viewed as a refined version of the table-based ANS encoder and is proven to be equivalent in terms of representation quality. Comprehensive experimental analysis further confirms the improved efficiency of the modified encoder, showcasing its ability to achieve representations of near-optimal length on a wide range of random input datasets. In contrast to the original ANS encoder, the proposed scheme offers versatility in initialization values, thus facilitating the development of ANS representations of minimal length. In addition, the paper investigates various table sizes for the ANS encoder, illustrating how different sizes impact representations, while empirical results demonstrate the potential benefits of using multiple representations to improve compression performance on random datasets. Ultimately, the modified encoder poses an intriguing research question: Can the redundancy of the ANS encoder be made arbitrarily small, thus facilitating efficient compression schemes? This fundamental question is shown to have far-reaching implications in the fields of information theory, physics, and engineering. The proposed research framework is versatile, allowing it to be applied to various areas, such as the encoding of both large datasets and single large numbers. Interestingly, the modified encoder can also be utilized as a tool for the initialization of itself, resulting in a near-optimal length with high probability, thus providing insights into its general efficiency, while empirical results reveal the potential to achieve zero redundancy of measurement, thus appearing as a promising research challenge. In the realm of practical applications, the modified encoder can be used to achieve a near-optimal length with high probability, thus offering on-line compression capabilities, which are particularly valuable in fields such as robotics, wireless sensor systems, and data analysis. The proposed scheme allows for the compression of datasets of arbitrary size, while achieving a redundancy of 0.375 bits per symbol, which appears to be the minimal achievable redundancy for the ANS encoder. The modified encoder can also be utilized to efficiently compress graphs, which represent complex data structures consisting of interconnected elements, while achieving a near-optimal length with high probability,

When performing cosmological inferences based on the Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions, standard analyses usually only consider a specific feature related to baryon acoustic oscillations. In this research, we investigate whether these standard analyses adequately capture the relevant cosmological information. To address this, we directly fit multiple elements of the two- and three-dimensional Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions, in addition to BAO signals, to volume-averaged Lyman-$\alpha$ data from quasar pairs across a specific redshift range. Our analysis indicates that these additional signals can provide distinct constraints on $\Omega_m$ and $H_0$, while maintaining consistency with the standard BAO signal constraints on $H_0$, $d_A$, and $d_V$. Combining our analysis with two distinct sets of standard BAO signals, we observe equivalent limits on these parameters, but our method allows for significantly reduced systematics in the estimation of $H_0$, enabling a $2.2$σ discrepancy with the Hubble constant estimated in Planck 2018. Additionally, by leveraging the combined BAO, FOG, and NECD signals, we obtain highly restrictive limits on these parameters, reducing the systematics related to $H_0$ estimates to $0.7$σ. Furthermore, through the incorporation of these signals, we achieve highly restrictive limits on $f_{NL}^{local}$. Our research highlights that utilising the full shape of Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions, in addition to BAO signals, can enhance cosmological inference. The two-dimensional analysis reveals a $1.3\sigma$ and $1.9\sigma$ discrepancy with the Planck 2018 estimates of $H_0$ and $\Omega_m$ respectively, while the three-dimensional analysis reveals a $1.7\sigma$ and $1.1\sigma$ discrepancy for the same parameters. The three-dimensional analysis provides a $1.3\sigma$ constraint on $f_{NL}^{local}$. The research also indicates that the FOG and NECD signals can be utilized independently to constrain non-Gaussian features, with the results showing a $1.3\sigma$ discrepancy from zero for the local $f_{NL}^{equil}$ value and a $1.7\sigma$ discrepancy from zero for the $m_{\nu}$ value. We identify potential systematics in the Lyman-$\alpha$ data from the cross-correlation between quasars and galaxies

This innovative procedure, emittance exchange, requires precise control and, due to its complexity, has only been theoretically explored until now. The recent experiment, implemented without any significant adjustments to the accelerator component setup, has moved the field closer to practical applications. The new development has key implications for a variety of particle accelerator uses, such as advanced particle identification and future intensity upgrade projects. A specific potential application involves deep-learning-based particle identification, which could substantially benefit from this technique. Additionally, the new technique emittance exchange may facilitate enhanced sensitivity in certain particle physics experiments by reducing interaction time. Conversely, the new technique may also raise background event rates in certain intensity upgrade projects; therefore, it is crucial to understand and analyze these potential implications. Further sensitivity investigations are planned after completing a comprehensive simulation study. Over the past thirty years, various theoretical models have been introduced to analyze intricate systems. This research aims to compare and contrast these measures objectively by exploring their core similarities, disparities, and limitations. To achieve this, a Boltzmann machine architecture is employed as a reference model to analyze how system complexity evolves in response to variations in network dynamics and parameters. Furthermore, a variant of an information-based measure of complexity is applied to examine the process of incremental Hebbian learning in Hopfield networks, which mimic autoassociative memory through a fully recurrent structure. As the network learns to recognize patterns, total information flow consistently increases, mirroring an intrinsic growth in complexity. Conversely, when pattern recognition fails, an increase in network temperature corresponds to a decrease in total information flow, indicating an external disruption in learning. This reveals that an information-based measure of complexity can accurately characterize crucial aspects of learned dynamics. Additionally, an exploratory analysis of biological neural networks reveals that undirected connectivity in biological networks such as the cortex and allocortex tends to replicate internal information flows, both positively and negatively, providing insights into potential structural designs for neural networks that maximize complexity. Lastly, a geometric representation of complexity is proposed, leveraging an intersection of hyperbolic geometry and Maxwell's equations through the examination of the Gramian matrix in a Lorentzian metric. This approach successfully reduces the complexity of high-dimensional data and reveals a geometric relationship between Hopfield networks and the brain's neural networks. Geometric complexity in turn allows for identifying similarities and patterns within datasets, both biological and artificial. Furthermore, a high-dimensional geometric representation of learned Hopfield networks, both incremental and static, is achieved by mapping the Gramian matrix onto a hyperbolic surface. This yields surprising results in which similar network configurations, both static and dynamic, are closely proximal in a high-dimensional geometric space, while disparate configurations are distant from each other, demonstrating that an information-based measure of complexity provides valuable insights into the inherent structure of learned neural networks. The approach and findings presented here have the potential to contribute to understanding the intricate organization and function of the human brain. In particular, examining Hopfield networks across various scales and dimensions makes it possible to identify similarities and patterns within subsets of the brain's neural networks, both basic and complex. This paper showcases initial research on an innovative technique for facilitating communication between humans and a swarm of robots. Our solution involves merging a compact hand gesture recognition model with the advanced \emph{ros2} system, allowing a swarm of robots to execute complex actions in response to distinct hand signals. Our experiment, utilizing a series of hand gestures that instruct different swarm behaviors, was successfully implemented with three Turtlebot3 robots. This enabled these robots to automatically adjust their distances and evade collisions with obstacles in accordance with the detected hand signals. By leveraging this technology, we have developed a multi-faceted tool for controlling and analyzing robot swarms through non-verbal communication. This could have far-reaching implications, such as enabling disabled individuals to command larger robotic systems with intricate hand gestures. Furthermore, this technology can also be utilized for collecting valuable data to develop automated computer vision systems capable of identifying complex hand signals. Ultimately, our proposed approach has the potential to accelerate high-speed communication between humans and robot swarms over short distances. Moreover, it can facilitate complex interactions with these types of robots, as well as enable the design of more sophisticated computer vision systems able to recognize and interpret intricate hand signals. A key advantage of counterdiabatic protocols in driving quantum states involves the use of a supporting, auxiliary gauge potential. However, determining this potential requires the full Hamiltonian, posing a significant challenge for complex many-body systems. A recent approach, proposed by P. W. Claeys et al., utilizes an approximated, variational gauge potential. In the case of a two-component fermionic Hubbard model, this potential can be expressed using nested commutators. A critical insight in this context reveals that optimizing the variational parameters leads to a set of linear equations, whose coefficients are determined by these commutators. A newly devised method allows the nested commutators to be computed and evaluated exactly in the Hilbert space. A detailed investigation is conducted on driving a non-equilibrium insulator into a superfluid state using the prototypical two-component Hubbard model on a one-dimensional ring with six sites. A comparison is made between exact results and findings from applying the optimized variational method, indicating that the latter yields results of comparable accuracy. Furthermore, this study examines the constraints and limitations of the variational approach and explores the feasibility of developing more effective, higher-order methods for approximating the supporting gauge potential and, ultimately, improving the driving protocols. A code written in the NumPy/SciPy framework for calculating the commutators and optimizing the variational potential is also provided. A future update to include driving a Hubbard-triplet system using the optimized variational method is also envisioned. The study reports a significant advantage of using the variational method for Hubbard-like models, and a possibility of applying it to certain optical-lattice systems. A prospective update might involve utilizing it to drive a Hubbard-triplet configuration, realizing a Hubbard-model simulation on a multi-layered system, or employing it to launch a simulation of a novel scheme for topological vacuum entanglement swapping. Color-neutral images are a cornerstone in various image processing applications such as image compression, feature extraction, and printing due to their role in image representation. As a result of image acquisition processes, color images often contain gray tones that are essential for their meaning and quality. However, traditional color removal methods lead to significant information loss, particularly for images with notable color gradients. To overcome this limitation, a novel approach is proposed to remove colors from a single image, preserving its gray tones and texture while translating it into a composable binary image. This goal is achieved through a learned color space transformation applied to the image, allowing it to be converted into a binary composition of primordial colors. Additionally, a priority is set on maintaining image gray tones and texture in the proposed algorithm. For this purpose, a neural network is designed to map a color image to a binary composition, preserving its gray tones and features. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm delivers high-quality results, including accurate color removal, preservation of gray tones, and retention of valuable image information, while highlighting its applicability in various scenarios. Comparatively, existing methods incorporating neural networks fail to achieve comparable results. Our findings also reveal that the representation of colors in a specific color space makes it feasible to extract features based on color composition, including attributes related to weather, artifacts, and image style. Therefore, a control mechanism is introduced to balance color removal, gray tone preservation, and feature extraction simultaneously. Lastly, the proposed algorithm enables the conversion of an input color image to a binary composition with control over color composition, including the ability to extract features based on color properties. This capability is illustrated in our experiments with feature extraction based on color properties. With color space transformation, the proposed method can be applied in reverse to compose a color image from a binary composition, highlighting its applicability in image augmentation. To facilitate the implementation of the proposed algorithm, a parent-child disentanglement network is designed to isolate combinatorial features in image representation, contributing to the understanding of image depth complexity and the design of feature extraction algorithms. This research develops an expression to decompose infinitely differentiable complex-valued functions into a sum of exponentials along with a corresponding error term. Building upon this, a corresponding infinite series is derived for functions, and conditions are established to ensure convergence. Subsequently, these results are employed to categorize and analyze the convergence of different infinite series. Additionally, this decomposition is used to express and analyze the infinite series representation of logarithms and Bessel functions. Lastly, a novel infinite series expansion is developed for $e^{izx}$, specifically for magnetic fields and for a wide range of real values of $x$. A corresponding analysis of the convergence of this series is conducted. Our approach includes determining data validation zones, corresponding to first-order logic assertions, using an algorithm that calculates the various possible values for each IRI constructor within these validation zones. This process considers all partial and complete orders of the validation zones, leading to an algorithm with a computationally efficient single pass operation for determining valid solutions, using a finite tree language and special propagation mechanisms for annotated data. The origin of Be-type stars is still unclear with theories involving both single and dual star evolutions, however through 73 VFTS spectra analyses it has been observed that Be-type stars have higher rotational speeds. Calculations reveal that their estimated rotational speed has a mean value of 350km/s which is 30% lower than a random selection of B-type stars, suggesting a slower rotating population.  Further analysis found that Be-type stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud have slower surface rotations when compared to a random selection of B-type stars, suggesting they have existed for at least one million years before becoming Be-type stars, a process that requires the transfer of angular momentum from a companion star. Furthermore, it has been discovered that 60% of magnetic B-type stars in the database are identified as Be-type stars and a dual population has been defined.  Be-type stars in the magnetic group are more slowly rotating, however not as slowly as more normal Be-type stars, suggesting they have a full magnetic B-type star P Cygni sequence.  The source of Be-type stars' fast rotation remains unclear, however it is linked to a magnetic field. Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, are often difficult to understand. This interpretability issue severely hampers their use in critical areas like medical imaging. A promising approach, neural tangent kernel, offers some level of interpretation by mirroring a kernel machine's properties. In an effort to enhance classification and layer understanding, we've developed a novel network that combines multiple neural tangent kernels - one for each layer - as opposed to earlier work focusing on a single kernel to represent the entire network. We validate the effectiveness of this model on two datasets, revealing that it successfully reveals the network's layer-based organization and makes accurate predictions. As an additional contribution, we introduce a novel neural tangent kernel that has not been previously explored, demonstrated on a binary classification task. We hope that multi-kernel models, accompanied by this new kernel, will facilitate the development of more sophisticated, interpretable models. All code and models can be accessed at: https://github.com/ucasrl/MultiKT. Furthermore, it includes detailed instructions for creating visualizations, such as fitting and plotting kernel tangent spectra. We also provide access to the utilized datasets, namely CIFAR10 and CIFAR100. A tutorial video offering a visual explanation of the multi-kernel approach can be found at: https://youtu.be/0tIRF3u6tQ. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems, with a particular focus on the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems. Our results reveal that correlations cause a significant reduction in the topological classification from $\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ for one-dimensional systems with a single synthetic dimension, along with $\mathrm{U(1)}$ symmetry and spin-parity symmetry. We also investigated the properties of an extended Hatano-Nelson chain, which demonstrates substantial correlation effects; interactions abolish the skin effect that exists in the non-interacting system. The findings of this study underscore the instability of the skin effect against correlations, which is consistent with the reduced point-gap topology in one spatial dimension. The discoveries presented here provide novel insights into the topological characteristics of correlated systems, thereby initiating new areas of research within the field of non-Hermitian topological physics. Additionally, we propose potential experimental implementations using ultracold atoms. The creation of a chiral exceptional point via boundary interactions may pave the way for developing an interface that transmits signals of a specific rotation direction, thereby opening new avenues for lasing technologies that are chiral in nature. However, these findings raise concerns about the universe's trajectory in the distant past due to the influence of dark energy. A team of researchers has proposed a periodic cosmology model to address these concerns. The model introduces a temporal phenomenon, creating an illusion of time dilation, thereby dividing the universe into discrete segments. As the universe evolves, a portion of time is relived in a reverse sequence, affecting cosmic scales and relabeling events in each cycle. Using the Gaia's photometric data to about 25 million years ago, the researchers found consistency within three cycles, but the model needs further evaluation to eliminate ambiguities. Furthermore, the periodic cosmology model offers opportunities for novel investigations, including testing general relativity and examining the universe's parity symmetry. The proposed model also allows for the analysis of ancient asymptotic states, determining the probability distribution of lifetimes, and studying the segmentation pattern. The study leaves unanswered the primary question of whether the model accurately represents the universe's evolution before dark energy's dominance. The researchers intend to gather more data through the Gaia's extended mission to resolve the remaining uncertainties. The model's implications have also contributed to theories such as the Olber's paradox, a possible explanation for the horizon's origin, and the appearance of hierarchical structures at the cosmic background radiation level. The study suggests that a discrete pattern in the cosmic expansion history can be explored using the cosmic kinematic pantheon, a set of parameters including the Hubble parameter, deceleration, and curvature. The study also indicates that a discrete pattern in the cosmic expansion history, although consistent with Gaia's data, has not been identified in previous studies focusing on the cosmic kinematic parameters. This idea brings concepts from areas like chaos theory and dynamical systems into the study of quantum foundations. Despite this potential, developing realistic models within this framework has been a significant hurdle. To address this challenge, a concrete implementation of Invariant-set theory is being developed, one that aligns with established principles in physics and serves as a practical example of how the theory can explain observed quantum phenomena. This implementation utilizes a system of coupled pendula and is defined by specific mathematical equations, making it a concrete and quantifiable model that can be analyzed using current measurement techniques. Using this model, we have demonstrated that it's possible to reproduce Bell correlations without invoking hidden variables or violate established principles in physics. Instead, we identify issues related to common superdeterministic attempts to address this problem, and we argue that our model has a crucial distinction - it doesn't rely on untestable assumptions. Furthermore, we discuss how this model allows for dual explanations of nonlocality, making it compatible with established principles in physics, and we propose that these dual explanations could have distinct implications for tests designed to verify the reality of quantum correlations. We also outline how this model could be experimentally distinguished from other superdeterministic theories that attempt to explain quantum phenomena. By providing concrete details about how the model works and its composition, we are able to pinpoint the complexity associated with superdeterministic attempts to address Bell correlations without hidden variables. We argue that these attempts face a significant obstacle in explaining how fine-grained correlations are generated, and we propose that our model has a unique advantage in addressing this issue without relying on untestable assumptions. We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting on devices such as smart speakers and wearables. Our focus is on NN execution within devices with limited resources; thus, we suggest a Compact Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture. This CNN features (i) reduced computation requirements via limited multiplications, (ii) minimized memory needs through efficient weight storage, (iii) strict output constraints for hardware compatibility, and (iv) a limited number of layers for hardware implementability. Our findings show the CNN attains an accuracy of 86.7% at 1.3 million instructions, 0.57 million operations, and 7.KB memory usage on a field-programmable gate array (FPGA). When further optimized for power and accuracy, the CNN achieves 0.43 million operations, 86.7% accuracy, and 86.KB energy consumption on the same hardware platform. Our compact CNN achieves superior performance compared to existing NNs for keyword spotting. A new benchmark for FPGAs is developed, incorporating additional metrics to evaluate keyword spotting models. This benchmark applies the constrained architecture to enhance FPGA efficiency, a previously underutilized hardware platform for NN execution. Our work aims to provide a framework for NN compression and evaluation on the FPGA platform, a crucial step towards the development of smart audio devices. Our code and FPGA implementation are publicly accessible at https://github.com/appliedmachinelearning/KE. Our research data can be retrieved at https://doi.org/10.5068/W8VQZZ. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. The method's computational efficiency is further enhanced by parallel processing, demonstrating its scalability for large datasets. To address these requirements, a new approach called mixed criticality real-time systems has been developed, combining non-real-time and real-time tasks in a single system. To ensure the safety of critical tasks, a new hypervisor called T-Visor has been created.  Compared to other hypervisors, T-Visor has been designed specifically with embedded systems in mind, leading to a more efficient use of the host's resources and better performance. We present a multi-layer quiver in this paper, using which we can build a higher dimension (n+1) algebras of infinite complexity from a given n-dimensional quiver-based algebra. This process results in an (n+1)-dimensional quiver. To achieve this, we first establish the concept of a pre-quiver, which enables the construction of a pre-algebra, and subsequently, the integration of pre-algebras leads to the creation of a multi-layer quiver and its associated quiver-based algebra. This method allows us to simplify the classification of slice algebras by showing that certain types of quiver-based algebras do not support slice algebras of infinite complexity, whereas others do support such algebras; we will provide examples of both scenarios. Furthermore, we will classify multi-layer quivers for n=1, 2, 3, and establish the connection between these and previously classified quiver-based algebras of dimensions 1 to 3. To facilitate the classification, we will utilize Serre's congruence and the Hasse invariants for classification purposes. Additionally, we will provide the classification of multi-layer quivers for rank 2 and rank 3, and discuss some open questions. This work is an extension of earlier research, including a previous study on multi-layer quivers of dimension 1. To visualize the structure of multi-layer quivers, we have provided illustrations in the appendix. This research was completed under the supervision of Ryo Hanaki. Researchers have suggested the application of quantum interferometry and information processing in Bose-Einstein condensates. However, the current understanding of BECs relies on complex descriptions, often without a clear link to Noether's theorem. We propose a approach to represent the unitary evolution of a BEC's wave function using a Lie group and its corresponding Lie algebra. This framework provides a direct connection between conserved quantities, Lie groups, and Noether's theorem. By exploiting this connection, we uncover the origin of non-linear quantum mechanics in BECs, as well as the root cause of constraints on their dynamics. Furthermore, we outline the general framework for defining the Lie algebra associated with a BEC's symmetry, which has far-reaching implications for developing interferometry and information processing tasks within this quantum context. We also discuss initial implementations of this scheme on specific models, such as the Rabi model and the Jaynes-Cummings system. We believe our work serves as a foundational approach for managing BEC systems and exploring the interplay between symmetries, conserved quantities, and dynamic behavior. Moreover, it facilitates the design of interferometry and information processing tasks, leveraging the unique non-Gaussian correlations inherent in BECs. Current techniques often struggle to adapt or rely on the presence of similar examples during the training process. To overcome this issue, we have developed an innovative method that allows models to evolve gradually in a completely unsupervised manner. The proposed approach identifies and groups together exemplars sharing the same category, thereby facilitating the continuous evolution of the model. However, when the data sets of multiple categories are merged, the classical clustering problem becomes increasingly complex due to the absence of any prior knowledge. The proposed clustering objective evaluates the similarity between pairwise interactions within each class and maximizes the inter-class distance, while minimizing the intra-class variability. To achieve optimal results, we have incorporated a frequency-based objective that accurately reflects the true class probabilities. A comprehensive examination of pion-nucleon interactions at low energy is provided,
with the intention of offering a fundamental and educational overview relevant to current
research endeavors. Key topics addressed include the application of chiral effective
field theory, the significance of the sigma term, an understanding of the qualitative nature
of low-energy phase shifts, the physics governing the $\Delta$ resonance, and isospin violation.
It is emphasized that pion-nucleon scattering at low energy is intrinsically connected to QCD through effective
field theory. Furthermore, the need to incorporate the constraints of chiral symmetry in both theory and experiment
is stressed. Ultimately, the abstract argues that a multi-faceted approach, combining theoretical and experimental
knowledge, is essential for a deeper understanding of this complex system. This paper serves as a base for a more
extensive review on the subject, exploring the application of theory and experimental methods to analyze low-energy
pion-nucleon interactions. Such a review is anticipated to be published as an ARB article in the near future. 
A more detailed analysis will be available in the ARB series article, however some key resources and further reading are already accessible online, while key results from calculations and fitting procedures will be presented in an accompanying document. The PALEOCCENE concept has the potential to develop sensitive and efficient detection systems capable of identifying low-energy nuclear recoil events over extensive volumes. This capability could significantly contribute to various scientific applications such as geoseismic research, cosmic ray observation, oil exploration, and radioisotope tracing. A PALEOCENE module consists of two primary components: a large scintillator tank and a sophisticated silicon detector array. The module's design emphasizes the strategic integration of silicon sensors and scintillator materials to maximize the conversion of mechanical energy into electrical signals. Through comprehensive analysis of the silicon detector array's performance, researchers have established a standard model to predict mechanical vibrations and their resulting electrical signals within the scintillator. Employing extensive finite-element modeling, researchers analyzed various stimuli including seismic waves, air shockwaves, and impacts to simulate the entire PALEOCENE detection process. Simulation results indicate that even high-stress regions deep within the Earth's crust generate only negligible high-count rates, suggesting that PALEOCENE has the necessary sensitivity and extensive volume to effectively detect low-energy nuclear recoil events. Quantum process tomography is crucial for building quantum computers, establishing quantum networks, and developing quantum sensors. Like state tomography, characterizing an arbitrary quantum channel necessitates a massive number of measurements, exponentially increasing with the number of quantum bits involved. Recent advancements in shadow tomography, particularly in state measurement, have revealed the possibility of determining a quantum channel's behavior using only a fraction of the total measurements. This study adapts the concept of shadow tomography to tackle two-channel mixtures, leveraging the realignment operator to estimate the realignment of mixed states resulting from arbitrary channel applications. Previous research demonstrated that realignment is a highly invariant measure, making it resistant to channel applications. This work establishes that, statistically, estimates derived from shadow operators can accurately reconstruct the realignment of two-channel applications with high precision, offering a significant improvement over individual channels. Moreover, this study provides novel bounds on the precision achievable in reconstructing the realignment of multiple channels, expressed as a function of the total number of measurements. These new bounds surpass previous results, particularly in high-channel scenarios. Importantly, this research facilitates estimating the fidelity-weighed average gate set performance following partial channel applications, an essential metric in distributed quantum technology development. The proposed framework lends itself to sampling-based algorithms, including Markov Chain Monte Carlo, allowing the simulation of shadow operators to be executed in minutes or hours, depending on the channel count and system complexity. This method has substantial implications, as it enables estimating the fidelity-weighed average gate set performance using datasets comprising a small number of events, potentially exceeding the total number of measurements required for exact characterizations. This study further explores the scalability of the shadow operator approach, showing that its efficiency may experience a reversal compared to individual channels as channel complexity increases. The method proposed in this work can be accessed through the open-source Quantum Process Tomography Package available at https://github.com/Sothos/qpt. The research and associated code receive an open-data license, making all data, including raw datasets and shadow operator estimates, fully accessible to support reproducibility and transparency, fostering further advancements in quantum computing, networkin, and sensing applications. The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from various research areas.  By leveraging local data that captures the geometry of non-free actions and global data in the $C^*$-algebra framework, we establish a direct correspondence between the physical T-duality of string theory and the current C*-algebra approach.  Our work shows that T-duality commutativity is a consequence of almost abelianity, a geometric condition, rather than the specific T-duality isomorphism, and provides examples of geometric solvmanifolds that are not abelian but exhibit T-duality commutativity.  Additionally, the class of manifolds that are not abelian can be viewed as a step towards understanding three-dimensional T-duality non-commutativity, a phenomenon predicted in string theory.  Our work also explores the class of torus bundles as a special case within our framework, recovers the known T-duality isomorphisms, and demonstrates the failure of topological T-duality for certain non-free volume-preserving actions, as well as its potential extension to the non-trivial rational cohomology classes through the use of germs over a one-dimensional space.  Finally, the non-commutative T-duality of nilmanifolds is studied, providing evidence that a geometric, non-commutative T-duality is an extension of the classical, geometric T-duality.  Our work concludes with three open problems: investigating three-dimensional T-duality non-commutativity and developing a manifestly non-commutative T-duality for general torus bundles and nilmanifolds.  Although the current C*-algebra approach offers a non-commutative T-duality, it lacks the manifestly geometric aspect due to its reliance on local data; the last open problem seeks to address this issue.  Lastly, the broader implications and connections of topological T-duality have been placed beyond the scope of this dissertation; they are explored in 130, 131.

Instead of employing fermionic-excitation evolutions to construct the ansatz, we utilize a circuit consisting of qubit-excitation evolutions, which yields benefits in terms of circuit depth and as a result, circuit noise tolerance. Our approach successfully performs molecular chemistry calculations on IBM quantum processors without requiring complex and high-dimensional optimization of qubit coupling. We also introduce an automated method for determining the optimal circuit depth, which leverages the relationship between qubit excitation levels and the quantum computer's coherence time. This approach has been successfully tested on various molecular systems, including He$_2$, H$_2$ and HD. Our results demonstrate that utilizing a qubit-excitation evolution based ansatz coupled with the circuit learning technique and the determination of circuit depth can efficiently execute challenging chemical reactions on noisy quantum processors. This approach holds promise for molecular simulations due to its robustness and reduced requirement for optimization. We also provide guidance on accurately estimating ground-state energies from finite difference of energy estimates. We simulate the HD molecule using the fully connected Frei-Hammond parameterization, which requires deeper circuits than the qubit-excitation evolution ansatz, which results in significant precision losses for the Frei-Hammond parameterization when compared to the molecular Hamiltonian estimates. This result highlights the potential of the qubit-excitation evolution ansatz to perform molecular simulations on more complex quantum processors in the future. We find that the precision loss for QAOA is greater than that of the VQE under identical circuit depths for the He$_2$, H$_2$ and HD molecular systems. This result highlights the potential of the VQE under qubit-excitation evolutions as a intermediate-scale quantum technology for molecular simulations before widespread adoption of the more powerful QAOA. This approach leads to a DGD that learns a probabilistic mapping from a low-dimensional to a high-dimensional space, demonstrating better optimization and performance compared to VAEs. The discovery of a common-spectrum process in recent NANOGrav findings has led to theories suggesting it could be evidence of a primordial stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) that exceeds expectations based on standard inflationary models. If the SGWB is real, it would significantly impact our understanding of the Universe, forcing a re-evaluation of observations from cosmic microwave background radiation and the expansion history of the Universe. Given the potential for such a finding to greatly impact our understanding of the universe, we aim to thoroughly examine all possible signal models by applying the Bayesian F-test to pairs of EPT polynomials. However, an accurate model of the gravitational force between the Earth and the Sun (EPT) is essential to this endeavor. To this end, we undertake a comprehensive analysis to determine an accurate force model that meets three key criteria: it accurately aligns with the data from LARES16, must be computationally efficient, and robust against errors in orbital elements of the test masses. Using a Bayesian approach, we refine the LARES16 force model to develop the EPT, incorporating all relevant factors and solving for 16 parameters to establish a precise gravitational potential. Our investigation into potential sources of uncertainty in the LARES16 orbit reveals their effect on the estimation of the EPT. The refined EPT, in turn, serves as the basis for computing the gravitational force between the Earth and a generic object. A precise force model allows us to derive an accurate expression for the gravitational potential, solving for 10 parameters. Ultimately, we evaluate the computational cost of using the EPT to determine the gravitational force between the Earth and a generic object. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between the EPT and the gravitational potential. As a means to make the EPT broadly accessible, we implement it within the C Fund, a high-precision language designed for astronomical and atmospheric calculations. Lastly, we evaluate the EPT in relation to the gravitational potential at the surface of the Earth. However, our analysis reveals the primordial SGWB cannot be confirmed with the currently available data, prompting the consideration of reducing the EPT to better align with the data. Despite this, our refined EPT demonstrates equivalent or superior performance to previously developed models. If the SGWB is a reality, it far exceeds the predictions based on the standard inflationary model. We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a dictionary, our technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a prelabeled dataset. Human evaluation confirms the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised system is comparable to that of a traditionally trained model in terms of its naturalness and ease of understanding. Moreover, the unsupervised system we developed exhibits cross-language generalization capabilities, aided by the proposed multilingual dictionary creation process. This innovative unsupervised speech synthesis framework presents a groundbreaking solution for developing speech synthesis technologies in environments where data annotation expenses are exorbitant. The associated implementation can be accessed at: \url{https://github.com/michaelshelham/UNSPEECH}. This research received funding from the South African Research Chairs Company (SARChI) and the South African National Commission for UNESCO. These two approaches are expected to complement each other towards achieving state-of-the-art performance in speech synthesis. Despite the emergence of cost-free unsupervised speech synthesis techniques based on adversarial networks, research indicates that the generated speech from these models often requires post-processing and remains less natural when compared to speech produced by traditionally trained neural speech synthesis models. This study proposes an innovative unsupervised speech synthesis technique that leverages the strengths of adversarial networks and data-based approaches under a single framework. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a dictionary, this technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a prelabeled dataset. As a result, the proposed method facilitates the development of a large-scale unsupervised speech synthesis system that generates high-quality speech in any language, coupled with a multilingual dictionary creation process, which exhibits cross-domain generalization capabilities. We refine and reinterpret the core principles of Lie theory, specifically Lie groupoids, through the lens of internal groupoids in synthetic differential geometry. Key concepts are re-expressed, including path sources and integrated $A$-paths. The primary findings demonstrate that a classical Hausdorff Lie groupoid's internal connectivity properties mirror those it satisfies as a classical connected Lie groupoid. This has the consequence that a Lie groupoid's internal connectivity properties are indifferent to the choice of a Lie groupoid equivalent to it. Additionally, a Lie groupoid's local connectedness properties are encoded in its 1-connectedity species, and we establish that a simply connected Lie groupoid's path source corresponds to the source of its path space. The local connectedness properties of Lie groupoids are also studied, and it is found that a Lie groupoid is locally simply connected precisely when its 1-connectedness species' condition is satisfied. Finally, a Lie groupoid's $A$-connectedness properties are examined, and it is found that a Lie groupoid is $A$-connected if, and only if, its path source's $A$-source corresponds to the Lie groupoid's path space's source. This work ultimately reveals that a Lie groupoid's internal $A$-connectedness properties are insensitive to the choice of a Lie groupoid equivalent to it. The article concludes by making observations specific to 1-connected Lie groupoids. Detailed explanations of Lie groupoid properties, including their internal and local connectedness specifications, are provided in the appendix. The work is concluded with a comparison of Lie groupoids' local and internal connectedness properties. The author's hope is that a Lie groupoid theorist, familiar with classical Lie groupoids, will find this account a useful introduction to their internal and local counterparts. A reader interested in Lie theory, on the other hand, may use these speculations as a starting point to develop further generalizations. A significant portion of this work was written while the author taught a course on synthetic differential geometry, which provides additional Lie theory content. A Lie groupoid's internal and local connectedness properties were discussed in class, and the author hopes that this final version captures the essence of those lectures. Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews or social media content. Approximately one-third of reviews and statuses lack explicit opinion words, yet clearly convey human sentiment. Additionally, opinion words often convey nuanced sentiment meanings, which may not be explicitly stated ("lovely" implies pleasure, whereas "lovely" implies charm). We call this subtle sentiment conveyed by opinion words implicit sentiment. Unfortunately, existing approaches neglect implicit sentiment, resulting in incomplete analysis of sentiment. Our proposed model incorporates implicit sentiment inherent in opinion words, which significantly enhances accurate sentiment expression prediction. To achieve this, we developed a BERT-based model integrating explicit and implicit sentiment from opinion words. Specifically, we developed a unique rule-based method extracting explicit sentiment and a novel BERT-based model generating implicit sentiment word predictors. Through experiments on five datasets, we demonstrated the superiority of our approach over nine state-of-the-art baselines. Our source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/yangmingyu/IEAABSA. For convenience, we released five datasets and an annotation guide on https://www.pku.edu.cn/teacher/13871.html. Each dataset contains reviews with explicit sentiment annotations and a review without explicit sentiment with implicit sentiment annotations. Our objective is to facilitate research focused on these subtle sentiment meanings to ultimately achieve more accurate sentiment analysis. Implicit sentiment should not be disregarded; otherwise, it may hinder the ultimate pursuit of accurate sentiment analysis. The proposed model is the first to integrate explicit and implicit sentiment from opinion words, effectively enhancing sentiment expression prediction. Consequently, the total Acc of our model outperformed that of nine baseline approaches, including state-of-the-art models, on five datasets. Figure 1 provides an illustration of the proposed model's sentiment analysis results for a review mentioning a restaurant. Explicit sentiment words ("cheap", "main") convey sentiment towards the price but not the service; whereas, implicit sentiment words ("lovely", "charming") convey charm as the sentiment meaning. Therefore, the service likely receives more positive sentiment than the price. We hope our work inspires research focused on uncovering the subtle sentiment meanings inherent in opinion words to ultimately achieve more accurate sentiment analysis. This research delves into secure communication systems for multiple users that utilize reconfigurable intelligent surfaces to compensate for hardware limitations.
We simultaneously adjust the base station's beamforming vectors and the phase shifts on the RIS to achieve the highest possible weighted minimum secrecy rate.
We frame this problem as a non-linear optimization issue and use an algorithm that employs the accelerated gradient projection method to find an optimal solution with fewer iterations required.
We also prove that the proposed algorithm converges to a stable point.
Our simulation results show a substantial enhancement in secrecy performance compared to a system without RIS and better outcomes than a system that only adjusts the base station's beamforming vectors. Additionally, the accelerated gradient projection method offers a considerable reduction in computational complexity compared to other optimization techniques. This allows the algorithm to reach a stable point with a lower number of iterations required. As a result, the computational overhead is significantly decreased, providing a valuable trade-off between implementation complexity and system performance. This could lead to a substantial decrease in energy consumption by the base station and reduce energy consumption by the RIS. To further reduce energy consumption by the RIS, the phase shifts can be optimized using a constrained minimization problem as demonstrated in a corresponding study. The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the optical behavior within a linearly coupled $q$-deformed optomechanical system. Composed of two deformed cavities interacting with mechanical mirrors and coupled through a transmission parameter, this study reveals that $q$-deformation enhances the speed and magnitude of phase transitions during optical windows. Furthermore, for a specified range of $q$, these systems exhibit amplification of the optical signal. By manipulating parameters like tunneling strength and optomechanical coupling, one can cause the optical probe to be delayed or advanced by up to milliseconds, with even longer delays achievable through fine-tuning. This work also provides a link between the $q$-deformation in optical domains and non-linear optomechanical phenomena and offers a design strategy for the construction of $q$-deformed optical devices, potentially including optical memories and switches. The theoretical underpinnings of $q$-deformation in optical engineering are established, laying the groundwork for the analysis of optical behavior within this framework. The resulting theoretical models can inform the development of novel optomechanical devices featuring distinct optical properties. Additionally, the research explores the broader implications of $q$-deformation in optical science, revealing connections to Engle field theory and inspiring further study of the mathematical structure behind this concept. The final step outlines hypothetical approaches for realizing $q$-deformation in optical technology. Although currently beyond our capabilities, the optical realization of $q$-deformation holds significant promise for the future. The research concludes by identifying open questions and suggesting avenues for further investigation into the intersection of $q$-deformation and optomechanical systems. The study ends with an analysis of the potential role of $q$-deformation in the advancement of optomechanical science. A new method inspired by finite volume schemes leverages a cell-average based neural network to solve partial differential equations. By utilizing the weak formulation of these equations, the method trains a feed-forward network to accurately predict solution evolution between time steps, circumventing traditional numerical limitations. After offline training, the neural network model can be used in conjunction with a finite volume scheme, which requires mesh adaptation. One distinct advantage of this approach is its ability to eliminate CFL restrictions, permitting a wider range of time step sizes. Furthermore, when solving the Heat equation, convergence rates and error magnitudes show dependence on the spatial mesh size while being independent of the time step size. Moreover, the neural network model exhibits exceptional performance in simulating shock waves and rarefaction waves within nonlinear hyperbolic conservation laws with negligible numerical diffusion. Although some loss occurs in accurately capturing the sharp transition region, the neural network model demonstrates superior ability to resolve the flow field compared to traditional numerical methods, utilizing a Schur polynomial-based finite volume scheme framework. Notably, the neural network model shows promising generalization even on unseen mesh topologies, whereas performance significantly deteriorates when the neural network is trained with faulty data. Therefore, the neural network model's effectiveness relies heavily on data purity. Lastly, the neural network model's ability to solve a variety of one and two-dimensional problems is demonstrated with promising results. However, the neural network model's effectiveness for multi-species and multi-dimensional conservation laws requires further investigation. More importantly, the neural network model holds vast potential for real-world applications by addressing the present limitations. Future research aims to address these issues. The formation of magnetically-driven jets from a spinning black hole following a compact binary merger event is a significant aspect of optically thick gamma-ray bursts, especially in relation to the characteristics of the resulting ejecta. To examine this process, we utilized the numerical simulations of a multimessager model to explore three different black hole spins before the ejecta was fully expelled. We found that the mass and angular momentum of the ejected matter show notable correlations with the black hole's spin, which could influence the characteristics of the gamma-ray burst and the properties of the merger event's remnant system. Notably, the orientation of the ejected matter's angular momentum vector is highly dependent on the initial black hole spin, which may impact the direction of the gamma-ray burst jet. We discussed how these findings can be applied to the analysis of gamma-ray bursts originating from similar events, which could result in more accurate constraints on the properties of black holes, especially in relation to their spin. Additionally, we examined the possible implications of the ejected matter's behavior on the properties of the merger event's remnant system, including the characteristics of the remnant black hole, the collapse of the ejecta into a secondary black hole, and the properties of the gamma-ray burst jet. The relationship between the ejecta and these properties was also investigated. We found that the properties of the merger event could be better understood if the spin of the black hole in a given event could be accurately constrained using data from observations. We have gathered a comprehensive dataset containing 35 optical observations of 17 fast radio burst (FRB) events observed across 8 distinct locations. The optical flares were detected using various methods, including enhanced optical transients similar to FRB afterglows, extended emission synchronized with FRB pulses, and optical bursts distinct from FRB pulses. The optical and radio flux patterns were analyzed, and the optical luminosities were measured to establish upper limits. Our findings imply that magnetic field dipole radiation may not be the primary mechanism powering optical emission during FRBs, unless these radio bursts occur at incredibly low distances. If these radio bursts have their origins in a common astrophysical setting, a novel mechanism must be responsible for producing the observed optical flux, at least for pulses exhibiting double-peak patterns. The possible connections between FRB origins and optical observations are discussed, suggesting that exploring the relationships between radio emission intensities, spectral compositions, and pulse structures could lead to a deeper understanding of optical-producing mechanisms. Furthermore, we present initial constraints on monochromatic radiation model parameters for three FRBs, and suggest potential observations to clarify the optical production of these enigmatic radio bursts. The optical data and associated analysis code are publicly accessible through the Kosma Telescope Archive, while relevant research is ongoing to investigate the optical properties of FRBs, particularly for the most luminous FRB known, FRB 20121102A. Multimodal language generation capabilities of models like GPT-2 and GPT-3 can be leveraged for producing high-quality text, but it is still uncertain how they can be directed by non-text modalities like images. We introduce a new framework called MAGIC that allows these models to perform tasks such as image captioning in the absence of textual inputs. By incorporating an image representation module, a text modification module, and a text generation module, MAGIC enables the model to focus on generating relevant content while adhering to given instructions and preserving image information. From a technical standpoint, MAGIC allows the image and text modalities to interact freely, eliminates the need for optimization objectives that require a shared, latent space, and uses the image representation module's output as a supplementary input for text generation. We compare the performance of MAGIC with other image-guided GPT-2 and GPT-3 approaches that use image-text fusion, finding that MAGIC consistently achieves better results on the image captioning dataset, MS-COCO. Notably, MAGIC also demonstrates robustness to unoptimized hyperparameters and the type of image encoder used, as well as the ability to integrate with GPT-2 and GPT-3 models of varying sizes. We also explore additional applications of MAGIC by guiding it with semantic masks rather than images, allowing it to capture meanings like "outdoor" and "indoor" from visual cues. The potential future research avenues include integrating MAGIC with other image-guided GPT-3 approaches that direct the model based on semantic masks, as well as the model's ability to generate long-form images descriptions. Furthermore, in-depth analysis of MAGIC is suggested to pinpoint its strengths and weaknesses, offering a basis for comparable future work. We strongly advise against using MAGIC for malicious applications such as image-based forgery and deceitful media generation, given its potential misuse. This study offers a pioneering approach to quantizing convolutional neural networks by enabling the direct conversion of 32-bit models to extremely compact, high-performance networks in a single step. By leveraging circuitry-friendly quantization, circuit implementation, and the trade-offs between latency and energy efficiency, we circumvent traditional accuracy loss issues associated with other quantization techniques. We apply circuit-friendly quantization to demonstrate accurate inference with minimal precision (4-8 bits) on the CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet datasets, thereby facilitating substantial storage and bandwidth reductions, as well as speedup. For instance, the ResNet50 model yields a 104 MB size reduction, a 16x speed increase on the ImageNet, and a 50% power savings when using a mobile platform. Our method also greatly simplifies model optimization, as evidenced by the fact that accuracy on the ImageNet dataset with 7-bit weights and 64 mixed scales requires only 5 hours, as opposed to typical iterative approaches that may take several weeks. The objective of metric learning is to establish a suitable embedding of image features so that their similarity can be effectively determined by query and retrieve relevant images within a dataset. The conventional pair-wise loss strategy aims to correct feature orientations through its directional component, but its efficacy is restricted by the non-conclusive aggregation of orientations and simultaneous positive pair learning, thereby neglecting the feature orientations' diversity. Current text-generation algorithms used in dialogue can be flawed. Specifically, optimizing task success through reinforcement learning often leads to increased, but unnecessary, grammatical error rate. To address this, we suggest fine-tuning language models with an editor's correction mechanism, where the editor prioritizes maintaining the dialogue's natural flow. We demonstrate this approach in a task-oriented dialogue dataset and a related challenge, achieving the goal of enhancing dialogue fluency while reducing excessive creativity in sentence formulations to improve comprehension. Furthermore, maintaining the original meaning and relevance of statements through the editing process is assessed, revealing that the editor's ideal intervention point can significantly impact the final outcome. Interestingly, the editor's role is not merely a grammar corrector, but rather a creative sentence reviser. Therefore, fine-tuning as proposed is beneficial not only for grammar, but also for sentence refinement. A comparison between the Rayleigh distribution and the Gamma distribution found that the Gamma distribution more accurately models the variability of these stresses.  This was because the Gamma distribution captures heteroscedasticity, a nonlinear phenomenon, better than the Rayleigh distribution, leading to a more accurate prediction of failures.  A study on generating synthetic data for the DeepDiver structure based on the Gamma distribution was conducted, resulting in the development of two methods: direct transformation and simulation.  Both methods were compared, with simulation being preferred due to its ability to model non-uniform randomness and heteroscedasticity, effectively accounting for the deep diving and loading dynamics of the reference structure.  A simulation was performed on the DeepDaver reference structure, also part of the DeepOcean initiative, demonstrating the capabilities of the deep diving and loading methods developed for the DeepDiver.  A study on predicting failures and costs on the DeepDaver revealed that the simulation models developed helped lower failure rates and costs by 4% and 2% respectively, with simulation-based approaches resulting in a 89% and 74% reduction in the variance of these metrics.  This resulted in an operating range that is 7% longer at sea level and 5% longer at its maximum depth.  This investigation also examines the variability of the DeepDaver's loads, failing to find a correlation between the turbulence of its waves and the heteroscedasticity of their responses.  A possible explanation for this could be the DeepDaver's high bandwidth and irregular sampling rate, which may be hiding this correlation.  This could also imply that the turbulence observed during the experiments may not accurately represent the deep diving conditions of the DeepDaver, suggesting that the simulation models developed for the DeepDiver and DeepDaver can be improved upon by accounting for this disparity and exploring frequency-based heteroscedasticity.  A proposed future study aims to investigate this frequency-based heteroscedasticity in both the DeepDiver and DeepDaver. Social media can provide valuable insights into public perception, beneficial for crisis communication and management. This research focuses on analyzing Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake, aiming to leverage these insights to infer real-time public opinions. By combining data mining and natural language processing techniques, we examine public sentiment and topic discussions following the earthquake. Our approach utilized LDA for topic modeling and BERT for sentiment analysis. Results show users shared supportive messages and engaged with relief efforts, expressing their desire to have their concerns heard by authorities. A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree by finding the least integer c such that the quotient $G/\gamma_{c+1}(G)$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property. In this research, we derive the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of general linear groups $G=GL_m(K)$ where K is a commutative ring. Additionally, we establish the same nilpotency degree for unimodular $R$-linear groups $G=GL_m(R)$, given that R is a domain. Specifically, we find that the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of $G=GL_m(K)$ or $G=GL_m(R)$ is equal to $\min\{m+1, \left[\frac{m}{2}\right]+2\}$, presented under the assumptions already stated. Consequently, we find that the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of finite groups is equal to 2. Moreover, we investigate the infinite residuated groups $G=GL_m(K)$ or $G=GL_m(R)$ and demonstrate that in such cases, the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree is equal to $\left[\frac{m}{2}\right]+1$. This paper presents SceNDD: a novel naturalistic driving dataset derived from
instrumented vehicle data collected in downtown Indianapolis over a period
of 12 years. As a unique data collection approach, we employ a naturalistic
driving dataset that features extensive participant information, thereby
accounting for demographic factors that are often absent in other driving
datasets. With a large collection of driving episodes (N = 6,428) spanning 65
hours, SceNDD offers a comprehensive dataset that incorporates various driving
parameters, including participant information, vehicle data, event markers,
performance metrics, and driving environment data. Furthermore, we establish key
statistical insights into critical driving events, such as crashes, near-crashes,
and critical maneuvers, which occur at rates consistent with real-world driving
settings. As a benchmark for performance assessment, we utilize the SafeAssess
toolkit to annotate driving behaviors in SceNDD, thereby creating opportunities
for new insights into critical driving events. With its extensive participant
information, comprehensive driving performance metrics, and comprehensive driving
data, SceNDD is poised to address existing research limitations and offer
customized driver training, safety assessment, and vehicle development
opportunities. The dataset is accessible at https://sites.google.com/view/scednd.

The inhomogeneous limit of A-twisted calibrated manifolds with an almost parallel G2 structure results in the emergence of a new, unique structure, referred to as G2*, which is associated with three real Killing spinors. A-twisted calibrated 3-forms play a crucial role in this process. The G2* structure has distinct properties from the G2 structure on the Euclidean domain $\mathbb{R}^7$ due to its dependence on a complete, minimal submanifold of codimension 4. We examine the G2* structure on the Euclidean domain $\mathbb{R}^8$ and determine its relationship with the G2 structure via the inhomogeneous limit of A-twisted calibrated manifolds. Furthermore, we identify distinct analogues of the G2 structure on the Euclidean domain $\mathbb{R}^8$ via the inhomogeneous limits of A-twisted calibrated 7-manifolds with a G2 structure. Ultimately, we establish the existence of A-twisted calibrated 7-manifolds with a G2 structure whose inhomogeneous limits yield G2*-structures on $\mathbb{R}^8$ and G2 structures on the Euclidean domain $\mathbb{R}^7$. These examples involve the use of minimal submanifolds with codimension 4 and 5, respectively. A comprehensive review of known G2 structures on the Euclidean domain $\mathbb{R}^7$ and 7-manifolds is also provided, along with the description of distinct A-twisted calibrated 7-manifolds with a G2 structure via the inhomogeneous limits of G2*-structures on $\mathbb{R}^8$. Lastly, several open questions and potential future research areas are posed. A comprehensive survey of the current literature on the inhomogeneous limits of A-twisted calibrated manifolds with a G2 structure is presented. The author's doctoral dissertation, which explores the concept of the inhomogeneous limit of A-twisted calibrated manifolds with a G2 structure, is also discussed. A more in-depth exploration of the physical implications of these structures can be found in the dissertation.
