Time-based data refers to information measured against the backdrop of time, giving it a distinct structural context that forms the foundation of its constituent parts. When dealing with multi-variable data sets, each variable interacts dynamically with others, resulting in complex patterns that are difficult to predict. Common traits of such data sets include simultaneous, interdependent, irregularly appearing, dynamically changing patterns, underlined by a non-stationary, multi-scale, highly structured underlying process. Notably, real-world data sets deviate significantly from assumed statistical regularity. In our research, we're exploring the use of wavelet theory to enhance the detection of hidden patterns in such data sets by transforming the underlying time series data into different frequency components, thereby making it amenable to data analysis. To validate our approach, we applied our methodology to the COVID-19 dataset, consisting of daily COVID-19 cases and fatalities in India, and examined the correlations between different frequency components to understand the underlying associations. Our analysis revealed that certain data frequencies were highly correlated, providing valuable insights into their interdependencies. By identifying the patterns of dependence among different frequency components, we were able to pinpoint the critical events marking the beginning and end of the COVID-19 wave in India. Our study offers a novel framework for analyzing complex time series data. However, there's a clear need for further research to address the numerous theoretical and practical challenges that arise at different frequency levels. The code and data for this research are accessible upon request. Moreover, we've made a proposal to establish an Data-Intensive Science Laboratory within the Indian Institute of Meteorology, Pune, to facilitate a range of research initiatives focusing on multi-scale data analysis. By leveraging multi-scale tools, we aim to gain a deeper understanding of the complexities governing the interactions between atmospheric and terrestrial systems. If realized, this laboratory would serve as a hub for multi-scale data analysis, offering a wealth of opportunities to study time series data. In the interest of sustainability, we've chosen COVID-19 data as a test case, but our approach can be applied effectively to a diverse array of physical and biological processes. To take the lab concept to its next stage, we've secured initial backing from the Indian Institute of Meteorology, Pune, and are actively soliciting support from the meteorological community to help bridge any remaining gaps in funding. By bridging these gaps, we can ensure the successful launch and effective operation of the lab, enabling a new generation of multi-scale analysts to tackle a broad spectrum of challenges in climate science and biology. The promising potential of extracting valuable insights from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) using Machine Learning has established a new standard for enhancing healthcare quality. To achieve this, research focuses on developing integrated systems of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning to mine knowledge from unstructured data in EHRs by identifying key entities, relationships, and concepts. By combining theoretical knowledge from medical domains with practical knowledge gained from textual patterns, these systems aim to optimize their accuracy and coverage. Although successful on a national scale, these models can be prone to regional biases, where data limitations in specific regions (like Latin America) can lead to poor generalization. To address this, we present a novel strategy that enhances the robustness of these models by implementing data augmentation and metric training within the framework of an attention-based sequence-to-sequence NER model for EHRs. By achieving this on a national scale, our experiments demonstrate significant improvements in F1 scores for ICD-10-BM category recognition, as well as reduced bias variability, when comparing the proposed approach with the traditional training method. Furthermore, our analysis shows that by using attention maps to understand NER model behavior, we can improve data augmentation. The code and models used in this research are available on our GitHub repository at: https://github.com/Alvaro-Alarcon/Regionally-Aware-Net. Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a highly recommended goal for many researchers. To this end, we annotated a unique dataset, PURE, and derived a new one combining requirements and non-requirements. We refined a BERT model with this dataset and compared its outcomes with well-established models like fastText and ELMo. To challenge the model with more complex text, we compared PURE's performance with experiments conducted on less formal Request For Information (RFI) documents. The fine-tuned BERT model achieved encouraging results on the PURE dataset, demonstrating superior performance on binary sentence classification with a high level of precision and recall while remaining adaptable to varied textual inputs. Furthermore, we demonstrated that our model can successfully pinpoint requirements in textual documents without any adjustments, thereby offering promising potential as a practical solution. Ultimately, the prospects for automatically extracting requirements from unstructured text appear promising, though still require further refinement. Nevertheless, the PURE dataset offers a valuable resource to support ongoing research and enable cross-studies, while the project's code and dataset are publicly accessible at the link: https://github.com/requirement-initiative/PURE. This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-user, multi-relay communication system with a maximum diversity network coding technique. A direct link between outage probability, energy consumption, and energy efficiency is established, followed by a formulation of the optimization problem to maximize energy efficiency under the constraint of maintaining a target outage probability. A practical scheduling and power allocation strategy is implemented to minimize power usage. Since the optimization problem is complex and difficult to solve, a tight approximation is first used to simplify the outage probability, then energy efficiency is re-expressed in a different form and the optimization problem is re-cast into a solvable form as a mixed-integer non-linear problem. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates energy-dependent and distance-dependent variations. By comparing our results with recent scanning tunneling spectroscopy data, we have identified key similarities between the theoretical spectra and the experimental results. Additionally, we have analyzed how slight fluctuations within material parameters can affect the resulting tunneling spectra. This theoretical approach may contribute to a new understanding of YSR states and their applications in this emerging field. Using this theoretical framework, we have generated tunneling spectrograms for Fe adatoms on Al and compared them with actual experimental findings, showing notable agreement. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that slight alterations in the Fe self-energy and YSR coupling strength are indeed minor and can be disregarded. Conversely, the spatial extent of the local density of states is significantly affected by variations in the exchange interaction between the magnetic impurity and the surrounding host material. This specific insight may aid in evaluating the theoretical precision of the developed approach. Lastly, we have explored the theoretical concept of environment-induced broadening of the local density of states, illustrating its applicability to this particular model. This research aims to bridge the theoretical divide between atomic-scale modeling and experimental scanning tunneling spectroscopy. However, it is essential to note that current atomic models are insufficient for accurately analyzing experimental data. Although the theoretical framework is capable of capturing material-specific characteristics, such models are still simplified and do not account for various complex phenomena, for instance, the subtle environmental effects of nearby magnetic impurities, which, despite being less pronounced, are also detectable through scanning tunneling spectroscopy. To tackle this specific issue, we have developed a theoretical framework focusing on the environmental effects of a single impurity embedded within a superconducting material. By analyzing this specific environment, we have discovered that the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities are significantly influenced by the presence of nearby environmental effects. This theoretical insight is reflected in the theoretical spectra, which show a significant shift in the YSR state energies as well as a notable broadening of the local density of states. By comparing our results with actual experimental findings, we have identified a significant correlation between the theoretical spectra and the experimental results, suggesting that the theoretical shift in the YSR state energies is indeed related to the experimental shift in the same state. Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) can efficiently register and accurately bound point cloud errors for relatively static scenes.  However, they fail to account for changing scenes where once registered points may have shifted due to motion.  Traditional methods like Submap Localizer (SL) address this by breaking down large-scale point clouds into smaller submaps and registering them one at a time.  Although effective, this process can be computationally expensive and impractical for processing point clouds in memory.  This work introduces a new approach called Buffer Triangulation (BT), which efficiently registers and accurately bound point cloud errors for dynamic scenes.  It achieves this by trading off some accuracy in point cloud registration for better efficiency.  This allows BT to run on lower-spec hardware, making it suitable for real-time applications.  Moreover, it enables accurate local bounding of point cloud errors, facilitating reliable self-diagnosis and fault detection.  This work also develops a diagnostic tool to monitor and analyze BT, providing users with meaningful error flags and measures of registration quality.  It further develops a method to estimate camera motion, facilitating fault detection in the process.  This work demonstrates the effectiveness and efficiency of BT in registering dynamic scenes, showcasing its potential for real-time diagnostic applications in planning and perception systems.  Additionally, it develops a method to integrate BT and NDT techniques, enhancing the robustness and accuracy of registration in the process.  This work further develops a framework for modeling and simulating distribution shapes, providing a foundation for modeling dynamic scenes and behavior.  This work presents results obtained using the simulated and real-world data obtained from the KITTI dataset, detailing the integration of BT with NDT for registration and fault detection purposes.  Lastly, it presents future avenues for research and development based on the proposed work.  This research was carried out within the context of the planning and perception laboratory at Carnegie Mellon University. Subjecting amorphous carbon and Ge to strong electron-phonon coupling via intense X-ray pulses can create highly non-equilibrium plasma. Research involving the non-equilibrium phase resulting from photoionization uses XANES, a technique that offers insights into electronic structure. However, changes observed in XANES are often attributed both to electronic structure changes and to structural modifications. An experiment was recently conducted at the L-Edge of Ge and at the C-K edge of amorphous carbon to investigate the phenomenon of non-linear XANES. Employing both experimental and computational methods, it was demonstrated that intensity-dependent changes can result solely from changes in the beam's absorption and scattering properties, eliminating the need to consider changes in the sample's structure. Calculations based on the multi-channel Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert model reinforced this conclusion, suggesting that observed magnetization dynamics are primarily influenced by non-linear beam-induced magnetization in ferromagnetic channels rather than by excitation of paramagnetic channels. Additionally, it was found that the ability of Ge to support stable and long-lived non-equilibrium magnetization, characterized by large angles of magnetization relative to the film's plane, is due to large channel splittings in ferromagnetic Ge. Conversely, carbon was found to support magnetization perpendicular to its planes only at much lower angles of polarization. An analytical model based on excitations and dissipation in a two-channel model also showed that the rates of decay in both channels are equal, leading to an extended lifetime of non-equilibrium states along paths with lower energies. These findings highlight the capability of XANES to study transient electronic states with high energy resolution, offering insights into the fundamental physics of photoexcitation, magnetization, and electronic screening. Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue that experts struggle with.
Recent studies propose the use of deep learning techniques for automated
segmentation of MS lesions, but they rely on large amounts of annotated data
or suffer from biased predictions. A primary challenge is combining the benefits
of recent state-of-the-art deep learning methods while reducing their data demands.
We address this challenge by developing a semi-supervised deep learning method
that automatically identifies and verifies MS lesions from a limited set of labeled
images. For verification, we employ a deep neural network, trained on synthetic
data, to assess the likelihood that an unsupervised region contains a genuine MS
lesion, thus enabling users to select and retain verified lesions for training the
primary unsupervised segmentation model. We validate our approach on a dataset
of 100 labeled images and compare its performance to that of recent deep
learning methods requiring substantial annotated data. Our approach shows a mean
diameter overlap of 73\% between the user-selected regions and the unsupervised
prediction, outperforming other deep learning techniques on the same dataset. A
further evaluation shows that two of three evaluated clinical user methods produce
better results when the proposed unsupervised verification method is applied
compared to a fully automated approach that does not involve user input. Importantly, our approach improves the user's ranking of overlap from 54\% to 73%. A
subsequent study indicates that increasing the number of verified lesions leads to
favourable shifts in the RoI (Region of Interest) overlap metric. Our findings
suggest that our approach may be beneficial in clinical practice, as confirmed by a
clinical user experiment. Upon reviewing the outcome, users prefer the proposed
unsupervised verification method with interactive retuning of verification outcomes
over the fully automated version. Consequently, MS lesion segmentation accuracy is
further enhanced when the user interactively refines the verification process,
demonstrating the value of human expertise in the cycle. Although not recommended
for general usage, our approach indicates a viable path to integrate deep
learning technology into clinical practice. Ultimately, a combination of both
technical advancements and clinical expertise contributes to achieve satisfactory
results in MS lesion segmentation. A significant challenge remains to further
develop multiple sclerosis lesion detection technology to address a range of
additional clinical challenges beyond lesion segmentation. In response, we propose a
Multiple Sclerosis lesion analysis challenge to foster future research along
these lines. A related manuscript is available online at https://

Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the special token embeddings, like separator and classification tokens in BERT, just before self-attention operations in each Transformer layer.
By doing this, PASTA can achieve performance on par with fine-tuning for natural language understanding tasks such as text categorization and named entity recognition while updating a mere 0.029% of all parameters.
Our contribution offers a straightforward yet efficient way to fine-tune models, with applications across various deployment scenarios for handling multiple tasks, and underlines the crucial importance of special tokens in pre-trained language models. The code and model weights are publicly available.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to identify relevant source context for target words. However, research reveals that target word generation solely depends on the previously generated words in the target sequence, not the current target word and corresponding source context. This phenomenon challenges the essence of the attention model in NMT. To address this, we propose a novel attention mechanism, referred to as the look-ahead attention, which allows the model to consider future target words during source context calculation. Experimental evaluations on the English-to-German and English-to-German datasets show substantial enhancements in translating in-domain and out-of-domain text, with notable improvements of  in terms of BLEU scores, particularly in the realm of low-resource machine translation. Additionally, we provide insightful qualitative analysis of the attention weights to demonstrate its enhanced performance. Furthermore, we conduct a thorough analysis, combining the proposed look-ahead attention with diverse choice of source and target sentence ordering, resulting in improved accuracy for 10 languages across the multiUN and WMT datasets. Results indicate that the best results are achieved on the english-german dataset with a siamese sequence-to-sequence model using choice of source and target sentence, while the look-ahead attention yields improved performance on all selected languages. On the multiUN dataset, the best results are achieved with a rank 4 of source and target sentence, while an rank 1 is preferred on the wmt datasets. The source behind the diffuse gamma-ray background is currently unknown. However, various galactic features such as star-forming and starburst galaxies, black holes, and cosmic clusters may all play a part in this phenomenon. In our research, we use the properties of galactic clusters to understand their gamma-ray emission and how it relates to their electron proton ratio. We analyze gamma-ray data from 0.1 to 50 GeV using 10 years of Fermi-LAT data, and our results show a strong correlation between gamma-ray emission and thermal sunyaev-zel'dovich effect in clusters. Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. Firstly, we consider oscillating primordial features, encompassing cases of massive field oscillations and oscillatory features in the inflationary potential. Secondly, we look at any sharp feature within an inflationary model. These features can induce unsuppressed quantum fluctuations in heavy fields, leaving detectable signatures in the tensor power spectrum. Our research collects the current understanding of these unconventional signatures, including their potential origins, advantages, and limitations, and discusses their feasibility through lensed CMB data, particularly using the cross-correlation of $E$- and $B$-modes to filter out common linear temperature fluctuations. This work aims to inspire future investigations into the signals generated by heavy localized fields or field oscillations in modulated inflation, leveraging the capabilities of the Simons Observatory and the ground-based CMBPol survey. Moreover, we suggest exploring primordial features as a means to constrain the spectral index and the primordial amplitude through the study of $TB$ cross-correlation data. This work supplements our companion paper, where the tensor power spectrum is derived for oscillating features, including oscillatory potentials and oscillatory features in the $f_{NL}$ term. Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain these models can be particularly challenging. To address this issue, a framework called LaViSE is proposed to enable convolutional neural networks to describe their internal workings in plain text. By using generic image data, this approach creates a link between visual and semantic information, allowing for generalization. The LaViSE framework has a flexible structure, making it possible to analyze any convolutional neural network, regardless of its purpose or domain. Furthermore, this technique can be used as a tool for identifying the weaknesses of visual models and developing new ones. To demonstrate its capabilities, this paper presents experiments explaining models in the fields of medicine, where expert feedback is provided for evaluation purposes. The code and model weights for the LaViSE framework are available for public access.

The ongoing Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) epidemic in sub-Saharan Africa has devastating consequences for the region's communities, with nations striving to enhance awareness as a key strategy to combat the disease. Previous studies on the topic have been conducted, including ours, which aimed to identify the current level of HIV awareness among young people in Ghana and explore factors influencing their awareness. Using a cross-sectional study involving 1020 students from three public universities in Ghana, we assessed their knowledge of HIV using a multiple-choice questionnaire and gathered demographic information via a self-administered questionnaire. Our findings revealed that overall HIV awareness among the participants was high, yet men were more informed than women. Additionally, we discovered that higher HIV awareness was associated with having completed secondary education and engaging in romantic relationships. Our study contributes to the understanding of the complex factors driving HIV awareness in Ghana and may help inform public health policies to combat the disease. It also sheds light on the effectiveness of prior awareness campaigns in the country, which have been implemented at significant cost, but have seemingly failed to yield the desired outcomes as evidenced by the participants' level of knowledge. We posit that these campaigns may have reached too narrow a scope and recommend targeting groups that are currently overlooked. We are confident that our research will stimulate further investigation into the efficacy of awareness campaigns in Ghana and the European Union's efforts to support the country in its efforts to combat HIV. A core tenet of Bayesian deep learning is the capacity to separate uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components. A network functioning under Bayesian principles serves as both a sampler for the posterior distribution of latent states and a approximation of the likelihood function, permitting the distinction between uncertainties arising from data (aleatory) and those stemming from the model itself (epistemic). We reveal, however, that this dual function allows for an exchange where model uncertainty is sometimes incorrectly classified as data uncertainty. This phenomenon occurs when the likelihood function incorporates the impact of the prior on the likelihood function, causing a blending of uncertainties. Through practical examples and theoretical justification, it is demonstrated that this merging of uncertainties leads to suboptimal decision-making, including inefficient evaluation of expected risks and inefficient sampling in Bayesian optimization. Proposed adjustments to existing predictive objectives can alleviate this error and provide an implementation of the maximum-normally-distributed-loss (MNDL) method to disentangle uncertainties based on the norm of the likelihood function. This approach is then applied to Bayesian optimization, offering an improved strategy that equals or improves existing results while relying on the same number of sampling steps. Furthermore, it is shown that the MNDL method equals or improves objective function estimates under comparable sampling requirements and offers an interpretable trade-off between objective function and predictive quality. The MNDL method is accompanied by complementary theoretical results, including lower bounds on Bayesian optimization loss for Bayesian networks and a novel objective function minimization algorithm. The theoretical work further bridges uncertainty analysis and optimization by establishing a correspondence between a probabilistic objective function and a Pareto-frontier of expected loss. The correspondence enables a trade-off between expected loss and posterior probability, and the work shows that the frequency of optimization failures decreases as the model gains experience. The research also reveals an unexpected equivalence relation between optimization failure and the blending of uncertainties. This equivalence implies that failure frequencies can be reduced by prioritizing the differentiation of uncertainties. A final evaluation demonstrates that the frequency of failure diminishes over time as the model becomes more discerning between uncertainties. The implementation of the MNDL method using variational auto-encoders as a prior sampler is illustrated through practical examples in the associated supplementary material. The research is applicable to a variety of real-world Bayesian optimization use cases, including commodity pricing, hyperparameter tuning, and autonomous racing strategies. The debate on turbulent effects influencing magnetic activity in stars is ongoing.
Our research uses global convective dynamo simulations to calculate transport coefficients
for magnetic field evolution, which vary based on the magnetic field's strength and structure.
To derive statistical insights, we employ a mean-field approach and observe the decay
of magnetic energy in solar-like stars, finding that the decay rate is dominated
by turbulent diffusion effects at early stages and by magnetic diffusion at later stages.
The associated magnetic field parameters show significant variations, which shift
from purely azimuthal to mixed azimuthal and poloidal patterns. By extrapolating our
results to the solar convective zone, we find that the characteristic timescales for
magnetic field adjustments within the convective zone are sufficiently short, but further
developments are necessary to capture the solar cycle's periodicity, energy distribution
and other characteristics. Therefore, we propose cycle asymmetries, statistical cycle
fluctuations and cycle irregularities as important topics for future star dynamo research.

By reducing the complex model into a non-interacting chain with varying site potentials, we demonstrate that despite the presence of bosonic excitations, quasiparticles are stable when the site potential is sufficiently positive. Furthermore, our research encompasses the braided Thompson groups $BF$, $\widehat{BF}$, and $\widehat{BV}$. Alongside existing results in \cite{Kodama:2020to}, our findings confirm that these braided groups display linear divergence as well. The same principle applies to the braided versions of $F_n$, $T_n$, and $V_n$. Lastly, our research also considers the wreath Thompson group $V_{\mathcal{W}}$. Although it has not been established whether it is linearly divisible, our results show that it is virtually linearly divisible. The same logic applies to the wreath versions of $F_n$ and $T_n$. In contrast, our calculations indicate that the wreath version of $T$ is not virtually linearly divisible. Utilizing crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk to acquire top-tier human annotations proves more complicated than initially thought, influenced by several key factors, such as task instructions and annotator compensation, among others. To prevent inaccurate annotations which could mislead automatic summarization systems, we develop a multi-stage recruitment process targeting high-quality MTurk workers. By establishing a rigorous evaluation pipeline, we demonstrate the ability to exclude unskilled workers before evaluation tasks are initiated, and subsequently collect reliable annotations while maintaining efficient resource allocation. The proposed approach serves as a model for selecting qualified annotators in other complex annotation endeavors. Additionally, since the automatic summarization field is particularly susceptible to biased summaries, we investigate the impact of biased summaries on annotator judgment and identify instances where annotators' judgments are inconsistent. The proposed method for selecting MTurk workers and annotating summaries is available online to support research in the field of automatic summarization. The associated dataset can be accessed at: https://github.com/ilec-frcn/MECHANISME. Text-video retrieval, an essential task of practical importance, has seen escalating interest, with the focus on crafting nuanced spatial-temporal video representations being a major research priority. Current state-of-the-art models for text-video retrieval primarily utilize pre-trained vision backbones with rigid network architectures, thereby hindering the ability to further refine the video representation and yielding suboptimal results. To overcome this limitation, we present TS2-Net, a groundbreaking transformer architecture incorporating dynamic token shifting and selection, which effectively tailors token sequences to capture the inherent motion in videos. By enabling flexible token selection, the proposed model effectively extracts relevant spatial-temporal video representations, thereby enhancing the overall retrieval performance. Extensive experiments validate the efficacy of TS2-Net, with its code being publicly available for review. This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 62171302), the Guangzhou Key Lab (Grant No. 2021B11T206030), and the CAAI Helixtren Research Foundation (Grant No.HCIC212013402). We are honored to receive the AAAI 2023 Best Paper Award courtesy of Association for Advancement of Artificial Intelligence. TS2-Net won the first place in two major challenges, Video-Text Retrieval and Action-Text Retrieval of ActivityNet, and is the state-of-the-art method of IBM Video-Text. It achieved the results on ActivityNet using an off-the-shelf model and hyperparameters. We used uniform weight distribution for token loss function and 2 as the shift multiplier. We used 128 tokens with 28 head attention in the transformer architecture and a patch size of 16 for tokenization. We used one token shift module and one token selection module per block and two TS2-Net blocks. We used an R50-C4 vision backbone with contrastive learning of ViT-B/32 for tokenization of our method. We used an off-the-shelf AdamW optimizer with weight decay of 0.1 and epoch of 36 for training. We used off-the-shelf memory efficient transformer and maximum pool for the token selection module. We used 2048 tokens (256 per frame) with 75 clips for evaluation of our method. We used 64 tokens with 10 clips for inference of our method. This project involves rectifying the inaccuracies in previous quantum mechanics interpretations, eliminating extraneous calculations and parameters that have complicated the field. We introduce more suitable approaches to understand how gravitational fields affect quantum system energy levels. This work specifically focuses on how gravitational fields affect particles in free fall and those that are stationary. We provide streamlined explanations for related concepts, eliminating distractions from irrelevant ideas and concentrations, and place them within the broader context of established quantum mechanics frameworks, including the relativistic theory of gravity. We then discuss recent discussions about the role of reality in quantum mechanics and the seemingly contradictory requirements of reality and relativity in quantum mechanics. We explore the implications of these ideas, including the end of matter existence at a certain distance from the center of the Earth's gravitational field, and the possibility that the ground state of certain quantum systems in gravitational fields is impossible to achieve. We also derive new mathematical equations that describe the impact of a pure gravitational field on quantum systems in free fall, and outline the challenges of extending existing quantum mechanics frameworks to accurately capture the impact of gravitational fields at various scales, from terrestrial to cosmic. We consider the relevance of quantum mechanics for objects of any size, and speculate about the applicability of quantum mechanics to the cosmos and subatomic particles. We explore the intriguing idea that quantum mechanics might reveal inherent flaws in the standard relativity theory model and the fundamental principles of Einstein. We then conclude the inquiry by outlining future projects aimed at understanding the impact of gravitational fields on quantum systems in free fall, while acknowledging existing research limitations due to incomplete knowledge of quantum mechanics for objects under the influence of both linear and rotational motions. Our research involves exploring the thermal behavior of the Bose-Hubbard model in a two-dimensional lattice with a mixture of bosons of different spin types. As the Rashba spin-orbit coupling increases, the thermal behavior of the system changes significantly due to its anisotropic nature. In a strong spin-orbit coupling setting, the system undergoes various phase transitions, starting with the superfluid phase, which then transitions into a Mott insulator phase, and ultimately may undergo a second superfluid transition. Our analysis reveals that a more substantial interaction level is required to trigger the superfluid to Mott insulator transition as Rashba coupling increases. In the Mott insulator phase, the different spin components of the bosons are spatially separated, and their densities are anisotropically distributed due to the influence of the Rashba coupling. Our findings also indicate that a disorder potential can have a substantial impact on the thermal behavior of the system, particularly in the vicinity of the superfluid to Mott insulator phase transition. Furthermore, in the disordered system, the critical interaction level for this phase transition decreases with growing spin-orbit coupling, and both spin types of the bosons remain condensed in the superfluid and Mott insulator phases, with their densities being anisotropically distributed due to the influence of the disorder potential and Rashba coupling. Our work involves an expansion of the Bose-Hubbard model in terms of the mean field theory, with the Rashba coupling being treated within the rotating frame formalism. Our research provides insights into the possible realization of the superfluid Mott insulator transition in the optical lattice by controlling the Rashba coupling and disorder potentials. Our findings may be extended to other spin-orbit coupled systems involving the Bose-Hubbard model. The intricate connection between many-body interactions and the spatial dimension of a system plays a pivotal role in various quantum phenomena that emerge from these interactions. A compelling example of this relationship is the behavior of a Bose gas confined to a one-dimensional space, where the presence of phase states and Regel branching points gives rise to non-analyticities in thermodynamic quantities, which could manifest as discontinuities in the system's internal energy upon heating. The existence of these discontinuities suggests that one-dimensional Bose gases do not fully thermalize when heated to high temperatures, unlike their higher-dimensional counterparts. To investigate this phenomenon further, we examined the relationship between the momentum distribution function and the internal energy of the system and discovered that it exhibits characteristic "sawtooth-like" patterns in addition to these discontinuities, indicating that the momentum distribution function may serve as a more robust "thermometry" for quantum many-body systems. Furthermore, through the application of the time-local Heisenberg matrix equation, we found that the correlation time in one-dimensional Bose gases displays pronounced oscillations when the ratio of interaction strength to confinement strength approaches a specific value. The unusual phenomenon of "thermodynamic discontinuity" in one-dimensional Bose gases is a distinct example of the complex and often counterintuitive effects that arise from confinement-induced multi-body correlations, which can be potentially exploited for the manipulation of attractors in a wide range of applications to active metasurface systems and nanophotonics. The study of "thermodynamic discontinuity" in one-dimensional Bose gases also sheds light on the broader implications of confinement on the thermodynamic properties of quantum few- and many-body systems, which is currently being investigated further. In particular, we have observed a similar phenomenon in a two-dimensional Bose gas confined to a square boundary, which is currently being prepared for publication separately. The generalization of our research to other types of quantum systems, including the study of Fermi gases, is also underway. The unique "thermometric" properties of the momentum distribution function could potentially be replicated in a range of experimental systems, such as those employing optical cavities, where the manipulation of atom-like modes using individual photons and quantum optical nonlinearities may allow for the realization of a "thermometer" that operates independently of energy. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified signal denoising and IBI estimation as a significant area of focus. Recent breakthroughs have involved the use of deep learning, which has significantly improved signal quality and diagnostic accuracy, far exceeding previous limitations. A novel deep learning approach is being developed using a Tiramisu autoencoder to effectively filter out motion interference in ECG signals and accurately estimate IBIs. Our research shows significant advancements in estimating IBIs from signals with signal quality that has been restored to an R-RR interval of at least 0.8. Our ECG denoising model outperformed the traditional Recurrent Neural Network in estimating IBIs, which showed a mean absolute error of less than 20 milliseconds when trained on 852 patients and 1300 corresponding R-RR time series. Our research shows that our approach can effectively estimate IBIs and restore signal quality on a variety of ECG datasets, which can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. It may also be used to enable remote monitoring of individuals by analyzing how effectively their ECG signals are restored and IBI estimates converge. To utilize contemporary computing systems efficiently, an important consideration is reducing random memory accesses, as they can lead to significant performance degradation. To address this challenge, an data compression method known as tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) can be employed to compactly store matrices and tensors while enabling fast access to the original data. Nevertheless, the efficacy of this approach depends on the efficiency of data compression, and poor compression rates result in substantial overheads in subsequent computations.

In this research, a data compression scheme that minimizes random memory accesses during the computation of t-SVD is proposed. To reduce overheads, an online data compression method that incrementally compresses input data is developed and incorporated into t-SVD computations. Specifically, an algorithm based on low-rank matrix completion is used to efficiently compress matrices, and an adaptive thresholding strategy is employed to further accelerate computations. The results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves comparable performance to standard t-SVD algorithms with optimal data compression, and outperforms them with less compression overheads. The proposed method also exhibits efficiency in handling real-world data with applications in image processing, video streaming, and graph analytics. To facilitate its adoption, an open-source implementation of the proposed scheme is provided. Additionally, the paper includes a supplementary section containing additional computational results, including comparisons with other compression methods, that further validates its effectiveness. This scheme can be extended to other compressed linear solvers, offering opportunities for future improvements. The paper also includes a public data repository containing input data used in the study, located at https://github.com/ponciano/t-SVD-compression. Specifically, the dataset includes the SIFT feature vectors used in image processing and the Compressed Sensing Data used in computer vision. The paper acknowledges the grant provided by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research. In conclusion, an implementation guide and code repository are made available at https://github.com/ponciano. Additionally, the research is further expanded upon in a related paper that investigates the application of t-SVD-based compression in image recognition. In this study, the computational efficiency of t-SVD is demonstrated through computational results and a case study on feature engineering in image recognition, and an implementation guide and code repository are provided at https://ponciano.github.io. The research gleans insights and future directions for efficient image recognition, and a publicly accessible repository containing the computational results can be found at https://ponciano.github.io.

This study enhances the field of Deep Metric Learning by proposing a new network design, known as the Large Margin Dissimilarity Network (LMDA). It seeks to widen the margin between dissimilar data, thereby enhancing the embedding space's discriminative properties. To achieve this goal, LMDA incorporates a new loss function that combines the features of siamese positive samples using a folding technique, resulting in more explicit negative sample separation. Additionally, the network utilizes a layer-wise strategy to widen the embedding space, incorporating a residual learning strategy to retain information from earlier layers. Comparisons with existing methods demonstrate that LMDA's large margin approach successfully improves the precision of metric learning on various datasets when considering traditional deep metric learning approaches. It also competes favorably with recent explorations in metric learning, while outperforming traditional deep learners on several benchmarks. Importantly, LMDA's design offers a straightforward and efficient implementation, thereby serving as an alternative to existing deep metric learning approaches. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Gimeteo/DeepMetricLearning.git. A pre-trained model for the MNIST dataset can also be accessed through the same GitHub repository. Lastly, the paper provides analyses and discussions of issues relating to margin in deep metric learning. In various fields such as medicine, psychology, and economics, researchers frequently assess the impact of interventions using randomized controlled trials, which often aim to establish cause and effect through randomized assignment. However, traditional methods used to analyze these trials are restricted to continuous outcome variables. We have developed a novel approach that extends the framework to binary and count outcome variables within the context of hidden variable models. We present mathematical proofs demonstrating that our method estimates the unconfoundedated average, direct effect, and mediated effects by incorporating multiple covariates to balance confounding factors. We also introduce a compact representation of the proposed estimator and provide the variance-covariance matrix of the estimate, which facilitates the assessment of statistical significance. Through a comprehensive empirical analysis across different scenarios, we have established the robustness and reliability of our approach. We have also presented two case studies showcasing the practical application of our method to real-world data. Furthermore, the source code and supplementary information are publicly available for download. 

The novel approach we have proposed builds upon existing work by valenzuela2021 addressing limitations in balancing confounding factors, minimizing compression artifacts, and generalizing the framework to multiple outcome types. Additionally, our contribution extends that of hotz2021 by balancing confounding factors, accounting for hidden variables, and generalizing the framework to binary and count outcome variables.

Determining the fundamental parameters of star clusters is a vital component of astrophysical research. Utilizing the Gaia DR2 survey provides an opportunity for precise assessments of star positions, parallax, and motion based on uniform photometric data, thus enabling the determination of accurate cluster membership probabilities. Focused on the Melotte 72 open star cluster, located 2345+/-108 parsecs away and 1.0+/-0.5 billion years old, our research leverages Gaia DR2 to derive valuable cluster metrics such as radial profile, reddening, luminosity, and mass functions. Additionally, total mass and galactic coordinates are calculated. Evaluating potential member candidates based on their luminosity and mass functions reveals 338 probable cluster members, comprising 75 faint objects below the Gaia's sensitivity limit. The analysis of cluster dynamics also shows no evident hierarchy in the velocity distribution of stars. What's more, a prominent mass function exhibits a power-law slope of 2.24±0.4, displaying a mass plateau in the mass range of 1.6 to 3 times the mass of the sun, indicating a significant ratio of brown dwarfs to the sun in Melotte 72. Moreover, mass function analysis reveals that the initial mass function is roughly 0.5-0.7 times the mass of the sun, indicating a moderate level of mass segregation. Despite initial signs of dynamic evolution in the cluster, our dynamical analysis failed to identify any ordered flow. Consequently, our research contributes new knowledge regarding the dynamics of the Melotte 72 star cluster. The Gaia survey is revolutionizing the field of star cluster astrometry, allowing derived parameters to match those extracted from the initial photometric analysis. Such comprehensive multivariate data offers novel opportunities for research, enhancing our understanding of star dynamics. Further comprehensive research of star dynamics, using initial photometric data, is inevitable. A significant challenge in analyzing complex information on a higher dimensional scale is developing suitable metrics for feature space dimensionality and topological characteristics. This work proposes an efficient, adaptive technique for computing a key set of topological metrics, namely Betti numbers, which quantify features such as holes and cavities within the data. Our approach leverages the simplicity of simplicial complexes and partitions the data into progressively larger subsets to construct an efficient, scalable algorithm. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed method demonstrates its effectiveness using a diverse range of data sets, and showcases significant performance improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we provide detailed mathematical justifications for handling specific data set challenges like noisy data points and irregular spatial relationships. Furthermore, we suggest potential applications of topological metrics in data set analysis, such as identifying data set scale, evaluating clustering performance, and revealing complex relationships in data sets. Finally, we propose a novel Python tool, 'gpflearn', which provides an implementation of the proposed method and other techniques for computing Betti numbers and Betti spectra, along with supporting supplementary material and a live demo. The 'gpflearn' library is available for download at https://github.com/krishanio/gpflearn. A curated version of the code is shared at https://github.com/krishanio/topological-metrics-repo, and the accompanying data sets can be accessed at https://github.com/krishanio/mt-datasets. A pre-print version of the paper is shared at https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.13204, and the research was supported by the grant number HA3019 from Institute of Science and Technology, University of Applied Sciences. A video explaining the research is available at https://youtu.be/6O9tB9BQ8E. A conference presentation is shared at https://youtu.be/6O9tB9BQ8E. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed adaptive technique in handling data set challenges and showcases its efficiency and scalability. Through its applications in feature space dimensionality and topological characteristic analysis, the research highlights the relevance of the proposed method to various machine learning domains. Our 'gpflearn' library provides a user-friendly implementation of the proposed method and other techniques to support future research in data set analysis. Our live demo at https://gpflearn-demo.io/ showcases the effectiveness of the proposed method in real-world scenarios. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent direct depth estimation, and a third method employing predicted semantic segments and point clouds. When comparing these approaches to traditional calibration techniques, the results indicated that the methods involving direct depth prediction and semantic segmentation produced more accurate outputs, with significant improvement when combining the two methods. Furthermore, the integrated framework demonstrated robust performance across various testing scenarios, yielding calibration results comparable to those obtained through traditional methods on average, with a notable margin of improvement in terms of accuracy when considering outliers. The implementation details can be found on the repository at https://github.com/fatemehkarimii/homecamera_calibration. We also developed a research pipeline to automatically prepare datasets for other cameras and scenes in addition to the previously mentioned code. Using a trained model as intermediate step has certain benefits such as bypassing the need to collect actual data, eliminating the requirement for pairs of images in the training process, and allowing for increased flexibility in terms of calibrating the camera's position after it has been trained. The corresponding framework can be accessed at https://github.com/fatemehkarimii/homecamera_calibration/tree/cc. Furthermore, the results indicate that the methods involving direct depth prediction and semantic segmentation, and combining them, can lead to accurate results with values up to 0.8 months in terms of time axis adjustment when analyzing the data plots. The framework and code utilized are based on versions 2.0.1 for KF-SLAM, 1.0 for PDC, and 1.0 for SSC. The corresponding zipped code sources for the project can be found at https://github.com/fatemehkarimii/homecamera_calibration/archive/main.zip. The research was supported by a grant from the Robotics Research and Training Center of Iran. The data preparation code can be found at https://github.com/fatemehkarimii/homecamera_calibration/tree/data. The corresponding video can be found at https://youtu.be/FgkOaOEyC9E. Reinforcement learning treats policies as black-boxes that take a state and output an action to maximize rewards, but it fails to consider the constraints that are inherent to most real-world applications. Constrained reinforcement learning addresses this shortcoming by incorporating systems constraints into the learning process, but it has been limited in its ability to handle complex constraints that are often present in applications such as power plants and data centers. To overcome this shortcoming, this research introduces an approach called Lagrangian learning for constrained reinforcement learning, which has been proven to be computationally efficient and effective in distributed settings. To further illustrate the versatility of the proposed approach, this research also presents case studies in the operation of power plants and data centers. Moreover, this research provides guidance on how to distribute Lagrangian learning across distributed systems in a manner that minimizes communication overhead. Results from simulation experiments reveal that the proposed learning method yields better performance outcomes compared to unconstrained reinforcement learning and other constrained learning methods, such as primal-dual reinforcement learning. The outcome of the research demonstrates the ability of the proposed learning method to reduce communication overhead while delivering performance outcomes that are on par with optimally configured policies for distributed settings. The research also includes an analysis of how to generalize the approach to multiple criteria and provides insights into future research directions. The study's efficacy in distributed systems further underscores the potential of the proposed learning method to tackle various real-world challenges. The research code is also made available to facilitate replication of the results. The research was conducted at Virginia Tech. The research was supported by the National Science Foundation Grant RII-1845183. The research corresponds to an arXiv e-print at arXiv:2107.04223. The research method can be applied to a wide range of real-world applications, including those with complex systems constraints that are difficult to optimize. The research method aims to improve policy optimization by providing an effective and efficient constraint handling mechanism. The research targets a broad class of reinforcement learning problems that are constrained. The research evidence demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed Lagrangian learning in constrained reinforcement learning. The research evidence further demonstrates the improved outcome of the proposed learning method over other methods. The European Space Agency's GAIA mission will create a detailed 3D chart of the galaxy by studying a small percentage of the 100 billion stars within it, with the ultimate goal of producing a map to an unparalleled degree of accuracy. This article will outline the mission's underlying concept, key objectives, and scientific goals, as well as highlighting the significant technological innovations and improvements that have been realized during the preparation phase for the mission. Ultimately, the article will discuss the prospective scientific outcomes that the mission is expected to yield. Nonetheless, the article will primarily concentrate on the methodology employed for the mission's primary parameter, parallax, with a focus on the technique of data processing, including preliminary results from mock data. Finally, the article will discuss the potential additional scientific benefits that can be derived from the data collected during the mission, with a special emphasis on the study of star clusters. This article is based on a comprehensive review that was prepared by the respective Working Groups within the Low-Latitude Giant Branch Baryon Science Group for GAIA. The key findings from this review are presented in a series of articles within this journal, with the present paper representing the first installment. The subsequent articles within this journal will delve into respective scientific topics, with the present paper serving as an introductory overview outlining the mission's concept, key objectives, and underlying scientific principles. A listing of the various key scientists associated with the Low-Latitude Giant Branch Baryon Science Group for GAIA, along with their respective areas of expertise, can be found within the appendix of this article. The subsequent articles within this journal will be identified by their respective DOIs, with the corresponding reference provided in the footer of each page. Since tree-width is a crucial characteristic determining the complexity of vertex separator in computational theory, we argue that our algorithm is nearly optimal in terms of both memory and time complexity. Furthermore, we claim that any algorithm achieving a time complexity of O(n) bits assisted by a data structure of a fixed size can be transformed into a program using a data structure of size linear to treewidth. A substantial portion of network information comes from edge weights that are frequently overlooked in network clustering. We introduce two fully weighted measures that enable us to capture both the strength and direction of network connections. We compare these measures to alternative, hybrid methods that incorporate both edge weights and graph structure. Our research examines the sensitivity of different methods to artificial and real-world networks, using communities and gene networks as reference points. The results show that fully weighted measures produce more consistent and stronger resolutions than expected (or "zonotopes") in comparison to hybrid methods, which often yield unclear or contradictory results. We further applied these measures to a set of datasets from diverse fields, including biology, social networks, and material science, and obtained meaningful results that align with available knowledge. Our findings also reveal distinct characteristics of network clusters using fully weighted methods that are not exposed by traditional structural methods. Ultimately, our work contributes to the understanding of network community assignment and refinement. One notable strategy to embed prior knowledge about physical systems into machine learning models is physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). These models have been observed to perform well with smaller training datasets, excel in generalizing outcomes, and reduce training time. This paper demonstrates the advantages of using PINNs compared to purely data-driven neural networks in terms of both training performance and gaining insights into the quality of the approximated solutions. By considering PINNs that are trained with an underlying ordinary differential equation, we derive a strict upper limit on their approximation error. This error estimate is expressed in terms of the predicted solution and the differential equation's initial conditions, evaluated at fixed points. To establish a reliable bound, we compute the maximum value of the error function and the derivative of the error function. Our results indicate that PINNs can effectively control the approximation error by adjusting the training parameters. By applying the Kalman filter method, we obtain a more efficient way to select the training parameters that result in the smallest error. Our method also contributes to data efficiency and reduces the training time of PINNs. The theoretical findings and the proposed algorithm are validated through comprehensive numerical experiments. Our methods have been successfully applied to learning solutions of both linear and nonlinear ordinary differential equations as well as their use in real-world predictive challenges. The associated code is freely accessible at https://github.com/Jing-Jing-Long/Deep-Neural-Error-Calculator. Furthermore, the model's implementation for the recent ITC2022 predictive challenge can be found at https://github.com/Jing-Jing-Long/Deep-IC-Pro. Moreover, the model's implementation for the recent Challenging Predictive Colloids prediction
challenge can be found at https://github.com/Jing-Jing-Long/Deep-Colloid/Deep-Colloid.html. Our research highlights the potential of integrating PINNs with the Kalman filter to increase transparency and trustworthiness of deep learning models for functional data analysis. Additionally, our method leverages the embedding of prior knowledge to derive bounds on the approximation error that are not feasible using purely data-driven neural networks. Lastly, our method can also be employed to predict unknown data points, providing a reliable upper limit on the error that decreases as the network gains experience. For epidemiologic studies of large populations, accurate air pollution modeling is crucial. Leveraging advances in high-performance computing and machine learning has led to breakthroughs in air pollution modeling frameworks, allowing for more detailed simulations of complex atmospheric processes. Nonetheless, accurately predicting ambient concentrations of critical air pollutants remains a significant challenge. This research outlines a novel ensemble approach that combines spatial and temporal machine learning models operating on grids of pollutant concentrations. By employing extensive computational simulations, machine learning algorithms are trained to improve outcomes at a detailed resolution, building upon a coarser air pollution model. This novel method enhances the predictive capability of traditional models and offers flexible modifications to accommodate specific data limitations or preferences. To validate this approach, which relies on a vast synthetic dataset of 1 TB, statistical analysis confirms its efficacy and reliability. Detailed evaluation of this novel method's performance is presented using three real-world datasets from the United States. Moreover, this approach is applied to a European city to generate high-resolution air pollution maps, providing a practical application of the methodology that showcases its value in generating accurate air quality forecasts. Overall, this novel method holds considerable potential as an innovative tool for producing high-resolution air pollution models. Existing models can benefit from this approach by incorporating it as an additive component, thereby enhancing their predictive capabilities. By doing so, accurate air pollution models and forecasts can be developed at a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. This research demonstrates a practical application of machine learning for air pollution modeling, which can be applied to noise modeling as demonstrated in a companion paper. Graphene with gaps has been proposed to showcase the valley Hall effect, where different types of electrons exhibit opposing Hall behaviors controlled by geometric properties, specifically the Chern number (C).  We suggest that the actual phenomenon being observed in experiments is actually the orbital Hall effect, where the orbital angular momentum takes the place of the valley index, governed by an entirely different physical quantity, the orbital Hall conductivity (Ω0).  We derive and calculate this conductivity for a specific model featuring two atomic orbital systems and find its dimensionality to be fundamentally distinct from the Chern number's, thereby making Ω0 a more precise experimental target to achieve the desired valley Hall effect.  Furthermore, our work highlights the feasibility of producing the orbital Hall effect in a more straightforward and efficient manner than the valley Hall effect, thereby providing a foundation for the development of robust quantum devices.  Since the orbital Hall effect is primarily linked to the near-field, interference-based properties of light, an alternative approach to trigger the orbital Hall effect by controlling light's polarization instead of exploiting photon spin is proposed.  We believe that combining circularly polarized light with the orbital Hall effect offers greater control over the orbital Hall conductivity to achieve robust quantum operations, thereby making this approach applicable to a broader range of quantum technologies.  By leveraging the distinct mechanisms that mediate the orbital Hall effect, we can achieve a level of control that far surpasses the conventional valley Hall effect, thereby opening the door to more sophisticated quantum technologies.  As a final note, our work offers a strategy to achieve a quantum Hall effect without relying on a band gap by harnessing the concept of orbital Hall effect, thereby providing innovative methods for the development of quantum devices based on graphene and other 2D materials.  By extending the principles of valley Hall effect into the realm of orbital Hall effect, we can achieve robust quantum operations that far surpass the limitations of conventional valley flipping techniques, thereby making this approach a groundbreaking feat in the field of spin-based quantum technologies.  Moreover, our work provides a framework to achieve precise control over the quantum Hall effect at a microscopic scale, thereby offering an entirely new approach to exploit the valley and orbital Hall effects as distinct entities, thereby providing innovative methods for the development of carbon-based quantum devices. The growing importance of Adversarial Machine Learning within Computer Science can be attributed to vulnerabilities in models and crowd-sourced attacks on data. Over the past two years, research has gained momentum in graph adversarial attacks but Graph Classification remains an understudied area. The indirect utilization of Reinforcement Learning methods for graph classification, given that datasets involve discrete graphs with labels, stands in contrast to traditional approaches that use direct gradient optimization. This work aims to explore the novel threat of data manipulation during training (Data Poisoning) targeting Graph Classification neural networks via Reinforcement Learning agents. Furthermore, we develop a framework to automatically identify the most effective poisoning strategies, employing techniques such as Reinforcement Learning and Genetic Algorithms. Moreover, we present a method to quantify the robustness of Graph Classification neural networks against Data Poisoning attacks. Specifically, we introduce a robustness metric related to the loss of accuracy that an model incurs when subjected to attacks. To achieve this purpose, we simulate the behavior of a malicious adversary using a Genetic Algorithm search to optimize the attack. Results demonstrate the ability to significantly enhance the robustness of Graph Classification neural networks by selecting robust models or utilizing transfer learning strategies. Additionally, we show the potential of combining Data Poisoning defences with robustness metrics and Reinforcement Learning-based attacks. All source code is made available online. Graph Classification neural networks have been implemented using Pytorch and Adversarial attacks as well as Reinforcement Learning agents were developed in the A2C framework. The research was facilitated using a high-performance computing cluster. This work was carried out within the context of the RobustGraphNeuralNetworks Challenge 2021. The challenge's findings are presented in a separate publication. The research presented was made possible by the grant awarded to the work within the context of the programme. The future research perspective involves exploring novel techniques to enhance the robustness of Graph Classification neural networks and developing novel methods to combine defences and attacks. The research presented aims to contribute to the creation of safer Machine Learning models capable of robust performance against the most effective adversarial attacks, including Data Poisoning. The approach developed enables the creation of more realistic scenarios to evaluate the robustness of Graph Classification neural networks by simulating the behaviour of a malicious adversary using Genetic Algorithms. The research perspective involves the exploration of the potential to employ generative models and combine Data Poisoning and Robustness metrics in a unified manner. The research also involves the enhancement of robustness metrics to account for the more complex threat of Information Poisoning. The research aims to facilitate empirical studies

The development of extensive photometric catalogues across numerous sky regions has increased the need for a practical and efficient source matching technique to link photometric catalogues and astronomical databases. Despite existing methods, matching sources between photometric catalogues remains a complex task, especially with varying magnitude ranges and different error margins. Most techniques rely on literal and/or metric matching, but do not consider magnitude, potentially leading to poor results. We introduce a novel probabilistic algorithm that employs a Rayleigh test for statistical analysis and magnitude-based weighting to enhance literal and metric matching, resulting in improved cross-matching of photometric catalogues. We validate this method using simulated and real data, and compare its performance with established cross-matching techniques on 5 million optical sources. Our new approach successfully matches the Monte Carlo method, which serves as a baseline for comparison, by efficiently cross-matching the sources between two photometric catalogues with distinct magnitude ranges and different error margins. The proposed method is open-source, making it a practical and efficient tool for photometric catalogue cross-matching across various sky regions. It supports the spectroscopic follow-up observations component of the Revised Virtual Observatory Workshop (VOdw2) project, aiming to streamline the process of photometric and spectroscopic source association for astronomical research and spectroscopic follow-up efficiency. The cross-matching code is publicly available through the AstroPy package, at https://astropy.github.io/. Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, structured
conceptual frameworks called ontologies, which are used to improve efficiency and
accuracy in fields such as biology and medicine. However, as new knowledge emerges,
existing ontologies often require modification to accommodate this novel
information, which can be labor-intensive and costly if inaccurately applied. To
maximize the value of these frameworks, we developed an open-source tool to help
integrate new knowledge into them, minimizing the need for manual intervention.
This method relies on natural language processing technologies to identify and learn
new, previously undefined concepts from textual data, enabling us to incorporate
them into an existing ontology in an semantically meaningful way. The first public
evaluation of this approach was conducted, which involved integrating over 3,000 new
medical concepts into the NCI Biomedical Ontology (NCIT). Results showed a high
precision (91%) and exceptional recall (95%), which significantly outperformed
standard manual knowledge acquisition methods in terms of efficiency. The study
revealed the impact of partially applicable rules on recall rates and highlighted
the advantages of an ontology with a well-defined structure in the context of
knowledge automatic acquisition. The developed technique offers a cost-effective,
systematic way of integrating new knowledge into an existing ontology, which can be
utilized as an alternative to labor-intensive manual methods. The project is now
available for public use and future research aims to explore its applications in
other domains. The corresponding resources can be accessed at: \url{https://kangwoof.github.io/ KnowledgeGraphInjection/}. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views agents as constant seekers of information, with their brains equipping them to make inferences about the world by processing sensory data from external sources. Despite its wide applicability, active inference's biophysical roots remain unclear, with various implementations raising doubts about its broader potential. This study develops a unified framework for active inference, disentangling its intricacies and providing a mathematically coherent and easily implementable model that can be gradually refined to enhance its performance. We evaluate our framework's potential across different domains, successfully applying it to vision tasks and achieving a notable improvement in accuracy for a group of individuals who are blind and develop their own sensory interactions with the world through tactile feedback. We hope that our framework, built on a solid foundation of core concepts, will serve as a foundation for future explorations, with a vision for its applications extending beyond laboratory studies to real-world issues such as understanding and developing the sensory capabilities of human beings and developing AI systems that are autonomous and data-efficient. We make our code available for free, with a hope that it can facilitate replication, analysis, and further advancements in the field. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/joIncube/Active_Inference_Framework.

Our research focuses on the Soret effect in binary mixtures composed of smaller (dimer) and larger (monomer) units. The smaller molecules are assumed to be composed of two smaller units that can move independently, enabling them to interact with the larger molecules more efficiently. The Soret effect in this system is studied using molecular dynamics simulations and analyzed through various analytical methods. The results show a positive Soret effect at low concentrations of smaller molecules, but a reversal of this effect at higher concentrations. The underlying reasons for this phenomenon are explored through various theoretical approaches. The presence of an intense positive Soret effect at low concentrations of smaller molecules can be understood by considering the molecules as particles that must be completely disordered in order to interact. The efficient separation of these molecules in response to a temperature difference is only possible if they are moving freely, which implies that they are relatively small. The Soret effect reverses direction when the smaller molecules are not independent entities and are unable to escape the larger molecules. The identification of a critical concentration at which the Soret effect changes direction requires a detailed analysis of the thermodynamic properties of the system. The enthalpy and entropy of the system show distinct changes at the critical concentration, but these changes can be more accurately quantified using a temperature scale that factors in the molecular size. The Soret effect is more easily understood when considered in terms of an order parameter that reflects the tendency of the molecules to form ordered structures, or dimers. The formation of these structures is more prominent at higher concentrations of smaller molecules, but a reversal of this trend can be observed by accounting for the size of the molecules in the system. The presence of an intense positive Soret effect at low concentrations of smaller molecules and a reversal of this trend at higher concentrations suggests that the Soret effect in this system can be more easily understood if the size of the molecules is taken into consideration. The use of a temperature scale that factors in the size of the molecules provides valuable insights into the thermodynamic properties of the system, enabling a more accurate understanding of the Soret effect in binary mixtures composed of smaller and larger units. The presence of an intense positive Soret effect at low concentrations of smaller molecules and a reversal of this trend at higher concentrations is consistent with observations from experiments and simulations, providing valuable support for the theoretical approach. One of the most significant issues arising from agnostic domain shift in domain adaptive pedestrian detection is the prevalence of false positives.  As labeling each target domain's boxes is impractical, researchers focus on suppressing false positives in target domains using unsupervised methods.  To address this challenge, we transform the object detection task into a ranking task among positive and negative boxes, turning false positive suppression into an efficient box re-ranking problem without the need for manual annotation.  A secondary challenge in box re-ranking arises from the absence of labeled validation data, which is why we introduced the self-supervised evaluation metric from negative boxes and proposed a algorithm based on iterative optimization to automatically identify potential false positives and improve the accuracy of detection models.  Our approach is evaluated on the Caltech dataset and outperforms state-of-the-art models, with model$^{+}$ achieving an MAP of 34.7% and 42.1% in the minipeds and fullods of Caltech-10, respectively. This concept of "sibylvariance" holds that a well-intentioned NLP model should behave consistently across different inputs, even those outside its original scope. To address this, we developed a broadening technique that helps transfer learning by increasing the model's input range. Through experiments, we demonstrated the benefits of this technique and comparable approaches for NLP tasks, showcasing its potential to enhance NLP models' versatility and effectiveness. The code used in this research is available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/whw1996/sibylvariance. Additionally, we contributed a dataset of word replacement methods to aid further research in this area. To address this limitation, we established a dictionary of over 26 million word replacement suggestions, incorporating words across the entire English language spectrum.
