Researchers aim to create meta-learning algorithms that capitalize on previous experience to rapidly acquire new skills or adapt to new environments by utilizing representation learning techniques, which enable the transfer of knowledge across various tasks. As the interest in meta-learning grows, there is a pressing need to establish its theoretical foundations, particularly in terms of learning adaptable representations. In this research, we tackle the problem of multi-task linear regression where multiple related tasks share a common, low-dimensional linear representation. Our study provides effective, sample-efficient methods to address the dual challenges of learning a shared feature set from related tasks and transferring this knowledge to unseen tasks. This work sheds light on the central issue of meta-learning. Furthermore, we present theoretical limits on the minimum sample size required to learn a shared feature set for a set of N related tasks, with error rates proportional to 1/S^2 for N=S linear dimensions. Our results are demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments. Our study, therefore, contributes to the development of meta-learning as a field by establishing that linear regression can effectively learn a shared feature set to facilitate the transfer of knowledge across multiple related tasks. This study is further distinguished by its sample efficiency in learning a shared feature set for a large number of tasks, with error rates proportional to the inverse square of the number of tasks. We also investigate the effects of random Gaussian data on the performance of the developed methods. Our study provides the first analysis, to the authors' knowledge, of representation learning in the context of meta-learning. Our work has significant implications for understanding the central issue of meta-learning, specifically in the context of regression problems where the objective function is defined as the sum of task-specific loss terms. Each task loss function is assumed to be composed of a shared feature set shared by all tasks, leading to the emergence of a dual perspective, which is linear. Our study provides the first analysis, to the authors' knowledge, of representation learning in the context of meta-learning. Our work has a sample efficiency equivalent to the state-of-the-art in the context of regression problems, with certain assumptions composed of task-specific loss terms. Our study effectively addresses a particular instance of the general problem, specifically in the context of regression problems with linear objectives. The Turan number for an r-uniform graph F, denoted by ex(n, F), is defined as the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph on n vertices. The Turan density of F, denoted by pi(F), is defined as the limit of the maximum number of edges over the total possible number of edges as the number of vertices approaches infinity. Erdos-Stone-Simonovits' theorem established that the set of possible Turan densities for 2-uniform graphs is infinite, and for 3-uniform graphs, irrational Turan densities have been discovered, disproving a previous conjecture. We investigate whether irrational Turan densities exist in certain cases and show that the Lagrangian density of a specific 3-uniform graph is sqrt(3)/3, resulting in an irrational Turan density, which answers an open question posed by Baber and Talbot. We also show that the Lagrangian density of the graph obtained by adding an edge to the disjoint union of two complete graphs on n vertices is 2/n. The efficiency of deep learning semantic segmentation algorithms in identifying abnormalities on chest X-rays is limited by the laborious task of gathering annotated data. This study aims to explore how image enhancement techniques can alleviate this data labeling burden by facilitating the training of UNet-like neural networks on understaffed institutions. Initially, we assessed the impact of combining three image enhancement methods - color normalization, rotation, and flip - on reducing labeled data requirements, as these techniques are easily applicable and compatible with chest X-rays. By incorporating these methods as augmentations, we evaluated their contribution in decreasing the necessity for labeled data after the initial training of the network on a reduced dataset. Furthermore, we investigated the value of including rotation as an orientation augmentation. Ultimately, we analyzed the best approaches' performance in detecting pneumonia through semantic segmentation on the Mosaic Dataset, and compared them with a baseline model trained on the full dataset. This study's results and findings will guide institutions in determining which image enhancement techniques may replace labeled data, thereby optimizing resource allocation and efficiency. The data and code for this research are openly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/PerformanceAnalytics/ChestXRaySeg.git. This work has been presented at ECVA 2021. The related paper can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jim.2022.02.002. Experimental results indicate that using flip augmentation alone yields equivalent results to incorporating a range of both image enhancement methods and rotation as an orientation augmentation; notably, these approaches surpass the performance of the baseline model trained on the full dataset. These findings suggest that institutions may consider applying flip augmentation without needing labeled data to augmentations; by doing so, they can train a UNet-like neural network on a reduced dataset, thereby increasing efficiency. The proposed approach demonstrates potential in reducing the labeled data requirement by up to 100 data points, a reduction of considerable significance when considering the time-consuming process of annotating medical imaging data. This optimization not only accelerates the training process but also enhances the model's sensitivity to detect pneumonia through semantic segmentation on chest X-rays. The studies' outcomes and methods may inspire future research to uncover more sophisticated strategies to decrease the laborious task of data labeling in medical imaging. The related repository contains the time-consuming process of annotating chest X-rays for pneumonia detection, thereby making the study's findings relevant to a broader scope of researchers. As autonomous systems become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to establish a legal and regulatory framework for addressing harm caused by these systems to individuals. To establish a clear definition of harm, this study draws on concepts from causal models and utilitarianism by incorporating a metric known as harm's victim-centric value (HVC). The HVC calculation assesses harm by quantifying both the level of distress and the degree of deviation from an individual's expected outcome. We derive precise mathematical formulas to measure these aspects and illustrate the practical application of our method with a concrete example. Furthermore, this study investigates various modes of interference and establishes a universal formula for calculating harm in autonomous systems, specifically autonomous algorithms. To ensure the reliability of our measurement, it must align with the perceptions of those it quantifies. Crucially, we demonstrate that direct access to an autonomous system's decision-making process is necessary for an accurate assessment of harm. In addition, this study explores the algorithmic transparency required for equatable harm assessment and suggests a framework comprising four tiers of transparency, each providing an alternative method for evaluating harm in autonomous systems. Ultimately, we discuss the potential consequences and advantages of using our approach and highlight potential applications in managing liability, improving autonomous system performance, and developing policies, as well as identifying cases where our definition of harm and the associated value metric can be utilized. Ultimately, we discuss the significant implications and advantages of this method. In particular, it may serve as a useful tool for quantifying and optimizing liability, autonomous system performance, and policy development, as well as pinpointing instances where our definition and quantification can be applied. Notably, it may also facilitate the design of autonomous systems that cause less harm and enhance the way these systems operate. Interestingly, quantitative harm assessment could lead to an unexpected outcome: it may facilitate the creation of autonomous systems that cause less harm and lead to more efficient operations. In particular, it may encourage the design of autonomous systems that adopt operating protocols minimizing deviation from user expectations. Conversely, it may also enable fine-tuning of autonomous system settings to prevent harm and reduce responsibility and liability for such systems. Furthermore, it may facilitate informed consent by enabling the calculation of the potential harm and enabling individuals to make informed decisions about their interaction with autonomous systems. In particular, it may allow for the assessment of various interaction methods to identify which one poses the least risk. The MMLSpark library along with existing Spark features forms the foundation of the Deep Spark platform, a comprehensive machine learning system. To optimize performance, it features deep learning acceleration through employment of Spark's optimized execution mechanisms. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues, typically tackled with neural sequence-to-sequence models trained on extensive audio and text data. Although prior studies have been successful, they often require large datasets for training, which can't be applied to languages without sufficient resources. In an effort to bridge this gap, zero-shot speech-to-text translation has been explored where there's no prior knowledge about the audio and text streams. Previous research has made zero-shot translation possible between speech and text from the same language by leveraging large amounts of data for training speech and text recognition systems, which are then used to compute speech-to-text probabilities. However, extending zero-shot translation to translate between languages has proven difficult, particularly when it comes to English to non-English language translations, largely due to a lack of data. Our work reveals that, in fact, English to non-English translations are the easiest to translate zero-shot and that the problem gets progressively harder as we translate to languages further away from English. Our research also shows that translating zero-shot from speech to text across different languages is also easier when the target language is closer to English, and that the performance improves significantly when we increase the amount of data in the target language. Our best results were when we increased the amount of data in the target language, and when we increased the amount of data in the speech-to-text system, with the particular combination of these two factors greatly affecting the performance. Our best result was a the score that indicated very high accuracy, which suggests that zero-shot speech-to-text translation between languages is feasible, at least easily translating English to other languages. Our work also suggests that our speech-to-text system, which was trained using data from a large corpus of American English speech, was able to translate English to other languages better, at least easily. This work introduces a novel extension of the traditional heat conduction theory, encompassing cases with fading memory and incorporating the standard heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions as a particular instance. We delve into the well-posedness of systems comprised of equations akin to those by Coleman and Gurtin, further subject to dynamic boundary conditions with memory. These systems contain nonlinear elements situated both internally and on the boundary, with their behavior either dictated by classical dissipation principles or governed by a nonlinear balance condition. Moreover, we allow for disparate memory kernels between the interior and boundary of the domain. We prove the existence and uniqueness of solutions for these systems of nonlinear partial differential equations defined within a bounded open region in n-dimensional Euclidean space (where n is 1, 2, 3), allowing for arbitrary initial conditions and using methods applicable to nonlinear time-integral equations. This work builds upon previous work by the first author, initially published in 2013. We provide a comprehensive review, incorporating novel findings and additional commentary. Critical comments regarding the physical implications of these generalized models are also offered, alongside a discussion regarding their relevance, including comparison with measured data. Due to the highly interdisciplinary nature of this work, we touch upon applications from these fields, including elasticity for large deformations, damage in materials, electrically conducting fluids subject to dynamic boundary conditions, and generalized models of heat conduction. We refer to the contributions of other researchers in these respective disciplines. Furthermore, we outline open questions and possible avenues for future investigation. A substantial appendix is included, addressing issues such as the construction of appropriate function spaces and lemmas, essential for the novel contributions presented in this work. Comprehensive references to relevant literature are also provided. Due to space constraints, some unimportant details and secondary results are omitted, while their essence is captured through the use of interrelated comments and propositions. A list of names of individuals who provided feedback on earlier drafts is included, alongside an acknowledgement of financial support received during the completion of this work. Lastly, the Humanitarian Paper Award bestowed by the Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics (SIAM) is acknowledged. This work may be viewed as a research summary, incorporating the author's scholarly perspectives. Precise short-term forecasts of energy consumption are essential for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently, particularly with regard to highly disaggregated load distributions among a small number of customers, where individual behaviors tend to dominate aggregate consumption profiles. Since peak demand often drives energy distribution challenges, developing accurate timing and level predictions of daily peak demand is crucial, as traditional forecasting methods fail to live up to expectations due to their inherent limitations during peak hours. This research investigates the potential benefits and limitations of a graph convolutional network, dubbed identification of peak demand using GNNs or iGNET, when applied to time-series data to forecast peak demand, drawing comparisons with convolutional neural networks, long short-term memory networks, and Bayesian time-series models, specifically emphasizing the value of the neural network approach over the more conventional methods due to its data density capabilities and the superior forecasting results it provides when applied to data subsets, as well as its relative simplicity and abstracted data characteristics. Additionally, the study demonstrates the value of incorporating macropeak, or previously identified peak demand, as a supplementary input to enhance peak demand forecasting accuracy. Using real-world data from 1,700 low-voltage electricity networks, it was observed that macropeak identifies peaks with high accuracy about 5 days in advance, making it an essential component of the forecasting model. Applying iGNET to a dataset from a low-voltage network with 785 consumers showed that it yielded a 9.5% reduction in the forecast error when compared to the baseline, while achieving comparable results with aggregated energy consumption forecasts, often resulting in lower error values, as well as producing forecasts with reduced bias as the neural network's optimization objective naturally prioritizes minimizing the total forecast error, thereby implicitly reducing bias. Conversely, the peak demand forecasts derived from the LSTM model exhibited considerable bias, with higher error values than iGNET during morning peaks and lower error values at evening peaks, largely stemming from its failure to capture peak demand characteristics during midday hours. Similarly, the Bayesian time-series model, or BNS, demonstrated significant bias, with higher error values than iGNN during morning and lower error values at evening, largely resulting from its inability to capture peak demand at midday. The growth of machine learning algorithms has not entirely resolved the issues affecting AI performance, primarily due to limited data and insufficient resources. However, augmenting a model with relevant information can address some of these challenges to a degree. The difficulty in effectively integrating knowledge lies in the multiple forms of knowledge representation involved. This paper aims to provide an overview of various knowledge integration approaches and their effectiveness in machine learning applications. Furthermore, we intend to offer insights on the prospects of continuing research in this field and the potential benefits it could offer in the future. We also compile a list of prominent academic papers and conduct a systematic analysis of their key details and outcomes. Additionally, we outline several promising areas where further research is required to bring knowledge integration more thoroughly into the machine learning process. While these efforts still result in numerous open questions, we anticipate that significant advancements in natural language processing and machine learning will closely involve the effective integration of knowledge. Creating a reliable model for precise COVID-19 detection on chest CT scans poses significant difficulties despite considerable advancements. The issue often arises due to annotation biases affecting traditional supervised segmentation techniques, which rely on detailed boundary markings that are often unavailable for COVID-19. To overcome these challenges, we introduce an innovative framework that utilizes image-level labels, enabling the development of a highly accurate, unbiased detector. This novel approach leverages a unique two-stage process involving a novel self-supervised model and a deep learning framework for diffusion that rectifies diffusion bias. Notably, our solution outperforms current state-of-the-art methods utilizing either detailed boundary markings or weak labels, resulting in a 4.3% absolute percentage point improvement when using image-level labels, as well as reducing the average dice score by 0.038 when using full boundary markings. This superior performance, along with the elimination of diffusion bias, makes our solution a valuable resource for assessing COVID-19 through accurate lung lesion segmentation. The code and model for this solution are available on GitHub at https://github.com/berkantgul/COVID19-Lesion-Segmentation. We believe our work will contribute significantly to future research by offering a new image-level approach, which we plan to update as more data become available. Additionally, we will conduct thorough experimentation using more sophisticated techniques to expand the scope of our solution and advance the field. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge of the spine to accurately segment the vertebrae column. By employing a novel key-point localization network, the proposed method achieves the state-of-the-art results, yielding a very high identification accuracy rate of 98.77%, and outperforms existing approaches significantly, reducing the average number of identification errors per image to 0.223, with a corresponding significant increase in average classification precision to 98.77%, and overall computation time. The proposed method's efficacy has been successfully demonstrated on the publicly available dataset from the 2D Spine (2DSpine) Challenge. We extend this work to three-dimensional CT scans and conduct comprehensive experiments to further validate the method's reliability and scalability. Within an extremely high level of electron interaction with the surrounding electromagnetic field, temporary variations in the field energy lead to a steady state formation of an entwined state confined at the center of the barrier. As an incoming electron's energy aligns with that of this confined state, it undergoes rapid, inelastic scattering off the barrier, resulting in emission of a cavity-generated photon. This phenomenon is studied across varying barrier thicknesses, resulting in a range of photon energies from a few to multiple times the electron's kinetic energy. Furthermore, the probability of inelastic scattering events is found to depend inversely on the concentration of surrounding electrons, thus offering a potential approach to engineering and managing optical information transfer through a series of strongly interacting electron systems. The theoretical framework is grounded in a multi-electron variant of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation with an additional nonlinear element, induced by the electrons' feedback response on the cavity cavity. This paper outlines our method for utilizing central pattern generators (CPGs) in the control of a four-legged walking robot, which overcomes the limitations of pre-compiled gaits. By allowing the CPG learning algorithm to adapt pattern parameters in real time, the robot can seamlessly transition between diverse gaits without a need for explicit reconstruction. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by activating a set of physical actuators on our prototype robot that makes transitions to novel gaits based on predefined criteria. For instance, the robot can switch from a normal walking pattern to an escape gait triggered by an optical sensor detecting a barrier in its path. Furthermore, the fusion of CPGs and reinforcement learning holds promise in developing sophisticated multi-gait capabilities in robots. However, the current capability of reinforcement learning to generate stable gaits in robots is hindered by the extensive training time and instability during the learning process. To address this limitation, we developed an hybrid approach that combines model predictive programming and off-line reinforcement learning. By utilizing CPGs as starting points for gait configurations, we reduce the time and effort required for real-off-line reinforcement learning. As a result, the training time is significantly reduced and the learning process becomes more stable, which we demonstrate with our four-legged walking robot. The robot learns an "aggressive" gait for breaching tasks in a controlled environment. We believe that this approach can be applied to various legged robots and provide experimental validation of our method using our own four-legged walking robot. The video showcasing our robot's capabilities can be accessed at: https://youtu.be/9bMp8YXx1qM. A well-documented phenomenon, microtearing modes, occurs due to the electron temperature gradient in a plasma and causes fine-scale magnetic reconnections and the formation of magnetic islands. Prior research in a slab geometry setting showed that the drive mechanism requires collisions, but our simulations show that in the absence of collisions, there is still a small-scale, electron-driven tearing instability that exists. Detailed studies reveal that these modes are driven by electron temperature gradients but are influenced by electron finite radius effects and have properties that set them apart from larger-scale modes. Interestingly, these modes exist even in an electrostatic state and electromagnetic forces actually help stabilize them. Analytically, these modes match a previously studied type known as ETG modes and have been found to potentially be more unstable. They can contribute to the formation of magnetic islands, which have been linked to the enhancement of turbulent transport in magnetized plasmas. These findings could be important for understanding and addressing problems in magnetized plasmas, including those in tokamaks, by potentially controlling and suppressing the formation of magnetic islands. They also highlight the need to consider the interplay between ETG modes and other instability types, particularly ITG modes. By noting that these ETG modes require larger scales than typically associated with them and are influenced by collisionless processes, our results suggest that they could be more easily measured experimentally than previously thought. These findings also show that to mitigate the formation of magnetic islands, it may be effective to directly manipulate and manage the electron temperature gradient. However, an interesting observation from our research suggests that while altering the electron temperature could be effective, modifying the plasma's finite electron radius through additional injection, for example, may be more effective. Building upon this, the concept of fashion attribute manipulation, which modifies a specific attribute while retaining others, has emerged. This enables users to search not only identical items but also similar items with specific attributes. However, implementing fashion attribute manipulation in fashion databases poses a challenge due to the lack of accessible data and the high cost of manual annotation. To overcome these limitations, we utilize Amazon Mechanical Turk for crowdsourcing image data and develop a fashion image parsing system based on a conditional conditional generative adversarial network. This method allows for the accurate labeling of fashion items in images. Subsequently, we design a research framework for fashion attribute manipulation by combining parsed images with attribute information. Through this, we introduce a new concept of attribute manipulation for images, facilitating more precise search by image and retrieval tasks. To validate our approach, we introduce two datasets for parsing and manipulating fashion images, namely, FashionPara, and use our approach in fashion instance-level image retrieval tasks, including retrieval, novel view generation, and manipulating and searching by fashion attributes. The $\R$-optimal solution for the underdetermined equation $Ax=y$ where $A$ is a bounded linear operator mapping a Banach space to a Hilbert space, and $\R$ is a strongly convex function defined in that space, is considered in this research. Since the equation is underdetermined, a minimizer of $\R\circ ax$ in this context is, by Tukey's postulate, generally an ill-posed problem. Consequently, numerical approximations are also ill-posed; hence, regularization methods are applied. It is demonstrated that an $\R$-optimal solution exists and can be obtained using a Tikhonov regularized method, which is controlled by the regularization parameter. A scheme for selecting this parameter is developed, and it is proven that the proposed method results in converging sequences as the parameter value approaches zero. The research further examines Tikhonov regularization in a Banach algebra setting where the matrix $A$ is a finite-dimensional matrix, and it offers a convenient link with linear inverse problems that involve compact operators. An alternative, automatic method for selecting the regularization parameter is suggested, which involves the use of a scaled $L$-curve analysis. Finally, the research presents numerical examples to illustrate the practical applicability and efficiency of the developed theoretical findings. The research also provides a useful connection with existing approaches in inverse problems that involve penalty and augmented Lagrangian methods for underdetermined linear systems. Moreover, it is demonstrated that the developed theoretical findings generalize some of the penalty and augmented Lagrangian methods for underdetermined linear systems that result in strongly convex cost functions. Constructing the matching cost is a critical step in estimating light field depth but has received limited attention in the era of deep learning. The prevailing methods often rely on the Werlberger cost constructor, incorporating u-v warped previous and next frames to estimate occlusion. However, these modern deep learning-based approaches typically use simplified matching cost constructors, compromising both speed and effectiveness. To address this, our innovative cost constructor efficiently computes the depth disparity while minimizing occlusion, leveraging detailed feature maps. This is made possible by projecting features from each pixel onto its geometrically corresponding positions in the epipolar lines, and then calculating the maximum consistency across these positions. This constructor boasts superior speed and efficacy benefits over the Werlberger constructor and demonstrates substantial enhancements in estimation accuracy for both stereo and multi-view scenarios, and its remarkable ability to work in dense light field footage with zero additional parameters. Furthermore, our constructor can be easily integrated with existing deep learning-based depth estimation methods to achieve superior performance; for instance, it results in a substantial improvement of GE-NET to 0.8425 SSIM and 0.7557 MS-SSIM. This constructor is available at: \url{https://github.com/ashishji/Depth-from-light-field/tree/main/matching_constructor}. The project also hosts a vast collection of light field videos to support depth estimation research and evaluation. Additionally, our constructor's sources and data have been made available under a free license at the provided URL. Furthermore, our constructor has been successfully demonstrated on various light field datasets to estimate depth accurately and efficiently. To facilitate evaluation, our constructor can be easily integrated with other estimators by simply substituting the existing constructor to experience its superior performance. We are confident that our constructor will significantly benefit the light field depth estimation community and look forward to participating in future challenges to continuously enhance its performance. To validate this, our constructor has consistently outperformed the top submissions to the recent SAE challenge in the stereo and multi-view categories, and we are confident that it will continue to provide superior performance for other light field applications. This is made possible by our constructor's high speed which enables it to efficiently process the light field footage towards various computer vision tasks. To meet growing demands for next-generation home WiFi networks, it is essential to improve their performance capabilities. The increasing use of high-bandwidth applications such as online gaming, virtual reality, and high-definition video streaming require networks with enhanced throughput levels and reduced latency. One effective strategy for achieving these goals is to deploy multiple access points within a given area, but this also raises the challenge of identifying the most suitable access point for each device. 

This study explores the design of energy-efficient algorithms for solving joint downlink and uplink access point association problems in home WiFi networks that support multi-user, multi-band operation. We present two algorithms, namely MAXP and MEDP, that optimize energy consumption while ensuring throughput and latency meet specific quality of service requirements. We validate these algorithms by analyzing their impact on delay, throughput, and device energy consumption in home WiFi networks with mixed traffic loads. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of these algorithms in improving network performance by reducing average association times and boosting overall throughput levels. Furthermore, we show that the MAXP and MEDP algorithms can reduce energy consumption by up to 52% and 45% respectively, thereby enhancing their efficiency and competitiveness. We also find that these algorithms outperform other alternative approaches used for comparison, including the joint uplink-downlink association algorithm, and observe a direct relationship between the number of home WiFi devices present and the benefits derived from the algorithms for energy efficiency. Finally, we observe that the MAXP and MEDP algorithms offer competitive performance properties, but can incur substantial computational overhead during the uplink mode, particularly when the number of home WiFi devices is high. To address this issue, we also explore and evaluate the design of other alternative algorithms for access point association problems that support home WiFi networks with multiple access points and bandwidth aggregation capabilities. We present various trade-offs between algorithm design features such as complexity, device delay, and device energy consumption for each of the algorithms in question. Based on these findings, we also identify areas for further research and highlight important considerations that may affect the design of energy-efficient algorithms for home WiFi networks that support multiple access points and bandwidth aggregation. Overall, our analysis provides valuable insights into the design and development of energy-efficient algorithms that can improve the performance and efficiency of home WiFi networks in which a large number of home WiFi devices are present. We also explore and discuss the applicability and adaptability of these algorithms and their impact on the overall performance of the network in home WiFi environments.
